knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is monotone when every two graph points \((x,u)\) and \((y,v)\) satisfy \[\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\ge 0.\] Equivalently, the graph of \(A\) is a monotone subset of the product Hilbert space under the canonical dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is monotone when differences of inputs and corresponding outputs always have a nonnegative inner product.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Operators

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ordinary monotonicity of a set-valued mapping and locates cyclic monotonicity as a stronger condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(\rho:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) is monotone if, for every \((x_0,x_0^*),(x_1,x_1^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\rho\), \[\langle x_1-x_0,\,x_1^*-x_0^*\rangle\ge 0.\] Every cyclically monotone mapping is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is monotone when the inner product of the difference of any two input points and the difference of their corresponding values is nonnegative. Cyclic monotonicity implies ordinary monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho\text{ is monotone}\iff \forall (x_0,x_0^*),(x_1,x_1^*)\in\operatorname{gph}\rho,\ \langle x_1-x_0,x_1^*-x_0^*\rangle\ge0;\qquad \rho\text{ cyclically monotone}\implies\rho\text{ monotone}.

children.title: Strictly Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Strict monotonicity as a solution-separation regime.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is strictly monotone}\iff x\neq y\Longrightarrow\langle x-y,u-v\rangle>0\) for all graph points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictness concerns distinct input points, not distinct graph points.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is strictly monotone if, for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), \[x\neq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle x-y,u-v\rangle>0.\] This condition implies monotonicity because the pairing is positive for distinct inputs and equals zero when the inputs coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly monotone operator has a positive input-output difference pairing whenever the two inputs differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Monotone Operators

children.title: Paramonotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Paramonotonicity and its solution-identification consequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is paramonotone}\iff \langle x-y,u-v\rangle=0\Longrightarrow u\in Ay\text{ and }v\in Ax\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard set-valued Hilbert-space definition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A monotone operator \(A\) is paramonotone if, whenever \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) attain equality in the monotonicity inequality, the outputs may be exchanged: \[\langle x-y,u-v\rangle=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,v),(y,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A.\] Thus equality forces \(u\in Ay\) and \(v\in Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A paramonotone operator permits outputs to be exchanged between two graph points whenever their monotonicity pairing vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Paramonotone Operators

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Class Inclusions, Separations, Counterexamples
children.top_down_role: Logical relations and failure boundaries among the three classes.

assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R^2\) with its Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{strictly monotone}\}\subsetneq\{\text{paramonotone}\}\subsetneq\{\text{monotone}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional separations among baseline classes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every strictly monotone operator is paramonotone, and every paramonotone operator is monotone. Both inclusions are strict. The zero operator \(Z\) is paramonotone but not strictly monotone. The skew rotation \(S\) is monotone because \(\langle z,Sz\rangle=0\) for every \(z\), but it is not paramonotone: equality holds for all pairs while \(Sx=Sy\) need not hold. The identity \(I\) is strictly monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict monotonicity implies paramonotonicity, which implies monotonicity; the zero operator and a planar rotation show both inclusions are strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Class Inclusions, Separations, Counterexamples

children.title: Uniformly Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Uniform monotonicity moduli and their qualitative consequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is uniformly monotone with modulus }\phi\iff \langle x-y,u-v\rangle\ge\phi(\|x-y\|)\) for all graph points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform monotonicity expressed through a positive distance modulus.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is uniformly monotone with modulus \(\phi\) if every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) satisfies \[\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\ge \phi(\|x-y\|),\] where \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(\phi(t)>0\) whenever \(t>0\). The modulus supplies a positive separation depending only on the distance between inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform monotonicity lower-bounds the monotonicity pairing by a positive function of the distance between inputs.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Monotone Operators

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definitions of uniform monotonicity vary on whether the modulus must also be increasing or satisfy further regularity. A source specifically stating the adopted modulus convention is required.

children.title: Strongly Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Strong monotonicity parameters, uniqueness, and conditioning.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is }\mu\text{-strongly monotone}\iff \langle x-y,u-v\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|^2\) for all graph points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-modulus Hilbert-space definition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone if, for every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), \[\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\ge \mu\|x-y\|^2.\] Strong monotonicity is uniform monotonicity with the quadratic modulus \(\phi(t)=\mu t^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity lower-bounds the input-output difference pairing by a positive constant times squared input distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Monotone Operators

children.title: Quantitative Class Relations
children.top_down_role: Implications, separations, and parameter-sensitive relationships between the classes.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) acts on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu\text{-strong}\Longrightarrow\text{uniform with }\phi(t)=\mu t^2\Longrightarrow\text{strict}\Longrightarrow\text{paramonotone}\Longrightarrow\text{monotone}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implication chain for Hilbert-space monotonicity classes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, then it is uniformly monotone with modulus \(\phi(t)=\mu t^2\). Any uniformly monotone operator whose modulus is positive away from zero is strictly monotone. Strict monotonicity implies paramonotonicity, and paramonotonicity includes monotonicity by definition. Hence \[\mu\text{-strong}\Longrightarrow\text{uniform}\Longrightarrow\text{strict}\Longrightarrow\text{paramonotone}\Longrightarrow\text{monotone}.\] Reverse implications fail without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity implies uniform, strict, paramonotone, and ordinary monotonicity in sequence; the reverse implications generally fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Quantitative Class Relations

children.title: Geometric-Convergence Regime
children.top_down_role: Convergence consequences associated with quantitative monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_n-x_\star\|\le q^n\|x_0-x_\star\|\), where \(q=\sqrt{1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2}<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear convergence of the constant-step forward iteration.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_\star\) be the unique zero of \(A\), and generate \(x_{n+1}=x_n-\gamma Ax_n\). Then \[\|x_{n+1}-x_\star\|\le q\|x_n-x_\star\|,\qquad q:=\sqrt{1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2}<1.\] Consequently, \(\|x_n-x_\star\|\le q^n\|x_0-x_\star\|\), so the forward iteration converges geometrically to \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strongly monotone Lipschitz operator, a sufficiently small forward step is a contraction and converges geometrically to the unique zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Convergence Regime

children.title: Cocoercive Operators
children.top_down_role: Cocoercivity as a forward-evaluable regularity class.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is }\beta\text{-cocoercive}\iff \langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\ge\beta\|Bx-By\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued Hilbert-space definition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive if, for every \(x,y\in H\), \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\ge \beta\|Bx-By\|^2.\] This inequality implies monotonicity and, by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cocoercive mapping controls squared output differences by the inner product of input and output differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Operators

children.title: Inverse-Strongly Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Inverse-strong monotonicity within quantitative operator classifications.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is }\beta\text{-inverse-strongly monotone}\iff \langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\ge\beta\|Bx-By\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space convention for inverse-strong monotonicity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(B\) is \(\beta\)-inverse-strongly monotone if, for all \(x,y\in H\), \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\ge \beta\|Bx-By\|^2.\] The adjective “inverse-strongly” reflects that, on the range of \(B\), this is the strong-monotonicity inequality for the inverse relation \(B^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-strong monotonicity is the inequality that strongly controls output differences through their pairing with input differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Strongly Monotone Operators

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Hilbert-Space Terminology Equivalence
children.top_down_role: The geometry-dependent correspondence between the two class labels.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is }\beta\text{-cocoercive}\iff B\text{ is }\beta\text{-inverse-strongly monotone}.\)

notation.meaning: Common cocoercivity or inverse-strong monotonicity constant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of two names for one Hilbert-space inequality.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a single-valued mapping on a Hilbert space, “\(\beta\)-cocoercive” and “\(\beta\)-inverse-strongly monotone” denote the same condition: \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\ge \beta\|Bx-By\|^2\qquad(\forall x,y\in H).\] Thus the terminology changes neither the constant \(\beta\) nor the defining inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Hilbert spaces, beta-cocoercive and beta-inverse-strongly monotone are equivalent names for exactly the same inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space Terminology Equivalence

children.title: Averaged-Mapping Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections to averaged mappings and admissible forward evaluations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I-\gamma B\text{ is }\alpha\text{-averaged with }\alpha=\gamma/(2\beta)\in(0,1).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward steps generated by cocoercive mappings.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(T=I-\gamma B\) and \(\alpha=\gamma/(2\beta)\). Then \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and there exists a nonexpansive mapping \(R:H\to H\) such that \[T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R.\] Hence every forward step with \(0<\gamma<2\beta\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged. Equivalently, the averagedness inequality follows from the \(\beta\)-cocoercivity of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward step using a beta-cocoercive mapping is averaged whenever its step size lies strictly between zero and two beta.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaged-Mapping Interface

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Lipschitz Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Monotone operators controlled by Lipschitz regularity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) belongs to the class of monotone Lipschitz operators.

notation.meaning: inner product and induced norm on the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued, globally Lipschitz monotone operators on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(B\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, for some \(L\in[0,\infty)\), when every \(x,y\in H\) satisfies
\[
\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq 0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\|Bx-By\|\leq L\|x-y\|.
\]
The least admissible \(L\), when finite, is the Lipschitz modulus of \(B\). Monotonicity alone does not imply any finite Lipschitz modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is Lipschitz monotone when its increments have nonnegative pairing with input increments and are uniformly bounded in norm by a constant times those increments.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise, properly scoped to single-valued operators on a real Hilbert space, and uses an appropriate content kind. No source reference or inspectable locator is supplied, so the record cannot yet enter candidate review.

children.title: Skew Operators
children.top_down_role: Skew operator structure in monotone inclusion models.

assumptions_latex: \(S:H\to H\) is a bounded linear operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is skew precisely when \(S^*=-S\), equivalently \(\langle Sx,x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in H\).

notation.meaning: Hilbert-space adjoint of the linear operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linear skew operators on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(S\) is skew when
\[
S^*=-S.
\]
Equivalently, \(\langle Sx,y\rangle=-\langle x,Sy\rangle\) for all \(x,y\in H\), or \(\langle Sx,x\rangle=0\) for all \(x\in H\). Consequently,
\[
\langle Sx-Sy,x-y\rangle=0
\]
for every \(x,y\in H\), so both \(S\) and \(-S\) are monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded linear operator is skew when its adjoint is its negative. Its quadratic form vanishes, making both the operator and its negative monotone.
knowledge_statements.title: Skew Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalent characterizations and monotonicity consequence are correct for bounded linear operators on a real Hilbert space, and definition is suitable for this leaf. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Symmetric–Skew Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Structural decompositions separating monotone and skew contributions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=A+S\) uniquely, with \(A^*=A\) and \(S^*=-S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical decomposition of a bounded linear operator into symmetric and skew parts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
A=\frac{L+L^*}{2},\qquad S=\frac{L-L^*}{2}.
\]
Then \(A^*=A\), \(S^*=-S\), and \(L=A+S\). This decomposition is unique among representations of \(L\) as the sum of a bounded self-adjoint operator and a bounded skew operator. Moreover, \(L\) is monotone if and only if \(A\) is positive semidefinite, meaning \(\langle Ax,x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bounded linear operator uniquely splits into self-adjoint and skew parts; its monotonicity is determined entirely by the positive semidefiniteness of the self-adjoint part.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric–Skew Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The canonical symmetric-skew representation, uniqueness claim, and monotonicity characterization are correct in the stated real Hilbert-space setting. The representation content kind fits the leaf, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Forward-Correction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Why plain forward evaluation may be insufficient for these classes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\gamma\neq0\), the forward map \(I-\gamma S\) is expansive and hence nonexpansiveness cannot follow from monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity alone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp obstruction to using an uncorrected forward step for general monotone Lipschitz operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The rotation \(S\) is linear, skew, monotone, and \(1\)-Lipschitz. Nevertheless, for every \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\) and every \(x,y\in H\),
\[
\|(I-\gamma S)x-(I-\gamma S)y\|^2=(1+\gamma^2)\|x-y\|^2.
\]
Thus \(I-\gamma S\) has Lipschitz constant \(\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}>1\). A nonzero admissible forward step therefore requires structure stronger than monotonicity plus Lipschitz continuity, or an additional correction step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar skew rotation is monotone and Lipschitz, yet every nonzero explicit forward step is expansive. General forward splitting therefore needs stronger structure or correction.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Correction Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The planar rotation calculation correctly establishes the failure of nonexpansiveness for every nonzero forward step, and failure_boundary is the appropriate role for this leaf. The claim needs an authoritative source and specific locator.

children.title: Contractive Mappings
children.top_down_role: Strict metric contraction regimes and their uniqueness consequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is contractive with contraction factor \(q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global metric contractions, also called Banach contractions.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(T\) is contractive when there exists \(q\in[0,1)\) such that
\[
d(Tx,Ty)\leq qd(x,y)
\]
for all \(x,y\in X\). Any such \(q\) is a contraction factor. If \(X\) is complete and nonempty, the Banach contraction theorem additionally yields a unique fixed point and convergence of every Picard iteration to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contractive mapping reduces every pairwise distance by a uniform factor strictly below one. On a nonempty complete space it has one fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Mappings

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Nonexpansive Mappings
children.top_down_role: The boundary metric class without strict contraction.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global nonexpansiveness in a metric space.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(T\) is nonexpansive when
\[
d(Tx,Ty)\leq d(x,y)
\]
for every \(x,y\in X\). Equivalently, its global Lipschitz modulus is at most \(1\). Every contractive mapping is nonexpansive, but the converse fails because the defining inequality permits equality and supplies no uniform factor strictly below \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive mapping never increases pairwise distances. Unlike a contraction, it may preserve distances and need not have a unique fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexpansive Mappings

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Contraction-Factor Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior across strict, limiting, and degenerate contraction factors.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The values \(q=0\), \(0<q<1\), \(q=1\), and \(q>1\) delimit constant, contractive, nonexpansive-boundary, and potentially expansive regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by an admissible global Lipschitz factor, not necessarily the least one.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(q=0\), then \(T\) is constant. If \(0<q<1\), then \(T\) is contractive. If \(q=1\), the bound certifies only nonexpansiveness. If \(q>1\), the bound alone permits expansion and certifies neither nonexpansiveness nor contraction. Because a Lipschitz factor need not be minimal, classification by \(q\) is strongest when \(q\) denotes the exact Lipschitz modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factors below one certify contraction, one marks the nonexpansive boundary, and factors above one allow expansion. A zero factor characterizes constant mappings.
knowledge_statements.title: Contraction-Factor Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Uniqueness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of automatic uniqueness at the nonexpansive endpoint.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a nonempty complete metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A contraction has exactly one fixed point, whereas a nonexpansive mapping may have none, one, or many.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The strict factor-one boundary for fixed-point existence and uniqueness.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T:X\to X\) has a contraction factor \(q<1\), then \(\operatorname{Fix}T\) contains exactly one point. This conclusion fails at the nonexpansive boundary \(q=1\): the identity mapping on any non-singleton complete metric space is nonexpansive and fixes every point, while the translation \(T(x)=x+1\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is an isometry with \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict contraction guarantees one fixed point on a complete space. At factor one, the identity has many fixed points and a real translation has none.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.5 Contractive mappings p. 143
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Firmly Nonexpansive Mappings
children.top_down_role: The metric class associated with resolvents and projections.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space metric characterization used by resolvents and projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive when every \(x,y\in H\) satisfies
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|^2\leq\langle Tx-Ty,x-y\rangle.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|^2+\|(I-T)x-(I-T)y\|^2\leq\|x-y\|^2,
\]
or the reflected mapping \(2T-I\) is nonexpansive. Every firmly nonexpansive mapping is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is firmly nonexpansive when the squared norm of each output increment is bounded by its pairing with the corresponding input increment.
knowledge_statements.title: Firmly Nonexpansive Mappings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three firm-nonexpansiveness characterizations are equivalent in a real Hilbert space, and the definition fits the leaf and its resolvent/projection role. No source reference or locator is provided.

children.title: Conical Averagedness Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Classes supporting compositions and relaxation analysis.

children.title: Averaged Mappings
children.top_down_role: Standard averaged mappings and their fixed-point geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is averaged precisely when it admits a representation \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\) with \(0<\alpha<1\) and nonexpansive \(R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical averaged mappings with parameter strictly between zero and one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the mapping \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged when there exists a nonexpansive mapping \(R:H\to H\) such that
\[
T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R.
\]
A mapping is averaged when it is \(\alpha\)-averaged for at least one \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). In particular, a firmly nonexpansive mapping is \(1/2\)-averaged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged mapping is a strict convex combination of the identity and a nonexpansive mapping. Firm nonexpansiveness corresponds to averaging parameter one half.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Mappings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of alpha-averagedness and the one-half-averaged characterization of firmly nonexpansive mappings are correct in the stated Hilbert-space setting. A specific authoritative citation is required.

children.title: Conically Averaged Mappings
children.top_down_role: Extended averagedness beyond the ordinary parameter range.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is conically averaged precisely when \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\) for some \(\alpha>0\) and nonexpansive \(R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conical extension of averagedness allowing every positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha>0\), the mapping \(T\) is conically \(\alpha\)-averaged when there exists a nonexpansive mapping \(R:H\to H\) such that
\[
T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R.
\]
Equivalently, \((1-1/\alpha)I+(1/\alpha)T\) is nonexpansive. Classical \(\alpha\)-averagedness is recovered when \(0<\alpha<1\); conical averagedness also permits \(\alpha\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conically averaged mapping has the usual identity–nonexpansive representation but allows every positive coefficient, including parameters at or above one.
knowledge_statements.title: Conically Averaged Mappings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conical averagedness definition, equivalent rescaling, and parameter range are mathematically consistent, and definition is the correct content kind. No supporting source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Averaging-Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Ordinary, boundary, and conical parameter ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\), where \(R:H\to H\) is nonexpansive and \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intervals \(0<\alpha<1\), \(\alpha=1\), and \(\alpha>1\) correspond respectively to averaged, nonexpansive-component, and overrelaxed conical regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter boundaries for the identity–nonexpansive representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(0<\alpha<1\), the representation is a convex combination and \(T\) is classically averaged, hence nonexpansive. When \(\alpha=1\), one has \(T=R\), so the class is exactly nonexpansive mappings. When \(\alpha>1\), the representation is overrelaxed and certifies only conical averagedness: nonexpansiveness can fail, as shown by \(R=-I\), for which \(T=(1-2\alpha)I\) has Lipschitz modulus \(2\alpha-1>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameters below one give classical averagedness, one gives nonexpansiveness, and parameters above one describe overrelaxation that may be expansive.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaging-Parameter Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three parameter regimes are correctly distinguished, and the example with R=-I correctly shows that the overrelaxed regime may be expansive. Property fits the parameter-regime leaf, but the record lacks a source and specific locator.

children.title: Composition–Relaxation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Closure behavior under compositions and relaxation transformations.

assumptions_latex: \(T_i=(1-\alpha_i)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha_iR_i\), where \(R_i:H\to H\) is nonexpansive and \(0<\alpha_i<1\), for \(i=1,2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_1T_2\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged, and the relaxation \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)\operatorname{Id}+\lambda T_1T_2\) is conically \(\lambda\alpha\)-averaged.

notation.meaning: Identity mapping on the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-factor averaged composition followed by positive relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \[\alpha=\frac{\alpha_1+\alpha_2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2}{1-\alpha_1\alpha_2}.\] Then \(0<\alpha<1\), and there exists a nonexpansive mapping \(R:H\to H\) such that \[T_1T_2=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R.\] Consequently, for every \(\lambda>0\), \[T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)\operatorname{Id}+\lambda T_1T_2=(1-\lambda\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\alpha R,\] so \(T_\lambda\) is conically \(\lambda\alpha\)-averaged. It is ordinarily averaged whenever \(0<\lambda\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composition of two averaged maps is averaged with the displayed parameter; relaxing that composition multiplies its conical averaging parameter by the relaxation factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition–Relaxation Calculus

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the composition–relaxation leaf and the formulas are internally coherent, but no citation supports the composition parameter or conical-relaxation claim.

children.title: Quasi-Nonexpansiveness Strength Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point-relative classes used in Fejér analysis.

children.title: Quasi-Nonexpansive Mappings
children.top_down_role: Distance control relative to fixed-point sets.

assumptions_latex: \(T:H\to H\) has a nonempty fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive exactly when every fixed point is at least as close to \(Tx\) as to \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space definition with a nonempty fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive if \[\|Tx-z\|\leq \|x-z\|\qquad\text{for every }x\in H\text{ and }z\in\operatorname{Fix}T.\] Equivalently, each application of \(T\) does not increase the distance from the current point to any fixed point. No inequality between \(Tx\) and \(Ty\) is required when neither \(x\) nor \(y\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is quasi-nonexpansive when it never increases the distance to any of its fixed points.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Nonexpansive Mappings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Strongly Quasi-Nonexpansive Mappings
children.top_down_role: Strengthened fixed-point-relative decrease properties.

assumptions_latex: \(T:H\to H\) has a nonempty fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is \(\rho\)-strongly quasi-nonexpansive when the fixed-point distance decreases by at least \(\rho\|Tx-x\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The residual-decrease convention for strong quasi-nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(T\) is \(\rho\)-strongly quasi-nonexpansive if \[\|Tx-z\|^2\leq \|x-z\|^2-\rho\|Tx-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in H\text{ and }z\in\operatorname{Fix}T.\] It is strongly quasi-nonexpansive if such a constant \(\rho>0\) exists. Dropping the nonnegative residual term yields quasi-nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong quasi-nonexpansiveness requires a quantified decrease in squared distance to every fixed point, proportional to the squared fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Quasi-Nonexpansive Mappings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-decrease definition fits the leaf, but strong quasi-nonexpansiveness conventions vary and the stated parameterization has no cited source.

children.title: Fejér-Monotonicity Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of these mapping classes in Fejér-type convergence analysis.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct fixed-point iteration and Fejér monotonicity toward fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z\in C\) and every \(n\geq0\), quasi-nonexpansiveness gives \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|=\|Tx_n-z\|\leq\|x_n-z\|.\] Hence \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\). If \(T\) is \(\rho\)-strongly quasi-nonexpansive, then the stronger descent estimate \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|^2\leq\|x_n-z\|^2-\rho\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|^2\] holds for every \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration of a quasi-nonexpansive map is Fejér monotone toward any subset of its fixed points; strong quasi-nonexpansiveness also controls successive displacements.
knowledge_statements.title: Fejér-Monotonicity Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Fejér-monotonicity property fits the interface leaf and is mathematically standard, but it lacks a citation; the displayed derivation should also be recast as a direct statement rather than proof text.

children.title: Fixed-Point-Set Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limitations arising from empty or poorly behaved fixed-point sets.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nonempty real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-point inequality alone carries no information when \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonemptiness boundary in the definition of quasi-nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\), the quantified inequality \[\|Tx-z\|\leq\|x-z\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in H\text{ and }z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\] is vacuously true. For example, any nonzero translation \(Tx=x+a\), where \(a\in H\setminus\{0\}\), has no fixed point and satisfies this vacuous predicate despite increasing some pairwise distances neither more nor less than an isometry. Therefore the standard quasi-nonexpansive class explicitly requires \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a fixed point, the defining quasi-nonexpansive inequality is vacuous; a nonzero translation exhibits this boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point-Set Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and vacuity example fit the leaf, but the convention requiring a nonempty fixed-point set needs an inspectable citation.

children.title: Integrable Monotonicity Representation Theory
children.top_down_role: Integrability-oriented monotonicity classes and their representation boundary.

children.title: Cyclic Monotonicity Maximality Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Cyclic classes associated with convex potentials.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximal cyclic monotonicity and convex subdifferential representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization and uniqueness result, supported by extraction-grounded evidence without verified full-text span alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set-valued mapping \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\), there exists a closed proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \(T=\partial f\) if and only if \(T\) is maximally cyclically monotone. Moreover, if \(f\) and \(g\) are closed proper convex functions and \(\partial f=\partial g\), then \(f=g+c\) for some \(c\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping on finite-dimensional Euclidean space is the subdifferential of a closed proper convex function exactly when it is maximally cyclically monotone. A closed proper convex function represented by a given subdifferential mapping is unique up to an additive constant.
assumptions_latex: f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are closed, proper, and convex whenever invoked}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists f\text{ closed, proper, and convex}:T=\partial f\bigr)\iff T\text{ is maximally cyclically monotone},\qquad \partial f=\partial g\implies\exists c\in\mathbb{R}:f=g+c.

source_evidence.locator: Complete book / 24. Differential Continuity and Monotonicity / Theorem 24.9

children.title: Cyclic Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Finite-cycle compatibility within the monotonicity hierarchy.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cyclic monotonicity requires a nonnegative pairing sum around every finite cycle in \(\operatorname{gra}A\).

notation.meaning: Duality pairing between the Banach space and its dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space graph definition using finite cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is cyclically monotone if, for every integer \(n\geq2\) and every family \((x_i,x_i^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,n\), with \(x_{n+1}=x_1\), one has \[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle x_i-x_{i+1},x_i^*\rangle\geq0.\] Taking \(n=2\) recovers ordinary monotonicity, so every cyclically monotone operator is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is cyclically monotone when its duality-pairing sum is nonnegative around every finite cycle of graph points.
knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-cycle definition is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but no source supports the Banach-space formulation or sign convention.

children.title: Maximally Cyclic Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Graph completeness relative to cyclic monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximal cyclic monotonicity means that no strictly larger graph in \(X\times X^*\) remains cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximality is taken within the class of cyclically monotone graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone if, whenever a cyclically monotone operator \(B:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) satisfies \[\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}B,\] one necessarily has \(\operatorname{gra}A=\operatorname{gra}B\). Thus maximality concerns graph inclusion among cyclically monotone operators, rather than maximality among all monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cyclically monotone operator is maximal when its graph has no proper cyclically monotone extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximally Cyclic Monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximality definition correctly concerns inclusion among cyclically monotone graphs and fits the leaf, but it has no citation.

children.title: Convex-Potential Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between cyclic classes and convex-potential representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is cyclically monotone iff its graph lies in a convex subdifferential; it is maximally cyclically monotone iff it equals one.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar’s subdifferential representation in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is cyclically monotone if and only if there exists \(f\in\Gamma_0(X)\) such that \[\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f.\] Moreover, \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone if and only if there exists \(f\in\Gamma_0(X)\) such that \[A=\partial f.\] The potential is determined only up to an additive constant when its subdifferential is prescribed on the relevant connected domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cyclically monotone graphs are contained in convex subdifferentials, while maximal cyclically monotone graphs are exactly convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Potential Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the convex-potential interface, but the Banach-space theorem and the qualified additive-constant assertion require a precise authoritative source and hypotheses.

children.title: Cyclic Maximality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between ordinary maximal monotonicity and maximal cyclic monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J\) is maximally monotone but not cyclically monotone, so monotone maximality does not imply cyclic maximality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separation of maximal monotonicity from cyclic monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^2\), \[\langle x-y,Jx-Jy\rangle=0,\] and the everywhere-defined continuous linear monotone operator \(J\) is maximally monotone. Nevertheless, take \(x_1=(1,0)\), \(x_2=(0,1)\), and \(x_3=(0,0)\). Then \[\sum_{i=1}^{3}\langle x_i-x_{i+1},Jx_i\rangle=-1<0,\qquad x_4=x_1.\] Hence \(J\) is not cyclically monotone and cannot be a convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar quarter-turn is maximally monotone but violates a three-point cyclic inequality, separating monotone maximality from cyclic maximality.
knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Maximality Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quarter-turn counterexample is coherent and the counterexample kind fits the boundary leaf, but maximal monotonicity and the cyclic failure are uncited.

children.title: Rockafellar Cyclic-Monotonicity Principle
children.top_down_role: The representation bridge between cyclic graphs and convex potentials.

children.title: Convex-Potential Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: The reconstruction side of cyclic representation.

assumptions_latex: \(A:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is cyclically monotone with nonempty graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed supremum defines a convex potential \(f\) satisfying \(f(x_0)=0\) and \(\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar antiderivative normalized at one graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), define \[f(x)=\sup\left\{\langle x-x_n,x_n^*\rangle+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,x_i^*\rangle:\ n\geq0,\ (x_i,x_i^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\right\},\] where the term with \(n=0\) is \(\langle x-x_0,x_0^*\rangle\). Then \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, \(f(x_0)=0\), and \[\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f.\] If \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone, this inclusion is equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supremum of affine path sums reconstructs a normalized convex potential whose subdifferential contains the given cyclically monotone graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Potential Reconstruction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the reconstruction leaf, but the exact supremum formula, normalization, and Banach-space conclusions require a theorem-level citation.

children.title: Nonintegrable Monotone-Operator Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary between subdifferential-representable and general monotone graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A general maximally monotone operator need not admit any convex-subdifferential representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cyclic monotonicity is the integrability condition missing from general monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(J\) is maximally monotone, but it is not cyclically monotone. If a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\) satisfied \(\operatorname{gra}J\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f\), then \(J\) would be cyclically monotone because every convex subdifferential is cyclically monotone. This contradiction shows that no such potential exists. Thus maximal monotonicity alone does not provide convex-potential integrability; cyclic monotonicity is the additional necessary structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximal monotonicity does not ensure convex-potential representation; the planar quarter-turn is a concrete nonintegrable example.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegrable Monotone-Operator Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and quarter-turn example fit the leaf, but the maximal-monotonicity and nonrepresentability claims lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Rectangular Three-Star Terminology Pair
children.top_down_role: Range-sensitive subclasses used in sum theory.

children.title: Rectangular Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: The rectangular monotonicity class and its domain–range geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is rectangular precisely when its Fitzpatrick function is finite on \(\operatorname{dom}A\times\operatorname{ran}A\).

notation.meaning: Effective domain of an extended-real function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangularity stated through the Fitzpatrick-domain criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[F_A(x,x^*)=\sup_{(a,a^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A}\bigl(\langle x,a^*\rangle+\langle a,x^*\rangle-\langle a,a^*\rangle\bigr).\] The operator \(A\) is rectangular if \[\operatorname{dom}A\times\operatorname{ran}A\subseteq\operatorname{dom}F_A.\] Equivalently, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}A\) and \(x^*\in\operatorname{ran}A\), \[\sup_{(a,a^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A}\langle x-a,a^*-x^*\rangle<+\infty.\] This property is also commonly called three-star monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator is rectangular when its Fitzpatrick function is finite at every domain–range pair; equivalently, the displayed graph supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the rectangular-operator leaf and the two finiteness formulations are algebraically consistent, but the Fitzpatrick-domain criterion and three-star terminology equivalence require a precise citation.

children.title: Three-Star Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: The three-star formulation used across the literature.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
\(A:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone and has nonempty graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is three-star monotone exactly when the displayed supremum is finite for every point of \(\operatorname{dom}A\times\operatorname{ran}A\).

notation.meaning: graph of the set-valued operator A
duality pairing between X and its dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard Banach-space graph formulation of three-star monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(A\) is three-star monotone if, for every \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{dom}A\times\operatorname{ran}A\),
\[
\sup_{(a,a^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A}\langle x-a,a^*-x^*\rangle<+\infty.
\]
Equivalently, for every such \((x,x^*)\),
\[
\inf_{(a,a^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A}\langle x-a,x^*-a^*\rangle>-\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator is three-star monotone when its graph has uniformly finite cross-pairing against every domain-range pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Star Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed graph-boundedness condition is the standard form associated with three-star monotonicity, but no citation is supplied for the terminology or exact formulation. The plain statement's phrase "uniformly finite" may incorrectly suggest one bound uniform over all domain-range pairs; the displayed condition only requires pointwise finiteness.

children.title: Terminology Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence and convention differences between the two labels.

assumptions_latex: \(A:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone with nonempty graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For monotone operators, “rectangular” and “three-star monotone” name the same property.

notation.meaning: effective domain of an extended-real-valued function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies two standard names for one graph-boundedness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following conditions are equivalent:
\[
\operatorname{dom}A\times\operatorname{ran}A\subseteq\operatorname{dom}F_A,
\]
and, for every \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{dom}A\times\operatorname{ran}A\),
\[
\sup_{(a,a^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A}\langle x-a,a^*-x^*\rangle<+\infty.
\]
The first condition is called rectangular monotonicity, while the second is called three-star monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rectangular monotonicity and three-star monotonicity are equivalent terminology for the same finite cross-pairing condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminology Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Fitzpatrick-domain condition and finite cross-pairing condition are mathematically consistent, and the property kind fits the terminology leaf. However, the asserted correspondence between "rectangular" and "three-star monotone" has no cited source.

children.title: Sum-Theory Range Consequences
children.top_down_role: Range-sensitive consequences relevant to operator sums.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone and \(A+B\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The range of \(A+B\) is nearly equal to the Minkowski sum of the individual ranges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Brezis–Haraux-type range conclusion in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated hypotheses,
\[
\overline{\operatorname{ran}(A+B)}
=
\overline{\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B}
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{int}\operatorname{ran}(A+B)
=
\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B).
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{ran}(A+B)\) and \(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B\) have the same closure and interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under maximality, compatibility, and rectangularity, the sum operator’s range has the same closure and interior as the sum of the ranges.
knowledge_statements.title: Sum-Theory Range Consequences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \((x_k,x_k^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) and the sequence \((x_k,x_k^*)\) is bounded in \(X\times X\), then there are indices \(k_j\) and a pair \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) such that
\[
x_{k_j}\to x,
\qquad
x_{k_j}^*\to x^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, every bounded graph sequence has a strongly convergent subsequence whose limit remains in a closed graph.

children.title: Hilbert-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: The principal setting for metric resolvents and averaged operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resolvent is everywhere defined and firmly nonexpansive; its complement is also firmly nonexpansive.

notation.meaning: resolvent of A with parameter lambda

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty resolvent formulation in the Hilbert-space metric geometry.

source_refs.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(J_{\lambda A}:H\to H\) is single-valued and has full domain. For all \(x,y\in H\),
\[
\lVert J_{\lambda A}x-J_{\lambda A}y\rVert^2
\leq
\langle J_{\lambda A}x-J_{\lambda A}y,x-y\rangle.
\]
Consequently, both \(J_{\lambda A}\) and \(I-J_{\lambda A}\) are firmly nonexpansive, hence averaged and nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal monotone operator on a Hilbert space has an everywhere-defined, firmly nonexpansive resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space Regime

children.title: Reflexive Banach-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Dual-space and coercivity-based theory.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The duality-regularized operator \(A+\lambda J\) is surjective onto \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflexive Banach analogue of Hilbert resolvent surjectivity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{ran}(A+\lambda J)=X^*.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(x^*\in X^*\), there exist \(x\in X\), \(a^*\in Ax\), and \(j^*\in Jx\) such that
\[
x^*=a^*+\lambda j^*.
\]
Reflexivity supplies the weak compactness used by the coercive duality regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a reflexive Banach space, adding a positive multiple of the normalized duality mapping makes a maximal monotone operator surjective.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflexive Banach-Space Regime

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3

children.title: Nonreflexive Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compactness and duality limitations in nonreflexive spaces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reflexive-space compactness and surjectivity arguments cannot be transferred without additional hypotheses or bidual formulations.

notation.meaning: canonical embedding of X into its bidual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates nonreflexive weak-compactness failure from Hilbertian metric failure.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Versions of Extremal Principle in Banach Spaces p. 230
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonreflexivity means that \(\iota_X(X)\neq X^{**}\). Equivalently, the closed unit ball of \(X\) is not weakly compact. Hence a bounded sequence or net arising from a coercive monotone inclusion need not possess a weakly convergent subnet with limit in \(X\); a weak-star cluster point may exist only in \(X^{**}\). Therefore reflexivity-dependent existence and range arguments require extra compactness assumptions or an explicit bidual extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without reflexivity, bounded approximations may converge only in the bidual, so standard weak-compactness existence and surjectivity arguments can fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonreflexive Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Versions of Extremal Principle in Banach Spaces p. 230

children.title: Non-Hilbertian Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of inner-product geometry in general Banach spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space not identified isometrically with a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hilbert resolvent identities do not transfer verbatim to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks the loss of inner-product resolvent geometry.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In general, \(X\) and \(X^*\) are distinct spaces and the normalized duality mapping \(J:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) need not equal \(I\), be single-valued, or be linear. Consequently, the Hilbert-space expression \((I+\lambda A)^{-1}:X\to X\), its firm-nonexpansiveness inequality, and the identity \(I-J_{\lambda A}\) are not intrinsic Banach-space constructions without added smoothness, convexity, and duality-map hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside Hilbert spaces, primal and dual spaces differ and the duality map may be nonlinear or multivalued, invalidating metric resolvent formulas.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Hilbertian Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3

children.title: Duality-Mapping Substitutes
children.top_down_role: Geometric replacements used outside Hilbert spaces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized resolvent replaces the Hilbert resolvent whenever the inverse is well defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the normalized duality mapping as the Banach-space metric substitute.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\lambda>0\), the duality-map resolvent is represented by
\[
R_{\lambda A}=(J+\lambda A)^{-1}J.
\]
Thus \(z=R_{\lambda A}x\) precisely when there exist \(j_x^*\in Jx\), \(j_z^*\in Jz\), and \(a^*\in Az\) satisfying
\[
j_x^*=j_z^*+\lambda a^*.
\]
If \(X\) is Hilbert and identified with its dual, then \(J=I\) and \(R_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing the identity by the normalized duality mapping yields a Banach-space generalized resolvent that reduces to the Hilbert resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Mapping Substitutes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112

children.title: Combined Geometric Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Settings where nonreflexivity compounds non-Hilbertian limitations.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonreflexive, non-Hilbertian Banach space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither Hilbert metric-resolvent theory nor reflexive compactness arguments apply automatically.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Versions of Extremal Principle in Banach Spaces p. 230
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two independent obstructions coexist: \(J\) may be nonlinear or multivalued, so \((I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) lacks the Hilbert firm-nonexpansive interpretation; and \(\iota_X(X)\neq X^{**}\), so bounded approximation nets may have weak-star cluster points outside \(X\). Accordingly, a Banach-space resolvent or existence theorem must separately impose geometry ensuring suitable behavior of \(J\) and compactness or representability ensuring that limiting points belong to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonreflexive non-Hilbert space, both metric resolvent identities and weak-compactness limit arguments may fail, requiring separate geometric and compactness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Combined Geometric Obstructions

children.title: Maximal Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Graph completeness, extensions, localization, and domain-range geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximal monotonicity induced by a saddle subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A saddle-function construction of a maximal monotone operator, including its smooth, everywhere-finite specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed proper concave-convex function on \(\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \(\rho(u,v)=\{(-u^*,v^*):(u^*,v^*)\in\partial K(u,v)\}\). Then \(\rho\) is a maximal monotone mapping from \(\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\) to itself. In particular, if \(K\) is everywhere finite and differentiable, then \((u,v)\mapsto(-\nabla_1K(u,v),\nabla_2K(u,v))\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing the sign of the first dual component of the saddle subdifferential produces a maximal monotone mapping. If the saddle function is everywhere finite and differentiable, its correspondingly signed partial-gradient map is maximal monotone.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a closed proper concave-convex function on }\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho\text{ is maximal monotone};\qquad K\text{ everywhere finite and differentiable}\implies (u,v)\mapsto(-\nabla_1K(u,v),\nabla_2K(u,v))\text{ is maximal monotone}

children.title: Monotone Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions that preserve monotonicity without requiring maximality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is a monotone extension of \(A\) exactly under graph inclusion and monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic definition of a monotone extension.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(B\) is a monotone extension of \(A\) if \(B\) is monotone and
\[
\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}B.
\]
Equivalently, every pair belonging to \(A\) also belongs to \(B\), and every \((x,x^*),(y,y^*)\in\operatorname{gra}B\) satisfies
\[
\langle x-y,x^*-y^*\rangle\geq0.
\]
The extension is proper when the graph inclusion is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone extension enlarges an operator’s graph while preserving monotonicity; it is proper when at least one graph point is added.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Extensions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83

children.title: Maximal Monotone Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions complete relative to the monotonicity ordering.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) possesses a maximal monotone extension.

notation.meaning: family of monotone graphs containing the graph of A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence by maximal graph inclusion, without uniqueness.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists a maximally monotone operator \(M:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) such that
\[
\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}M.
\]
Here maximality means that whenever a monotone operator \(N:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{gra}M\subseteq\operatorname{gra}N,
\]
then \(\operatorname{gra}N=\operatorname{gra}M\). The assertion is only existential; distinct maximal monotone extensions may occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every monotone operator has a graph-inclusion-maximal monotone extension, although that extension need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Monotone Extensions

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of every closed proper convex function on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is a maximal monotone set-valued mapping.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is maximal monotone}

knowledge_statements.title: Extension Existence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic existence in a Banach space; neither uniqueness nor constructive computability is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every monotone set \(A\subset X\times X^*\) is contained in a maximal monotone set \(M\subset X\times X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every monotone graph in a Banach space has at least one maximal monotone extension; uniqueness and constructive computability are not asserted.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
\(A\subset X\times X^*\) is monotone: \(\langle x-y,x^*-y^*\rangle\ge 0\) for all \((x,x^*),(y,y^*)\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a maximal monotone set \(M\subset X\times X^*\) satisfying \(A\subset M\).

notation.meaning: dual pairing between the Banach space and its dual
a maximal monotone extension of the initial graph

children.title: Extension Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity and selection issues among admissible extensions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distinct graphs \(M_0=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\) and \(M_1=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb R\}\) are maximal monotone and satisfy \(A\subset M_0\cap M_1\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional example showing that maximal monotone extensions generally are not canonical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(A=\{(0,0)\}\) is monotone. Both \(M_0=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\) and \(M_1=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb R\}\) contain \(A\). Each is maximal monotone on \(\mathbb R\), while \(M_0\ne M_1\). Hence maximal monotone extension of a monotone graph need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The single point (0,0) has both the zero operator and the identity operator as distinct maximal monotone extensions.

children.title: Global Maximality Tests

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(T:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator \(T\) is maximal monotone if and only if \(\operatorname{gra}T=(\operatorname{gra}T)^\mu\).

notation.meaning: monotone polar of a subset of the product space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: defining monotone-polar characterization of maximality
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global graph test using every point monotonically related to the operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\subset X\times X^*\), define its monotone polar by \[A^\mu=\{(x,x^*)\in X\times X^*: \langle x-y,x^*-y^*\rangle\ge 0\ \text{for every }(y,y^*)\in A\}.\] A monotone operator \(T\) is maximal monotone exactly when every pair monotonically related to its entire graph already lies in that graph, equivalently \(\operatorname{gra}T=(\operatorname{gra}T)^\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone operator is globally maximal exactly when every point monotonically related to its whole graph already belongs to the graph.

children.title: Local Maximality

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space, \(U\subset X\) is open, and \(T:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph is maximal relative to \(U\) precisely when \((x,x^*)\in U\times X^*\) and \(\langle x-y,x^*-y^*\rangle\ge0\) for every \((y,y^*)\in\operatorname{gra}T\cap(U\times X^*)\) imply \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}T\).

graph restricted to base points in the region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative maximality is tested only against graph points whose primal coordinates lie in the chosen open region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\operatorname{gra}_U T=\operatorname{gra}T\cap(U\times X^*)\). The operator \(T\) is maximal monotone relative to \(U\) when \(\operatorname{gra}_U T\) is monotone and no pair in \(U\times X^*\) can be adjoined while preserving monotonicity. Equivalently, every \((x,x^*)\in U\times X^*\) monotonically related to all of \(\operatorname{gra}_U T\) belongs to \(\operatorname{gra}_U T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local maximality globalizes when the tested open regions cover the entire primal space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\{U_i\}_{i\in I}\) is an open cover of \(X\) and a monotone operator \(T:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is maximal monotone relative to every \(U_i\), then \(T\) is maximal monotone on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a monotone operator is relatively maximal on every member of an open cover of the whole space, then it is globally maximal.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(T:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone.
\(\{U_i\}_{i\in I}\) is an open cover of \(X\).
For every \(i\in I\), \(T\) is maximal monotone relative to \(U_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator \(T\) is maximal monotone on \(X\).

notation.meaning: an open cover of the primal space

knowledge_statements.title: Test Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A proper local testing region cannot detect monotone extensions outside that region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(U=(-1,1)\), the operator \(T:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) defined by \(T(x)=\{0\}\) for \(x\in U\) and \(T(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise is maximal monotone relative to \(U\), but it is not maximal monotone on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero operator restricted to a proper open interval is locally maximal there but admits a proper monotone extension to the whole line.

children.title: Bounded-Domain Extension Regime

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a monotone set \(M_C\subset C\times X^*\), maximal among monotone subsets of \(C\times X^*\), such that \(A\subset M_C\).

notation.meaning: initial monotone graph over the bounded domain
a maximal relative extension within the bounded cylinder

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This records relative extension inside a bounded domain, not a verified formulation of the named Debrunner–Flor theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Within the family of monotone subsets of \(C\times X^*\) that contain \(A\), ordered by inclusion, every chain has a monotone union. Hence a maximal member \(M_C\) exists and satisfies \(A\subset M_C\subset C\times X^*\). Its maximality is relative to the bounded cylinder \(C\times X^*\); the statement alone does not establish maximal monotonicity in \(X\times X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone graph over a bounded domain has an inclusion-maximal extension within that domain, but this is only relative maximality.

convex-analytic normal cone to the interval

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty's Hilbert-space equivalence for a fixed positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a monotone operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(\lambda>0\), \[A\text{ is maximally monotone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H.\] If these conditions hold, they hold for every positive resolvent parameter, and \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}:H\to H\) is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone Hilbert-space operator, maximality is equivalent to surjectivity of a positive identity shift; under these conditions, every positive-parameter resolvent is everywhere defined, single-valued, and firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is maximally monotone}\iff\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Type restriction behind the identity-shift form of Minty's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a general Banach space, a monotone operator naturally maps \(X\) into \(X^*\), while the identity maps \(X\) into \(X\). Thus \(I+\lambda A\) is not a type-consistent sum unless an additional identification \(X\cong X^*\) is supplied. Hilbert spaces provide this identification through the Riesz map. Banach-space analogues instead use a duality mapping \(J:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) and formulate surjectivity of \(J+\lambda A\), with reflexivity or geometric assumptions imposed as required by the chosen theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The identity-shift version is intrinsically Hilbertian. In Banach spaces, operators take values in the dual, so a duality map and extra hypotheses are needed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two logically distinct properties support Minty parametrization. If \(A\) is monotone, then \(I+\lambda A\) is injective as a relation in its first component, so \(J_{\lambda A}\) is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive on \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)\). If \(A\) is also maximal, Minty's theorem gives \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H\). Thus failure of monotonicity can destroy uniqueness or firmness, whereas failure of maximality preserves restricted uniqueness but can destroy full parameter coverage.

children.title: Fitzpatrick Function Family
children.top_down_role: Canonical convex graph representatives.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi_A=\min \mathcal F_A\), and \(\operatorname{gra}A=\{(x,x^*):\varphi_A(x,x^*)=\langle x,x^*\rangle\}\).

notation.meaning: duality pairing between the space and its dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Fitzpatrick family for a maximal monotone operator on a real Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\varphi_A(x,x^*)=\sup_{(a,a^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A}\bigl(\langle x,a^*\rangle+\langle a,x^*\rangle-\langle a,a^*\rangle\bigr).\] The Fitzpatrick family \(\mathcal F_A\) consists of all proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions \(h:X\times X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfying \(h(x,x^*)\geq\langle x,x^*\rangle\) everywhere and equality on \(\operatorname{gra}A\). For maximal monotone \(A\), \(\varphi_A\in\mathcal F_A\), and \(\varphi_A\leq h\) pointwise for every \(h\in\mathcal F_A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fitzpatrick function is the smallest lower-semicontinuous convex majorant of the duality pairing that equals the pairing exactly on a maximal monotone graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Fitzpatrick Function Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and minimality claim are mathematically standard and fit the container, but no inspectable citation supports the Fitzpatrick-family characterization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex representatives under the standard duality-product convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bivariate representative of \(A\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(h:X\times X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \(h(x,x^*)\geq\langle x,x^*\rangle\) for every \((x,x^*)\in X\times X^*\), while \(h(x,x^*)=\langle x,x^*\rangle\) whenever \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). Maximal monotonicity then implies that equality holds only on \(\operatorname{gra}A\), so the equality set recovers the represented operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representative is a convex function majorizing the duality pairing whose contact set is exactly the maximal monotone graph.
