children.title: Autoconjugate Representatives
children.top_down_role: Representative functions invariant under the relevant conjugation transform.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space.
\(h:X\times X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate on the product dual, followed by transposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autoconjugacy using product-space Fenchel conjugation and coordinate transposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The product conjugate is \[h^*(x^*,x)=\sup_{(y,y^*)\in X\times X^*}\bigl(\langle y,x^*\rangle+\langle x,y^*\rangle-h(y,y^*)\bigr).\] The function \(h\) is autoconjugate when \(h(x,x^*)=h^*(x^*,x)\) for all \((x,x^*)\). It represents the operator \(A\) determined by \(x^*\in Ax\) exactly when \(h(x,x^*)=\langle x,x^*\rangle\). Autoconjugacy implies \(h(x,x^*)\geq\langle x,x^*\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An autoconjugate representative equals its product Fenchel conjugate after exchanging primal and dual coordinates; its contact set with the pairing defines a monotone graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Autoconjugate Representatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The autoconjugacy convention and majorization consequence are plausible and locally appropriate, but no source is supplied for the product-dual formulation or representation claim.

children.title: Self-Dual Representatives
children.top_down_role: Self-dual representation conventions for monotone graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space.
\(L:X\times X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L^*(p,x)=L(x,p)\) for every \((x,p)\in X\times X^*\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate with respect to both variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality in the self-dual-Lagrangian coordinate convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[L^*(p,x)=\sup_{(y,q)\in X\times X^*}\bigl(\langle y,p\rangle+\langle x,q\rangle-L(y,q)\bigr).\] The function \(L\) is self-dual when \(L^*(p,x)=L(x,p)\) for every \((x,p)\in X\times X^*\). Its derived vector field is \(\bar\partial L(x)=\{p\in X^*:L(x,p)=\langle x,p\rangle\}\); equivalently, equality holds precisely when \((p,x)\in\partial L(x,p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-dual representative equals its full Fenchel conjugate after the conjugate variables are written in dual–primal order.
knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Representatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The self-dual-Lagrangian definition fits the leaf, but the derived-vector-field and subdifferential equivalence need an authoritative source using this exact coordinate convention.

children.title: Duality-Convention Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections and distinctions between autoconjugate and self-dual terminology.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space.
Product conjugation pairs \((x,x^*)\) with \((p,x^{**})\) through the canonical dualities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h=h^{*\top}\iff L^*(p,x)=L(x,p)\) when \(L=h\).

notation.meaning: transpose converting dual–primal order to primal–dual order
canonical embedding of the space into its bidual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of autoconjugate and self-dual terminology under coordinate transposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h:X\times X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(h^{*\top}(x,x^*)=h^*(x^*,J_Xx)\). Reflexivity identifies \(J_Xx\) with \(x\), so the autoconjugacy identity \(h^{*\top}(x,x^*)=h(x,x^*)\) becomes \(h^*(x^*,x)=h(x,x^*)\). Renaming \(h\) as \(L\) and \(x^*\) as \(p\) yields the self-dual-Lagrangian identity \(L^*(p,x)=L(x,p)\). Thus the two formulations differ by the ordering convention for product-dual coordinates, not by their mathematical content.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Autoconjugacy and self-duality are the same product-conjugacy identity, expressed respectively in primal–dual and dual–primal coordinate conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Convention Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The correspondence is mathematically plausible and duality is the correct content kind, but the claimed terminological equivalence requires a source fixing both conjugation conventions.

children.title: Representative Existence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Operator classes and ambient settings affecting representative existence.

assumptions_latex: Autoconjugacy is interpreted through the canonical embedding \(J_X:X\to X^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) reflexive guarantees an autoconjugate representative; without reflexivity, \(h^*(x^*,J_Xx)=h(x,x^*)\) is not automatic for every maximal monotone \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflexive-space existence theorem and the bidual obstruction beyond reflexivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is reflexive, every maximal monotone \(A:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) admits a proper lower-semicontinuous convex representative \(h\) satisfying \(h^*(x^*,x)=h(x,x^*)\) and \(h(x,x^*)=\langle x,x^*\rangle\) exactly on \(\operatorname{gra}A\). If reflexivity is removed, the conjugate naturally lives on \(X^*\times X^{**}\); hence the same identity must use \(J_Xx\), and unrestricted existence for every maximal monotone operator does not follow from the reflexive theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reflexivity guarantees autoconjugate representatives. Without it, product conjugation lands in the bidual, and the reflexive existence theorem no longer applies automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Representative Existence Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the universal reflexive existence theorem and the precise limitation beyond reflexivity require a specific authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Canonical Monotone Operator Constructions
children.top_down_role: Standard sources and transformations of maximal monotone operators.

children.title: Convex Subdifferential Operators
children.top_down_role: The subdifferential source class.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f\) is monotone; under the stated hypotheses it is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convex subdifferential on a real Banach space.

source_refs.locator: A. Convex Sets and Functions p. 38
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), define \[\partial f(x)=\{x^*\in X^*: f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle y-x,x^*\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in X\},\] with \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) when \(f(x)=+\infty\). For any \(x^*\in\partial f(x)\) and \(y^*\in\partial f(y)\), adding the two subgradient inequalities gives \(\langle x-y,x^*-y^*\rangle\geq0\). The operator \(\partial f:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex subdifferential collects supporting slopes. It is monotone, and every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function generates a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subdifferential Operators

source_witnesses.locator: A. Convex Sets and Functions p. 38
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited Rockafellar–Wets locator does not establish the stated general Banach-space maximal-monotonicity theorem, and the statement includes proof text that must be removed after an appropriate source is supplied.

children.title: Normal-Cone Operators
children.top_down_role: The constraint-geometry source class.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C=\partial\delta_C\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic normal cone to a closed convex set.

source_refs.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[N_C(x)=\begin{cases}\{x^*\in X^*: \langle y-x,x^*\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in C\},&x\in C,\\ \varnothing,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] If \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, then \(N_C=\partial\delta_C\). Consequently \(N_C\) is maximal monotone, and \(0\in N_C(x)\) holds for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cone contains dual vectors supporting the convex set at a point. It is the indicator function’s subdifferential and is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Operators

source_witnesses.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-cone definition is standard and fits the container, but the cited finite-dimensional treatment does not support the asserted arbitrary-Banach-space scope.

children.title: Linear-Relation Symmetric-Skew Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Linear, affine, and multivalued relation classes.

children.title: Monotone Linear Relations
children.top_down_role: Linear and multivalued monotone graph structures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is monotone exactly when \(\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\) for every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).

notation.meaning: value of the relation at zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone linear relations on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear relation is a set-valued operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) whose graph \(\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq H\times H\) is a linear subspace. It is monotone when \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\) for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). Because the graph is linear and contains \((0,0)\), this is equivalent to \(\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\) for every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\). Maximal monotonicity means that no strictly larger monotone linear relation contains its graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear relation is monotone precisely when its graph’s quadratic pairing is nonnegative; maximality prohibits any proper monotone graph extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Linear Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity criterion is correct for a linear-subspace graph, but no source is supplied and maximal monotonicity must exclude every larger monotone graph, not merely larger monotone linear relations.

children.title: Skew Components
children.top_down_role: Skew contributions within linear-relation representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is skew exactly when \(\langle x,u\rangle=0\) for every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Skewness for possibly set-valued linear relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear relation \(S\) is skew when \(\langle x,u\rangle=0\) for every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}S\). Polarization on its linear graph then gives \(\langle x,v\rangle=-\langle y,u\rangle\) whenever \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}S\). With the adjoint relation defined by \((y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}S^*\) exactly when \(\langle v,x\rangle=\langle y,u\rangle\) for every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}S\), skewness implies \(S\subseteq-S^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A skew linear relation has zero quadratic pairing on its graph; cross-pairings are antisymmetric, and the relation lies in the negative of its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Skew Components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The skewness and cross-pairing statements fit the container, but the adjoint-relation convention and inclusion in the negative adjoint require an inspectable source.

children.title: Symmetric–Skew Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Separation of dissipative and skew structure in linear settings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A=A_++A_\circ\), with \(A_+^*=A_+\), \(A_\circ^*=-A_\circ\), and \(A\) monotone iff \(A_+\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded single-valued Hilbert-space decomposition; unbounded relations require domain qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[A_+=\frac{A+A^*}{2},\qquad A_\circ=\frac{A-A^*}{2}.\] Then \(A=A_++A_\circ\), \(A_+^*=A_+\), and \(A_\circ^*=-A_\circ\). Moreover \(\langle x,A_\circ x\rangle=0\) and \(\langle x,Ax\rangle=\langle x,A_+x\rangle\) for every \(x\in H\). Hence \(A\) is monotone if and only if its symmetric part is positive semidefinite, meaning \(\langle x,A_+x\rangle\geq0\) for all \(x\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bounded linear Hilbert-space operator splits uniquely into symmetric and skew parts, and monotonicity is exactly positivity of the symmetric part.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric–Skew Decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded single-valued Hilbert-space decomposition is precise, and representation is the correct kind, but no source supports the formulas and monotonicity equivalence.

children.title: Multivaluedness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Domain and representation issues specific to multivalued linear relations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=u+A0\), and \(A\) is single-valued exactly when \(A0=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic boundary between operators and genuinely multivalued linear relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(u\in Ax\), linearity of the graph gives \[Ax=u+A0.\] Indeed, if \(v\in Ax\), then \((0,v-u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), while adding any \((0,w)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) to \((x,u)\) gives \(u+w\in Ax\). Thus every nonempty value is an affine translate of the fixed subspace \(A0\). Consequently \(A\) is single-valued on \(\operatorname{dom}A\) if and only if \(A0=\{0\}\); nonzero elements of \(A0\) are precisely the obstruction to single-valuedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value of a linear relation is a translate of its zero fiber. The relation is single-valued exactly when that fiber is trivial.
knowledge_statements.title: Multivaluedness Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic boundary and failure-boundary kind are appropriate, but no citation is supplied and the statement contains proof text beginning with “Indeed,” which is prohibited in a knowledge statement.

children.title: Partial-Inverse Product-Space Transformations
children.top_down_role: Transformations used for constrained and decomposable inclusions.

children.title: Partial Inverses
children.top_down_role: Partial inversion as a transformation of constrained inclusions.

assumptions_latex: \(V\subset H\) is a closed vector subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gra}A_V=\{(x,y):P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}x\in A(P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}y)\}\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto a closed subspace.
Partial inverse of \(A\) with respect to \(V\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Spingarn partial-inverse definition in a Hilbert space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the Hilbert-space partial inverse associated with an orthogonal decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The partial inverse of \(A\) with respect to \(V\) is the operator \(A_V:H\rightrightarrows H\) defined, for every \((x,y)\in H\times H\), by \[y\in A_Vx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}x\in A\bigl(P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}y\bigr).\] Thus the transformation interchanges the \(V^\perp\)-components of the argument and value while retaining their \(V\)-components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partial inverse swaps the orthogonal-complement components of an operator's argument and value while retaining their components in the selected subspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Inverses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, notation, scope, and content kind match the Partial Inverses leaf, but no inspectable citation is attached. The standard-field rationale is insufficient to establish source support.

children.title: Product-Space Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations for coupled or decomposable inclusions.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m\geq 2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\sum_{i=1}^m A_i u\) is represented by \(0\in \boldsymbol A_{\boldsymbol V}\boldsymbol x\) in \(H^m\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal subspace of the product space.
Partial inverse of the product operator relative to the diagonal.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard diagonal product-space reformulation of a monotone inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal lifting of a finite sum inclusion into a partial-inverse zero problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\boldsymbol H=H^m\) with its product Hilbert structure, set \(\boldsymbol A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_m\), and let \(\boldsymbol V=\{(u,\ldots,u):u\in H\}\). Then \(0\in\boldsymbol A_{\boldsymbol V}\boldsymbol x\) holds exactly when, writing \(P_{\boldsymbol V}\boldsymbol x=(u,\ldots,u)\) and \(P_{\boldsymbol V^\perp}\boldsymbol x=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), one has \[v_i\in A_i u\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0.\] Hence such a zero exists exactly when \(0\in\sum_{i=1}^m A_i u\) has a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum inclusion lifts to a product operator whose partial-inverse zeros encode a common primal point and component values summing to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Liftings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-space representation is mathematically coherent and fits the Product-Space Liftings leaf. It correctly encodes the finite sum inclusion through the diagonal subspace, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Constraint-Encoding Interface
children.top_down_role: How the transformations encode subspace and coupling constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(V\subset H\) is a closed vector subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in A_Vx\iff u=P_Vx\in V,\ v=P_{V^\perp}x\in V^\perp,\ v\in Au\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct constraint encoding furnished by the partial-inverse definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes a subspace-constrained primal-dual inclusion as an unconstrained zero problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in H\), set \(u=P_Vx\) and \(v=P_{V^\perp}x\). Then \[0\in A_Vx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in V,\quad v\in V^\perp,\quad v\in Au.\] Thus \(x\mapsto(u,v)\) identifies \(\operatorname{zer}A_V\) with the set of pairs \((u,v)\in V\times V^\perp\) satisfying \(v\in Au\). The corresponding points \(u\) satisfy \(0\in Au+N_Vu\), and every such solution together with \(v\in Au\cap V^\perp\) corresponds to \(x=u+v\in\operatorname{zer}A_V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of the partial inverse correspond to pairs consisting of a point in the constraint subspace and an operator value in its orthogonal complement.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Encoding Interface

children.title: Transform Preservation Properties
children.top_down_role: Monotonicity and maximality behavior under the transformations.

assumptions_latex: \(V\subset H\) is a closed vector subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is monotone, respectively maximally monotone, iff \(A_V\) has the same property; moreover \((A_V)_V=A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard isometric graph transformation for partial inverses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation under the Hilbert-space partial-inverse transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partial inversion relative to \(V\) is involutive: \[(A_V)_V=A.\] It preserves monotonicity and maximal monotonicity: \[A\text{ is monotone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A_V\text{ is monotone},\] and \[A\text{ is maximally monotone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A_V\text{ is maximally monotone}.\] These properties require no additional assumptions on the domain or range of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial inversion is involutive and preserves both monotonicity and maximal monotonicity without additional domain or range assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Transform Preservation Properties

children.title: Graphical Convergence of Monotone Operators
children.top_down_role: Convergence structures for operator graphs and their resolvents.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Variational Analysis
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

children.title: Graph-Resolvent Convergence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Equivalent and comparative convergence viewpoints.

children.title: Graph Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence viewed through limiting monotone graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\xrightarrow{g}A\iff \operatorname*{Li}\operatorname{gra}A_n=\operatorname{gra}A=\operatorname*{Ls}\operatorname{gra}A_n\) in the strong product topology.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: strong graphical convergence of set-valued operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence in the strong topology of \(H\times H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((A_n)\) converges graphically to \(A\), written \(A_n\xrightarrow{g}A\), when \[\operatorname*{Li}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gra}A_n=\operatorname{gra}A=\operatorname*{Ls}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gra}A_n\] in the strong topology of \(H\times H\). Equivalently, every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) is the strong limit of some \((x_n,y_n)\in\operatorname{gra}A_n\), and every strongly convergent subsequence \((x_{n_k},y_{n_k})\in\operatorname{gra}A_{n_k}\) has its limit in \(\operatorname{gra}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph convergence means inner and outer set limits of the operator graphs coincide with the limiting graph in the strong product topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently specifies strong Painleve-Kuratowski convergence in the product Hilbert space, and its sequential formulation agrees with that definition. No inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Resolvent Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence viewed through associated single-valued resolvent mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\lambda A_n}x\to J_{\lambda A}x\) for every \(x\in H\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pointwise strong resolvent convergence for maximally monotone operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise strong convergence of full-domain Minty resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because each operator is maximally monotone, its resolvent \(J_{\lambda A_n}=(I+\lambda A_n)^{-1}\) is a single-valued mapping from \(H\) to \(H\). Resolvent convergence of \(A_n\) to \(A\) at parameter \(\lambda>0\) means \[J_{\lambda A_n}x\longrightarrow J_{\lambda A}x\quad\text{strongly in }H\quad\text{for every }x\in H.\] For maximally monotone operators, convergence at one positive parameter determines convergence at every positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolvent convergence is pointwise norm convergence of the full-domain resolvent maps; for maximal monotone operators one positive parameter suffices.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of pointwise strong resolvent convergence fits the leaf and the maximal-monotonicity assumptions make the resolvents full-domain single-valued maps. The additional assertion that one positive parameter determines every positive parameter requires an authoritative citation, but none is attached.

children.title: Graph–Resolvent Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Conditions relating the two convergence viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\xrightarrow{g}A\iff J_{\lambda A_n}x\to J_{\lambda A}x\) for every \(x\in H\).

notation.meaning: Graphical convergence in the strong product topology.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical graph–resolvent convergence theorem for maximal monotone operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong graph–resolvent correspondence on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For maximally monotone operators on \(H\), the following are equivalent: \[A_n\xrightarrow{g}A,\] and \[J_{\lambda A_n}x\longrightarrow J_{\lambda A}x\quad\text{strongly for every }x\in H.\] The equivalence holds for any fixed \(\lambda>0\); if the resolvent convergence holds for one positive \(\lambda\), it holds for every positive parameter. Maximal monotonicity ensures that all resolvents appearing here are single-valued and defined on all of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximal monotone operators, strong graph convergence is equivalent to pointwise norm convergence of resolvents at any one positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph–Resolvent Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and stated maximal-monotone graph-resolvent equivalence fit the correspondence leaf. An inspectable source is required for the strong-product, potentially infinite-dimensional formulation and the one-parameter assertion.

children.title: Correspondence Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Limits of equivalence outside suitable maximality or geometric settings.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nonzero real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is monotone but \(J_A\) has domain \(\{0\}\), so full-domain resolvent convergence cannot represent arbitrary monotone graph convergence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit nonmaximal monotone graph showing loss of full-domain resolvents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why maximal monotonicity is essential for the standard correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be given by \[A0=\{0\},\qquad Ax=\varnothing\quad\text{for }x\neq0.\] This operator is monotone but not maximally monotone, and its resolvent relation satisfies \[J_A=(I+A)^{-1},\qquad \operatorname{dom}J_A=\{0\}.\] It is therefore not a full-domain self-map of \(H\). This example marks the failure of the pointwise full-domain resolvent formulation for general nonmaximal monotone relations; maximality or a suitable surjectivity assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmaximal monotone operator can have a resolvent defined only at zero, so the full-domain graph-resolvent correspondence does not extend to arbitrary monotone relations.
knowledge_statements.title: Correspondence Failure Regimes

children.title: Function-Operator Convergence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between function convergence and operator convergence.

children.title: Mosco Convergence
children.top_down_role: Variational convergence of convex functions in weak–strong topology.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) iff the weak liminf and strong recovery conditions both hold.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Hilbert-space definition of Mosco convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mosco convergence for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((f_n)\) Mosco-converges to \(f\), written \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\), if both conditions hold: \[(\mathrm{M1})\qquad x_n\rightharpoonup x\ \Longrightarrow\ f(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n),\] and \[(\mathrm{M2})\qquad \text{for every }x\in H\text{ there exists }x_n\to x\text{ such that }f(x)\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n).\] Thus the lower bound is tested along every weakly convergent sequence, while recovery is required along at least one strongly convergent sequence for each point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence combines a weak sequential lower bound with a strongly convergent recovery sequence at every point.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak liminf and strong recovery conditions give the standard Hilbert-space definition of Mosco convergence and match the plain statement. No inspectable source is attached.

children.title: Subdifferential Convergence
children.top_down_role: Graphical convergence behavior of associated subdifferential operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) implies \(\partial f_n\xrightarrow{g}\partial f\) and \(J_{\lambda\partial f_n}x\to J_{\lambda\partial f}x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Attouch-type implication from Mosco convergence to subdifferential convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward Attouch implication for convex subdifferentials on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\), then \[\partial f_n\xrightarrow{g}\partial f.\] Equivalently, for every \(\lambda>0\) and every \(x\in H\), \[J_{\lambda\partial f_n}x\longrightarrow J_{\lambda\partial f}x\quad\text{strongly in }H.\] With \(J_{\lambda\partial f}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\), the same conclusion is \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_n}x\longrightarrow\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}x\quad\text{for every }\lambda>0\text{ and }x\in H.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence of proper closed convex functions implies graphical convergence of their subdifferentials and pointwise convergence of all associated proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Convergence

children.title: Function–Operator Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Passage from function convergence to operator convergence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\iff e_\lambda f_n(x)\to e_\lambda f(x)\) for every \(x\in H\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Moreau-envelope form of the Attouch function–operator correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized correspondence retaining function values, not merely subdifferential graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any fixed \(\lambda>0\), \[f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e_\lambda f_n(x)\longrightarrow e_\lambda f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in H.\] Under these equivalent conditions, \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_n}x\to\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}x\) for every \(x\), and hence \(\partial f_n\xrightarrow{g}\partial f\). The envelope values retain the additive normalization discarded by the subdifferential operator, which is why envelope convergence gives a function-level equivalence whereas graph convergence alone does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence is equivalent to pointwise convergence of Moreau envelopes; proximal and subdifferential convergence follow while additive normalization is retained.
knowledge_statements.title: Function–Operator Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and function-level normalization emphasis fit the correspondence leaf. The claim that pointwise Moreau-envelope convergence at one fixed positive parameter is sufficient in an arbitrary Hilbert space is sensitive to the precise Attouch theorem formulation and cannot be accepted without an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Correspondence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Hypothesis-sensitive limitations of the function–operator passage.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f_n=\partial f\) for every \(n\), but \((f_n)\) does not Mosco-converge to \(f\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive constants provide the canonical obstruction to recovering functions from subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits the additive-constant boundary of subdifferential convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_n\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(c_n\to+\infty\), and define \(f_n=f+c_n\). Then, for every \(n\), \[\partial f_n=\partial f,\qquad J_{\lambda\partial f_n}=J_{\lambda\partial f}\quad\text{for every }\lambda>0.\] Nevertheless, \((f_n)\) does not Mosco-converge to \(f\), and \[e_\lambda f_n=e_\lambda f+c_n\quad\text{for every }\lambda>0.\] Thus convergence of subdifferentials or their resolvents does not determine Mosco convergence without additive normalization data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding divergent real constants leaves every subdifferential and resolvent unchanged but prevents Mosco convergence, demonstrating the loss of additive normalization at the operator level.
knowledge_statements.title: Correspondence Boundary

children.title: Zero-Set Solution-Limit Stability
children.top_down_role: Stability questions induced by graphical limits.

children.title: Zero-Set Stability
children.top_down_role: Set convergence and persistence of zeros under operator limits.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(A_n,A:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximal monotone and \(A_n\to_g A\), meaning \(\operatorname{gra}A_n\) converges to \(\operatorname{gra}A\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{zer}A_n\subseteq \operatorname{zer}A.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: closed-graph consequence of Painlevé--Kuratowski graphical convergence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer zero-set stability under finite-dimensional graphical convergence; inner stability is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x_{n_k}\in\operatorname{zer}A_{n_k}\) and \(x_{n_k}\to x\), then \((x_{n_k},0)\in\operatorname{gra}A_{n_k}\). The outer-limit implication in graphical convergence gives \((x,0)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), hence \(x\in\operatorname{zer}A\). Equivalently, every finite cluster point of zeros of the approximating operators is a zero of the graphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite cluster point of zeros of graphically convergent monotone operators is a zero of the limiting operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Set Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outer zero-set inclusion is mathematically consistent with Painleve--Kuratowski graph convergence and the property kind fits the Zero-Set Stability leaf. However, no inspectable citation is attached, and statement_latex contains proof-style derivation rather than only the knowledge statement.

children.title: Solution Stability
children.top_down_role: Behavior of selected solutions under perturbation and graphical limits.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(A_n,A:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximal monotone, \(A_n\to_g A\), and every \(A_n\) and \(A\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for one \(\mu>0\).
Each \(A_n\) has a zero \(x_n\), the sequence \((x_n)\) is bounded, and \(A\) has a zero \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_n\to x_\star,\qquad \operatorname{zer}A=\{x_\star\}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: strong monotonicity gives uniqueness and graphical convergence identifies cluster points
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional stability with existence, boundedness, and a uniform strong-monotonicity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong monotonicity makes the zero of each operator unique. Every subsequence of \((x_n)\) has a convergent subsubsequence by boundedness. Zero-set outer stability identifies its limit as an element of \(\operatorname{zer}A\), while strong monotonicity makes that set the singleton \(\{x_\star\}\). Consequently all cluster points equal \(x_\star\), and therefore the entire sequence converges to \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded zeros converge to the unique limiting zero when graphical convergence is combined with a common positive strong-monotonicity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution Stability

children.title: Solution-Loss Regimes
children.top_down_role: Escape, disappearance, or instability of solutions under operator convergence.

assumptions_latex: The ambient Hilbert space is \(H=\mathbb R\).
For each \(n\ge1\), define the maximally monotone constant operator \(A_nx=\{1/n\}\), and define \(Ax=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A_n\to_g A,\qquad \operatorname{zer}A_n=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{zer}A=\mathbb R.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit constant-operator counterexample verified directly

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical convergence alone does not ensure existence or inner convergence of exact zero sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphs are \(\operatorname{gra}A_n=\mathbb R\times\{1/n\}\), which converge in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense to \(\mathbb R\times\{0\}=\operatorname{gra}A\). Hence zeros may appear only in the limit, and graphical convergence provides no inner zero-set stability without an additional solvability or regularity hypothesis.

children.title: Resolvent Metric Geometry
children.top_down_role: Firm nonexpansiveness and related metric structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|J_{\lambda A}x-J_{\lambda A}y\|^2\le \langle J_{\lambda A}x-J_{\lambda A}y,x-y\rangle\quad(x,y\in H).\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical resolvent characterization of maximal monotonicity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Firm nonexpansiveness of a maximal monotone operator's everywhere-defined resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}:H\to H\) is single-valued, everywhere defined, and firmly nonexpansive. Equivalently, \(J_{\lambda A}\) is \(1\)-cocoercive and its reflected mapping \(2J_{\lambda A}-I\) is nonexpansive. In particular, \(J_{\lambda A}\) is nonexpansive: \(\|J_{\lambda A}x-J_{\lambda A}y\|\le\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a maximal monotone operator is everywhere defined and firmly nonexpansive; its reflection is nonexpansive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The firm-nonexpansiveness claim and its stated metric consequences are standard and property fits Resolvent Metric Geometry. No authoritative source and specific locator are attached, so the source requirement is unmet.

children.title: Operator Reconstruction from Resolvents
children.top_down_role: Recovery and comparison of operators through resolvents.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A=\lambda^{-1}(J_{\lambda A}^{-1}-I),\qquad \operatorname{gra}A=\{(J_{\lambda A}x,\lambda^{-1}(x-J_{\lambda A}x)):x\in H\}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic inversion of the resolvent definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph and operator recovery from one resolvent parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,z\in H\), the equivalence \(z=J_{\lambda A}x\Longleftrightarrow x-z\in\lambda Az\) reconstructs every graph pair of \(A\). Thus one resolvent determines the operator uniquely. In particular, if maximal monotone operators \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(J_{\lambda A}=J_{\lambda B}\) for one \(\lambda>0\), then \(A=B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal monotone operator and its graph are recovered exactly from any one of its positive-parameter resolvents.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator Reconstruction from Resolvents

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reconstruction identities are mathematically consistent, and representation is appropriate for this leaf. The record supplies no citation, while statement_latex contains an algebraic derivation.

children.title: Reflected Resolvents
children.top_down_role: Reflected forms of resolvent mappings used in splitting constructions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_{\lambda A}:=2J_{\lambda A}-I,\qquad \|R_{\lambda A}x-R_{\lambda A}y\|\le\|x-y\|.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard reflected-resolvent definition and firm-nonexpansiveness equivalence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention reflection equals twice the resolvent minus the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reflected resolvent of \(\lambda A\) is the mapping \(R_{\lambda A}:H\to H\) defined by \(R_{\lambda A}x=2J_{\lambda A}x-x\). Since \(J_{\lambda A}\) is firmly nonexpansive, \(R_{\lambda A}\) is nonexpansive. Conversely, a mapping \(T:H\to H\) is firmly nonexpansive exactly when \(2T-I\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reflected resolvent is twice the resolvent minus the identity and is nonexpansive for every maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflected Resolvents

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is a suitable primary kind for Reflected Resolvents, although the record also bundles the nonexpansiveness property and a general equivalence. These standard claims have no inspectable source citation.

children.title: Cayley Transforms
children.top_down_role: Cayley-transform representations of monotone operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_{\lambda A}:=(I-\lambda A)(I+\lambda A)^{-1}=2(I+\lambda A)^{-1}-I.\]

notation.meaning: Cayley transform under the stated sign convention

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard nonlinear Cayley-transform convention expressed through the resolvent
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adopts the Cayley convention \((I-\lambda A)(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\); opposite-sign conventions also occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in H\), let \(z=J_{\lambda A}x\) and choose \(a\in Az\) so that \(x=z+\lambda a\). Then \(C_{\lambda A}x=z-\lambda a=2z-x\). Consequently \(C_{\lambda A}=2J_{\lambda A}-I\), and maximal monotonicity of \(A\) implies that \(C_{\lambda A}\) is an everywhere-defined nonexpansive mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated sign convention, the Cayley transform is the reflected resolvent and is therefore nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.title: Cayley Transforms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the Cayley Transforms leaf, but for a set-valued nonlinear operator the expression (I-lambda A)(I+lambda A)^{-1} requires an explicitly sourced relational convention; ordinary composition can be multivalued and need not equal 2J-I. The sign and composition convention is therefore unreliable without a source, and statement_latex contains derivation.

children.title: Reflection–Cayley Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Convention-sensitive relationships between the two transforms.

assumptions_latex: The Cayley transform is defined by \(C_{\lambda A}:=(I-\lambda A)(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_{\lambda A}=R_{\lambda A}=2J_{\lambda A}-I,\qquad R_{(\lambda A)^{-1}}=-R_{\lambda A}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic Cayley-reflection identity and resolvent inversion symmetry
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence for the explicitly stated Cayley sign convention, including inversion symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reflection and Cayley constructions are the same mapping under the stated convention. Moreover, the resolvent identity \(J_{(\lambda A)^{-1}}=I-J_{\lambda A}\) yields \(R_{(\lambda A)^{-1}}=2(I-J_{\lambda A})-I=-R_{\lambda A}\). Thus operator inversion corresponds to sign reversal of the reflected resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The chosen Cayley transform equals the reflected resolvent, while inversion of the scaled operator negates that reflection.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflection–Cayley Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Duality is an acceptable kind for the reflection--Cayley and inversion correspondence. The inversion identity is standard, but the Cayley equality inherits the unsourced nonlinear composition and sign convention from the preceding record; statement_latex also contains derivation.

children.title: Two-Operator Splitting Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of transformed resolvents in two-operator splitting structures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{\mathrm{DR}}:=\tfrac12(I+R_{\lambda B}R_{\lambda A}),\qquad x\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\Longrightarrow J_{\lambda A}x\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B).\]
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point interface underlying Douglas--Rachford splitting for a two-operator monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in H\), iterate \(x_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{DR}}x_k\). If a stopping rule returns an exact fixed point \(x\), output the shadow point \(z=J_{\lambda A}x\), which satisfies \(0\in Az+Bz\). Conversely, if \(z\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\) and \(a\in Az\) with \(-a\in Bz\), then \(x=z+\lambda a\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) and \(J_{\lambda A}x=z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas--Rachford averages the identity with two reflected resolvents; fixed points yield solutions through the first resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Operator Splitting Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Douglas--Rachford fixed-point interface and shadow-solution implication are correctly scoped, and algorithm fits this terminal container. No authoritative source with a precise locator is cited, and statement_latex includes algorithmic justification rather than only the statement.

children.title: Resolvent Scaling Relations
children.top_down_role: Effects of operator and argument scaling on resolvent representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_{\lambda B}(x)=b^{-1}J_{\lambda abA}(bx),\qquad J_{\lambda(aA)}=J_{\lambda aA}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct change-of-variables identity in the resolvent inclusion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive input and output scaling of an operator and its resolvent parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in H\), the relation \(p=J_{\lambda B}x\) is equivalent to \(x-p\in\lambda aA(bp)\). Multiplication by \(b\) gives \(bx-bp\in\lambda abA(bp)\), hence \(bp=J_{\lambda abA}(bx)\). The displayed scaling formula follows whenever the relevant resolvents are single-valued; maximal monotonicity of \(A\) guarantees this everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling an operator's values rescales the resolvent parameter, while scaling its argument also conjugates the resolvent by the same coordinate dilation.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Scaling Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The input-output scaling formula is algebraically plausible and representation fits Resolvent Scaling Relations. The second displayed identity merely restates notation, the record has no source, and statement_latex contains a derivation.

children.title: Resolvent Inversion Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between an operator, its inverse, and their resolvents.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_{\lambda A}(x)+\lambda J_{\lambda^{-1}A^{-1}}(x/\lambda)=x\qquad(x\in H).\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical resolvent decomposition for an operator and its inverse
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-explicit resolvent inversion, also called the nonlinear Moreau decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Writing \(p=J_{\lambda A}x\) gives \((x-p)/\lambda\in Ap\), hence \(p\in A^{-1}((x-p)/\lambda)\). Therefore \((x-p)/\lambda=J_{\lambda^{-1}A^{-1}}(x/\lambda)\), which yields the decomposition. At \(\lambda=1\), it reduces to \(J_A+J_{A^{-1}}=I\), and consequently \(R_{A^{-1}}=-R_A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point decomposes into the resolvent of an operator plus a scaled resolvent of its inverse.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Inversion Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parameter-explicit resolvent decomposition is standard and duality fits Resolvent Inversion Relations. The record lacks an inspectable source citation and includes proof-style derivation in statement_latex.

children.title: Resolvent Parameter Relations
children.top_down_role: Comparisons across different positive resolvent parameters.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_{\lambda A}x=J_{\mu A}\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\lambda}x+\left(1-\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\right)J_{\lambda A}x\right).\]

notation.meaning: Identity mapping on the Hilbert space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard resolvent identity for maximally monotone operators on Hilbert space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-parameter identity relating two resolvents of the same operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\) and all \(\lambda,\mu>0\), the resolvents of \(A\) satisfy
\[J_{\lambda A}x=J_{\mu A}\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\lambda}x+\left(1-\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\right)J_{\lambda A}x\right).\]
No ordering between \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolvents at any two positive parameters are related by evaluating one resolvent at an affine combination of the point and the other resolvent value.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Parameter Relations

children.title: Degenerate Parameter Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limiting behavior near vanishing or unbounded parameter regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard resolvent calculus is restricted to \(\lambda>0\); assigning \(J_{0A}=I\) requires an additional zero-scaling convention, and negative parameters can destroy invertibility.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: boundary analysis of the resolvent definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention dependence at zero and possible failure of invertibility at negative parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard maximally monotone resolvent calculus uses \(\lambda>0\). At \(\lambda=0\), the expression \((I+0A)^{-1}\) is convention-dependent: if \(0A\) is declared to be the everywhere-defined zero operator, then \(J_{0A}=I\), which contains no information about \(A\); under literal pointwise scaling of a relation, \(0A\) retains the domain of \(A\), so the same conclusion need not hold. In either interpretation, the Yosida quotient \(\lambda^{-1}(I-J_{\lambda A})\) is undefined at \(\lambda=0\). For the maximally monotone operator \(A=I\), the negative parameter \(\lambda=-1\) gives \(I+\lambda A=0\), whose inverse is not an everywhere-defined single-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero is outside the standard positive-parameter calculus and requires an explicit scaling convention; negative parameters can destroy invertibility even for the identity operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Parameter Boundaries

children.title: Product-Space Resolvents
children.top_down_role: Resolvents of operators represented on Cartesian product spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a finite Hilbert product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_{\lambda(A_1\times\cdots\times A_m)}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=(J_{\lambda A_1}x_1,\ldots,J_{\lambda A_m}x_m).\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard componentwise resolvent formula on finite Hilbert products
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-product formula for an uncoupled Cartesian-product operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_m\) by \(A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=A_1x_1\times\cdots\times A_mx_m\). Then \(A\) is maximally monotone on \(H\), and its resolvent separates exactly by coordinates:
\[J_{\lambda A}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\bigl(J_{\lambda A_1}x_1,\ldots,J_{\lambda A_m}x_m\bigr).\]
Thus evaluating the product resolvent requires only the independent component resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a Cartesian product of maximally monotone operators is the Cartesian product of their component resolvents.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Resolvents

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-product representation is mathematically standard, introduces its objects, and fits Product-Space Resolvents. No cited source or inspectable locator supports the claim, so source review is required.

children.title: Block Resolvents
children.top_down_role: Resolvent structure induced by block operator representations.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a finite Hilbert product.
\(A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_m\), where each \(A_i:H_i\rightrightarrows H_i\) is maximally monotone.
\(M=\operatorname{diag}(M_1,\ldots,M_m)\), where each \(M_i:H_i\to H_i\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_A^M(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\bigl(J_{A_1}^{M_1}x_1,\ldots,J_{A_m}^{M_m}x_m\bigr).\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard block-diagonal variable-metric resolvent representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-diagonal metric resolvents for an uncoupled finite-product operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(J_A^M=(I+M^{-1}A)^{-1}\) and \(J_{A_i}^{M_i}=(I+M_i^{-1}A_i)^{-1}\). These mappings are everywhere defined and single-valued, and for every \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in H\),
\[J_A^M(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\bigl(J_{A_1}^{M_1}x_1,\ldots,J_{A_m}^{M_m}x_m\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an uncoupled finite-product operator and a strongly positive block-diagonal metric, the metric resolvent decomposes into the independent block metric resolvents.
knowledge_statements.title: Block Resolvents

children.title: Separable Component Structure
children.top_down_role: Componentwise behavior under separable product constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a finite Hilbert product.
\(A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_m\), where each \(A_i:H_i\rightrightarrows H_i\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}=\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{zer}A_1\times\cdots\times\operatorname{zer}A_m.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard zero-set and fixed-point separation for product operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate separation of membership, zeros, and resolvent fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in H\) and \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in H\),
\[u\in Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_i\in A_ix_i\ \text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.\]
The zero and fixed-point sets satisfy
\[\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}=\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{zer}A_1\times\cdots\times\operatorname{zer}A_m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite Cartesian-product operator, membership, zeros, and resolvent fixed points are determined independently in each component.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Component Structure

children.title: Block-Coupling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Effects of off-diagonal coupling on simple resolvent decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R^2\) with its Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_A=(I+A)^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\] and each output coordinate depends on both input coordinates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit finite-dimensional monotone linear counterexample
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A skew block coupling destroys componentwise resolvent separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(A(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,-x_1)\) is a full-domain maximally monotone skew linear operator on \(\mathbb R^2\). Its unit-parameter resolvent is
\[J_A=(I+A)^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\]
so
\[J_A(x_1,x_2)=\left(\frac{x_1-x_2}{2},\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right).\]
Thus a product-space ambient domain alone does not imply componentwise resolvent evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximally monotone skew coupling on two blocks has a nondiagonal resolvent, so an ambient product space alone does not provide componentwise evaluation.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Coupling Boundary

children.title: Average-Parallel Resolvent Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Averaging and parallel combinations represented through resolvents.

children.title: Resolvent Averages
children.top_down_role: Weighted combinations formed through resolvent representations.

assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_m:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal R_\mu(\boldsymbol A,\boldsymbol\lambda)=\frac1\mu\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iJ_{\mu A_i}\right)^{-1}-I\right).\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of the weighted resolvent average
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted finite-family resolvent average with a common positive scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The resolvent average of \(\boldsymbol A=(A_1,\ldots,A_m)\) with weights \(\boldsymbol\lambda\) and scale \(\mu\) is
\[\mathcal R_\mu(\boldsymbol A,\boldsymbol\lambda)=\frac1\mu\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iJ_{\mu A_i}\right)^{-1}-I\right).\]
Equivalently, it is the unique maximally monotone operator whose \(\mu\)-resolvent is
\[J_{\mu\mathcal R_\mu(\boldsymbol A,\boldsymbol\lambda)}=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iJ_{\mu A_i}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted resolvent average is the operator whose scaled resolvent equals the weighted arithmetic mean of the component resolvents.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Averages

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and equivalent resolvent characterization are consistent and appropriately classified as a definition. The record has no citation or specific locator, so it remains source-dependent candidate knowledge.

children.title: Parallel Constructions
children.top_down_role: Parallel operator combinations expressed through inversion and summation.

assumptions_latex: \(B_1,\ldots,B_m:H\rightrightarrows H\) are set-valued operators on a real vector space \(H\).
Indices with \(\lambda_i=0\) are omitted from the relation sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbin{\|}_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i,B_i):=\left(\sum_{i:\lambda_i>0}\lambda_iB_i^{-1}\right)^{-1}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted parallel composition of relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted parallel composition defined through inverse relations, with zero-weight indices omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I_+=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\lambda_i>0\}\). The weighted parallel construction of \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\) is
\[\mathbin{\|}_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i,B_i):=\left(\sum_{i\in I_+}\lambda_iB_i^{-1}\right)^{-1}.\]
Equivalently, for \(x,u\in H\),
\[u\in\mathbin{\|}_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i,B_i)(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{there exist }x_i\in B_i^{-1}u\ \text{for }i\in I_+\ \text{with }x=\sum_{i\in I_+}\lambda_ix_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted parallel construction averages the inverse relations over the positive-weight indices and then inverts the resulting relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Constructions

children.title: Average–Parallel Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relations between resolvent averaging and parallel combination structures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal R_\mu(\boldsymbol A,\boldsymbol\lambda)+\mu^{-1}I=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iB_i^{-1}\right)^{-1}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic correspondence between resolvent averages and weighted parallel constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shifted-operator form of the average-parallel correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(B_i=A_i+\mu^{-1}I\), the inverse relations satisfy
\[B_i^{-1}(z)=J_{\mu A_i}(\mu z)\qquad(z\in H).\]
The resolvent average and the weighted parallel construction are related by
\[\mathcal R_\mu(\boldsymbol A,\boldsymbol\lambda)+\mu^{-1}I=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iB_i^{-1}\right)^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the reciprocal-scale identity to the resolvent average gives the weighted parallel construction of the shifted operators, with the required argument scaling in each inverse relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Average–Parallel Correspondence

children.title: Weight Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundary behavior under zero, limiting, or singular weights.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Within the probability simplex, zero weights omit components and a unit weight selects one component; outside the simplex, negative weights can destroy the resolvent property.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simplex endpoint identities and explicit negative-weight counterexample
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint behavior within the probability simplex and failure when negative weights are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose first that \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\). If \(\lambda_k=0\), the term involving \(A_k\) is absent from \(T=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iJ_{\mu A_i}\). If \(\lambda_k=1\), then all other weights are zero, \(T=J_{\mu A_k}\), and the resolvent average equals \(A_k\). Nonnegativity cannot in general be dropped: for \(A_1=0\), \(A_2=N_{\{0\}}\), \(\lambda_1=-1\), and \(\lambda_2=2\), one has \(T=-I\), which is not firmly nonexpansive and hence is not the resolvent of a maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the probability simplex, zero weights omit components and a unit weight selects one operator; permitting negative weights can produce a mapping that is not a resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight Degeneracy Regimes

children.title: Yosida Regularity
children.top_down_role: Single-valuedness and continuity features of Yosida operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Yosida approximation \(A_\mu=\mu^{-1}(I-J_{\mu A})\) is everywhere defined, single-valued, monotone, \(\mu\)-cocoercive, and \(\mu^{-1}\)-Lipschitz.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Hilbert-space regularity of the Yosida approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global regularity of the Hilbert-space Yosida approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Yosida approximation \(A_\mu=\mu^{-1}(I-J_{\mu A})\) is an everywhere-defined single-valued mapping from \(H\) to \(H\). For all \(x,y\in H\),
\[\langle A_\mu x-A_\mu y,x-y\rangle\geq\mu\|A_\mu x-A_\mu y\|^2\]
and
\[\|A_\mu x-A_\mu y\|\leq\mu^{-1}\|x-y\|.\]
In particular, \(A_\mu\) is monotone, \(\mu\)-cocoercive, and \(\mu^{-1}\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Yosida approximation is globally single-valued, monotone, cocoercive with constant equal to its parameter, and Lipschitz with reciprocal parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Yosida Regularity

children.title: Graph Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation of the original monotone graph through regularized operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gra}A=\{(J_{\mu A}x,A_\mu x):x\in H\},\qquad x=J_{\mu A}x+\mu A_\mu x.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard resolvent parametrization of a maximal monotone graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph parametrization and its bounded-value small-parameter displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\mu>0\), the graph of \(A\) has the exact parametrization
\[\operatorname{gra}A=\{(J_{\mu A}x,A_\mu x):x\in H\},\]
with
\[x=J_{\mu A}x+\mu A_\mu x\quad\text{and}\quad A_\mu x\in A(J_{\mu A}x)\qquad(x\in H).\]
For a fixed \(x\in H\), if the family \(\{A_\mu x:0<\mu<\mu_0\}\) is bounded for some \(\mu_0>0\), then
\[J_{\mu A}x-x=-\mu A_\mu x\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\mu\downarrow0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive parameter, resolvent and Yosida values exactly parametrize the graph; for a fixed base point, bounded Yosida values force the resolvent displacement to vanish with the parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Approximation

children.title: Regularity–Fidelity Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Balance between improved regularity and representation of the original graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity–Fidelity Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space Yosida regularization: smaller parameters worsen the global Lipschitz bound while reducing graph-point displacement whenever the corresponding Yosida values remain bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,y\in H\), the Yosida approximation satisfies \(\|A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y\|\leq \lambda^{-1}\|x-y\|\). It also satisfies \[(J_{\lambda A}x,A_\lambda x)\in\operatorname{gra}A,\qquad x=J_{\lambda A}x+\lambda A_\lambda x.\] Thus its global Lipschitz bound scales as \(1/\lambda\), while the distance from \(x\) to the represented graph point is \(\lambda\|A_\lambda x\|\). In particular, this displacement vanishes along any parameter sequence for which \(\lambda\downarrow0\) and \(A_\lambda x\) remains bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Yosida approximation has Lipschitz bound 1/lambda and represents an exact value of the original operator at a point displaced by lambda times that value; the displacement vanishes when those values remain bounded as lambda tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_\lambda\) is single-valued and \(\lambda^{-1}\)-Lipschitz, while \((J_{\lambda A}x,A_\lambda x)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) and \(x-J_{\lambda A}x=\lambda A_\lambda x\).

notation.meaning: resolvent of the maximally monotone operator

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A=I\), one has \(J_{\lambda A}=(1+\lambda)^{-1}I\) and hence \[ A_\lambda=\frac{1}{1+\lambda}I. \] Consequently, \(A_\lambda x\to Ax\) as \(\lambda\downarrow0\), while \(A_\lambda x\to0\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\). The latter boundary therefore maximizes smoothing but generally destroys fidelity to \(A\); no assertion that large-parameter Yosida approximations recover the original operator is valid without additional rescaling or structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the identity operator, the Yosida approximation tends to the identity as lambda vanishes and to zero as lambda diverges, exposing the fidelity boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise preservation of solutions under resolvent and Yosida regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in H\), the following assertions are equivalent: \[A_\lambda x=0,\qquad J_{\lambda A}x=x,\qquad 0\in Ax.\] Therefore, for every \(\lambda>0\), replacing the inclusion \(0\in Ax\) by the regularized equation \(A_\lambda x=0\) neither creates nor removes a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point solves the original zero inclusion exactly when it is a resolvent fixed point and exactly when its Yosida value is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in H\), \(A_\lambda x=0\iff J_{\lambda A}x=x\iff0\in Ax\).

children.title: Penalization Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Use of regularized operators as penalty mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalization Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted representation of an inclusion penalized by a Yosida approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The penalized inclusion \(0\in Bx+\beta A_\lambda x\) is equivalent to the existence of \(y\in H\) and \(a\in Ay\) satisfying \[x=y+\lambda a,\qquad 0\in Bx+\beta a.\] Under this correspondence, \(y=J_{\lambda A}x\) and \(a=A_\lambda x\). Thus the Yosida penalty uses an exact graph value of \(A\), coupled to \(B\) at the displaced point \(x=y+\lambda a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Yosida-penalized inclusion has an exact lifted form using a graph point of the original operator and a displacement equal to lambda times its value.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, and \(B:H\rightrightarrows H\) is arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in Bx+\beta A_\lambda x\) if and only if there exist \(y\in H\) and \(a\in Ay\) with \(x=y+\lambda a\) and \(0\in Bx+\beta a\).

notation.meaning: resolvent graph point associated with x

children.title: Zero-Set Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between original and regularized zero sets.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}A_\lambda=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}=\operatorname{zer}A\).

notation.meaning: set of points whose operator value contains zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-level form of zero preservation for every positive regularization parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero and fixed-point sets coincide exactly: \[ \operatorname{zer}A_\lambda=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}=\operatorname{zer}A. \] This equality holds for every \(\lambda>0\), including when \(A\) is multivalued. In particular, the solution set is independent of the Yosida parameter even though the values, Lipschitz modulus, and graph displacement of \(A_\lambda\) vary with \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Yosida approximation, its resolvent fixed-point equation, and the original operator all have exactly the same solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Set Correspondence

children.title: Penalty-Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Qualitative behavior across weak, finite, and vanishing regularization scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Parameter Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter effects that hold identically, without asserting convergence of solutions of an additional penalized problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\beta>0\) and \(\lambda>0\), the weighted penalty \(P_{\beta,\lambda}=\beta A_\lambda\) obeys \[\operatorname{zer}P_{\beta,\lambda}=\operatorname{zer}A,\qquad \operatorname{Lip}(P_{\beta,\lambda})\leq\frac{\beta}{\lambda}.\] Its underlying exact graph point is \((J_{\lambda A}x,A_\lambda x)\), whose displacement from \(x\) is \(\lambda\|A_\lambda x\|\). Thus \(\beta\) scales the penalty values, while \(\lambda\) controls both the Lipschitz bound and graph displacement. Convergence under joint parameter limits requires additional assumptions on the surrounding inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The penalty weight scales the values and Lipschitz bound, while lambda also controls graph displacement; conclusions about joint parameter limits require assumptions on the surrounding problem.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone, and \(\lambda>0\), \(\beta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}P_{\beta,\lambda}=\operatorname{zer}A\), \(P_{\beta,\lambda}\) is \(\beta/\lambda\)-Lipschitz, and the displacement to its represented graph point is \(\lambda\|A_\lambda x\|\).

children.title: Vanishing-Regularization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic regimes as regularization changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Regularization Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong pointwise vanishing-parameter limit at points in the operator domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}A\), let \(A^0x=P_{Ax}0\). Then \[A_\lambda x\longrightarrow A^0x,\qquad J_{\lambda A}x=x-\lambda A_\lambda x\longrightarrow x\quad\text{as }\lambda\downarrow0.\] Moreover, \(\|A_\lambda x\|\leq\|A^0x\|\) for every \(\lambda>0\). The value convergence is restricted to \(x\in\operatorname{dom}A\); outside the domain, boundedness or convergence of \(A_\lambda x\) need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any domain point, vanishing Yosida regularization recovers the minimum-norm operator value, and the associated resolvent point converges to the original point.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
\(x\in\operatorname{dom}A\), and \(A^0x\) is the minimum-norm element of the nonempty closed convex set \(Ax\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\lambda\downarrow0\), \(J_{\lambda A}x\to x\) and \(A_\lambda x\to A^0x\) strongly.

notation.meaning: minimum-norm value of A at x
