children.title: Epsilon-Enlargement Family
children.top_down_role: Canonical approximate monotone graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\), and \(A:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^\varepsilon(x)=\{x^*\in X^*: \langle x-y,x^*-y^*\rangle\geq-\varepsilon\ \text{for all }(y,y^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\}\).

notation.meaning: duality pairing between X and its dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard additive-error enlargement of a monotone graph in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), the \(\varepsilon\)-enlargement of \(A\) is defined by \[ A^\varepsilon(x)=\left\{x^*\in X^*: \langle x-y,x^*-y^*\rangle\geq-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }(y,y^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\right\}. \] The family is nested: if \(0\leq\varepsilon_1\leq\varepsilon_2\), then \(A^{\varepsilon_1}(x)\subseteq A^{\varepsilon_2}(x)\). If \(A\) is maximally monotone, then \(A^0=A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-enlargement permits a monotonicity deficit of at most epsilon against every exact graph point; larger epsilon gives a larger approximate graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Enlargement Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, nesting property, and maximal-monotonicity identity are standard and the definition kind fits the family leaf, but no inspectable citation or standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Brøndsted–Rockafellar Approximation Principle
children.top_down_role: Approximation and graph-recovery organization.

children.title: Approximate-to-Exact Graph Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery relations between enlarged and exact graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \((\bar x,\bar x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) such that \(\|x-\bar x\|\leq\rho\) and \(\|x^*-\bar x^*\|\leq\varepsilon/\rho\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space Brøndsted–Rockafellar recovery with reciprocal primal and dual error scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\rho>0\), an enlarged graph point \((x,x^*)\) with \(x^*\in A^\varepsilon(x)\) admits an exact graph point \((\bar x,\bar x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) satisfying \[ \|x-\bar x\|\leq\rho,qquad \|x^*-\bar x^*\|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{\rho}. \] In particular, choosing \(\rho=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) for \(\varepsilon>0\) gives simultaneous primal and dual errors bounded by \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every enlarged graph point can be recovered by an exact graph point, with primal radius rho and reciprocal dual error epsilon divided by rho.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-to-Exact Graph Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the recovery leaf, but the exact reciprocal constants and stated generality require authoritative support. The statement also contains the malformed token `qquad`; no replacement is returned because source uncertainty controls the mathematical version.

children.title: Enlargement Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Operator classes distinguished by enlargement behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(A:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Non-enlargeability means \(A^\varepsilon=A\) for all \(\varepsilon\geq0\); Brøndsted–Rockafellar regularity means every enlarged point admits exact recovery with reciprocal error bounds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two distinct enlargement regimes: no enlargement and quantitative recovery from enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A\) is non-enlargeable when \[ \operatorname{gra}A^\varepsilon=\operatorname{gra}A\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon\geq0. \] It has the Brøndsted–Rockafellar enlargement property when, for every \(x^*\in A^\varepsilon(x)\) and every \(\rho>0\), there exists \((\bar x,\bar x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) such that \[ \|x-\bar x\|\leq\rho,qquad \|x^*-\bar x^*\|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{\rho}. \] Non-enlargeability is an exact rigidity condition, whereas the second condition permits enlargement but requires quantitative exact-graph recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-enlargeable operators admit no new enlarged points; Brøndsted–Rockafellar operators may enlarge but allow quantitative recovery by exact graph points.
knowledge_statements.title: Enlargement Regularity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is an appropriate kind for classifying enlargement regimes, but the Brøndsted–Rockafellar recovery property with these constants for the stated Banach-space setting is not supported by a source and may require additional geometric hypotheses.

children.title: Inexact-Proximal Certificate Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of enlargements as computational certificates.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is monotone, and \(z,x,v\in H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple \((x,v,\varepsilon,r)\) certifies an inexact proximal step, with \(z-r=x+\lambda v\) and an explicit monotonicity deficit at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable residual-plus-enlargement certificate for an inexact resolvent evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tuple \((x,v,\varepsilon,r)\) is an inexact proximal certificate for input \(z\) and parameter \(\lambda\) when \[ v\in A^\varepsilon(x),qquad r=x+\lambda v-z. \] Equivalently, the reported quantities satisfy \(z-r=x+\lambda v\) and, for every \((y,y^*)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), \[ \langle x-y,v-y^*\rangle\geq-\varepsilon. \] The norm \(\|r\|\) measures failure of the resolvent equation, while \(\varepsilon\) measures failure of exact graph membership; both are directly checkable from the declared certificate and the enlargement oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact proximal certificate separates equation residual from graph error: r measures the resolvent mismatch, while epsilon bounds the monotonicity deficit.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Proximal Certificate Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate fits the computational-interface leaf, but no source establishes that this exact tuple and residual convention is a recognized inexact-proximal certificate. The statement also contains the malformed token `qquad`.

children.title: Proximal Specialization
children.top_down_role: The subdifferential-resolvent specialization and its dual decomposition.

children.title: Proximal Maps as Resolvents
children.top_down_role: The proximal representation of subdifferential resolvents.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Maps as Resolvents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space proximal representation for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), the problem \[\min_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}\] has a unique minimizer \(p\), characterized by \[p=J_{\lambda\partial f}x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}.\] Consequently, \(J_{\lambda\partial f}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) on \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a convex subdifferential is exactly the proximal map, whose value is the unique minimizer of the quadratically regularized objective.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\lambda\partial f}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\), with \(p=J_{\lambda\partial f}x\iff p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in H}\{f(y)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|y-x\|^2\}\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of lambda times f

children.title: Moreau Decomposition Family

children.title: Primal–Dual Proximal Decomposition
children.top_down_role: The conjugate-pair specialization.

assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x)+\gamma\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma)=x\) for every \(x\in H\).

notation.meaning: Proximity operator of a scaled function

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical scaled Moreau decomposition for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled Hilbert-space Moreau identity for a Fenchel-conjugate pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), the primal proximal point \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x)\) and the dual proximal point \(d=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma)\) satisfy
\[
p+\gamma d=x.
\]
Equivalently, \(d=(x-p)/\gamma\), with \(d\in\partial f(p)\) and \(p\in\partial f^*(d)\). Thus the identity decomposes \(x\) into proximal components associated with the conjugate pair \(f\) and \(f^*\), using reciprocal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point splits into a proximal component for a convex function and a reciprocally scaled proximal component for its Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Proximal Decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled Moreau identity is mathematically standard and fits the duality container, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied. The plain statement also omits the subgradient equivalences asserted in the LaTeX statement.

children.title: Cone-Projection Specialization Pair
children.top_down_role: Polar and dual-cone specializations.

children.title: Cone Specializations
children.top_down_role: Moreau-type structures specialized to closed convex cones.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_K^*=\sigma_K=\delta_{K^\circ}\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma_K}=P_{K^\circ}\).

notation.meaning: Polar cone of K under the nonpositive-pairing convention

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard conjugacy of a cone indicator and its support function
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-indicator specialization under the nonpositive polar convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Fenchel conjugate of the cone indicator satisfies
\[
\delta_K^*(y)=\sigma_K(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\in K^\circ,\\+\infty,&y\notin K^\circ,
\end{cases}
\]
so \(\delta_K^*=\delta_{K^\circ}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_K}=P_K\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_K^*}=P_{K^\circ}\). Substitution into the unit-scale primal–dual proximal decomposition yields \(P_Kx+P_{K^\circ}x=x\) for every \(x\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex cone, the conjugate of its indicator is the indicator of its polar, so both proximal terms are projections.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone Specializations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cone-indicator conjugacy and projection specialization are correct under the stated nonpositive-polar convention and fit this container, but the record has no cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Projection Specializations
children.top_down_role: Proximal decompositions expressed through metric projections.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_C}=P_C\) and \(x=P_Cx+\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma_C}(x)\) for every \(x\in H\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard proximal characterization of metric projection and indicator-support conjugacy
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection form of Moreau decomposition for an arbitrary closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because minimizing \(\delta_C(z)+\tfrac12\lVert z-x\rVert^2\) is precisely the metric-projection problem, \(\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_C}(x)=P_Cx\). Since \(\delta_C^*=\sigma_C\), the unit-scale Moreau identity gives
\[
x=P_Cx+\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma_C}(x),
\]
for every \(x\in H\). The second component is therefore \(x-P_Cx\), but it need not be a projection onto a fixed set unless additional structure, such as conicity, is present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map of a closed convex set's indicator is its metric projection, and the complementary Moreau term is the proximal map of its support function.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Specializations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection specialization is mathematically correct, but it lacks a source and the statement contains proof-style justification beginning with the minimization argument.

children.title: Polar-Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Primal and polar cone roles in specialized decompositions.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=P_Kx+P_{K^\circ}x\) and \(\langle P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in H\).

notation.meaning: Metric projection onto a closed convex set S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Moreau decomposition theorem for mutually polar cones
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal decomposition by a cone and its nonpositive polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), let \(u=P_Kx\) and \(v=P_{K^\circ}x\). Then
\[
x=u+v,\qquad u\in K,\qquad v\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=0.
\]
Conversely, if \(u\in K\), \(v\in K^\circ\), \(x=u+v\), and \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\), then \(u=P_Kx\) and \(v=P_{K^\circ}x\). Hence membership, summation, and orthogonality characterize the polar-cone projection pair uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point decomposes uniquely into orthogonal projections onto a closed convex cone and its polar; the decomposition also characterizes both projections.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polar-cone projection characterization is correct and appropriate as a property, but no source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonconic Projection Boundary
children.top_down_role: Features that do not persist beyond cone-based projection settings.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\{1\}\), which is closed and convex but not a cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma_C}(x)=x-1\) whereas \(P_{C^\circ}(x)=\min\{x,0\}\), so the polar-projection formula fails.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing why polar projection requires conicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C=\{1\}\), one has \(P_Cx=1\), \(\sigma_C(y)=y\), and \(C^\circ=(-\infty,0]\). Direct minimization gives
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma_C}(x)=x-1,
\]
while \(P_{C^\circ}(x)=\min\{x,0\}\). These expressions disagree, for example at \(x=2\). The valid Moreau identity remains \(x=P_Cx+\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma_C}(x)\), but replacing the support-function proximal map by projection onto \(C^\circ\) is invalid for this nonconic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the singleton set containing one, the complementary support-function proximal term is not projection onto the polar, showing that conicity is essential.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconic Projection Boundary

children.title: Contractive Fixed-Point Regime
children.top_down_role: The contractive fixed-point regime.

children.title: Contractive Iteration Regime
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point iteration behavior under strict contraction.

assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) satisfies \(d(Tx,Ty)\le qd(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in X\), where \(0\le q<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is \(x^*\in X\) with \(Tx^*=x^*\), and \(d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach contraction theorem with Picard iteration and geometric error estimates.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Picard sequence converges to a fixed point \(x^*\) of \(T\). For every \(n\ge0\),
\[
d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*)
\]
and
\[
d(x_n,x^*)\le \frac{q^n}{1-q}d(x_1,x_0).
\]
Thus every initial point produces a convergent iteration, and the contraction factor supplies both an a priori geometric rate and a bound expressed through the first observed step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration of a contraction on a complete metric space converges from every starting point to its fixed point at a geometric rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Iteration Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed-point existence in an incomplete invariant metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=(0,1)\) with the Euclidean metric and let \(T(x)=x/2\). Then \(T:X\to X\) is a contraction with factor \(1/2\), but \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\). For every \(x_0\in X\),
\[x_n=2^{-n}x_0\]
converges to \(0\) only in the completion, not in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an incomplete space, a strict contraction can converge only to a missing boundary point and have no fixed point in the space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\), although \(x_n=2^{-n}x_0\to0\) in the completion.
knowledge_statements.title: Completeness Boundary for Contractive Iteration

children.title: Fixed-Point Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Uniqueness consequences of contractive geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness component of the Banach contraction principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A contraction \(T:X\to X\) with factor \(q<1\) has at most one fixed point:
\[
\lvert\operatorname{Fix}T\rvert\le 1.
\]
Completeness of \(X\) is not required for this uniqueness assertion; it is required by the full Banach contraction theorem to guarantee existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict contraction has at most one fixed point, and this uniqueness assertion does not require completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) satisfies \(d(Tx,Ty)\le qd(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in X\), where \(0\le q<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{x\in X:Tx=x\}\) contains at most one point.

children.title: Contraction-Factor Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of stability and convergence behavior on contraction strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Contraction-Factor Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of Picard convergence guarantees on the contraction factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*).
\]
If \(q\in(0,1)\) and \(0<\varepsilon<d(x_0,x^*)\), then the sufficient iteration count
\[
n\ge \left\lceil\frac{\log(d(x_0,x^*)/\varepsilon)}{-\log q}\right\rceil
\]
guarantees \(d(x_n,x^*)\le\varepsilon\). The guarantee worsens as \(q\) approaches \(1\); when \(q=0\), one iteration reaches the fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometric error and sufficient iteration count worsen as the contraction factor approaches one; a zero-factor map reaches its fixed point in one step.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) is a contraction with factor \(q\in[0,1)\) and fixed point \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*)\), so smaller \(q\) yields a uniformly sharper geometric guarantee.

children.title: Nonexpansive Endpoint Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of contractive conclusions at the limiting metric regime.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At Lipschitz factor \(q=1\), neither fixed-point existence nor uniqueness follows from nonexpansiveness alone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of Banach conclusions at Lipschitz factor one.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strict inequality \(q<1\) is essential. On any complete metric space \(X\) containing at least two points, the identity \(I_X\) is nonexpansive with factor \(1\) and every point is fixed, so uniqueness fails. On \(X=\mathbb R\), the translation \(T(x)=x+1\) is an isometry and hence nonexpansive with factor \(1\), but \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\), so existence fails. Thus completeness does not restore the Banach conclusions at the endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At Lipschitz factor one, the identity has many fixed points and a translation of the real line has none, despite completeness.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexpansive Endpoint Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Picard-Convergence Failure at the Nonexpansive Endpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unrelaxed Picard convergence despite existence and uniqueness of a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(X=\mathbb R\), let \(T(x)=-x\). Then \(T\) is an isometry, \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\), and for every \(x_0\ne0\),
\[x_n=T^nx_0=(-1)^nx_0.\]
Thus the Picard sequence does not converge even though the nonexpansive map has a unique fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At factor one, reflection has a unique fixed point but every nonzero Picard orbit oscillates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\), but \((x_n)\) does not converge.
knowledge_statements.title: Picard-Convergence Failure at the Nonexpansive Endpoint

children.title: Perturbation Error-Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Stability and computable certification consequences.

children.title: Perturbation Stability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of contractive fixed points to mapping perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform perturbation bound for fixed points of contractions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The fixed points satisfy
\[
d(x_T^*,x_S^*)\le\frac{\eta}{1-q}.
\]
Thus, under the uniform metric on mappings, the fixed point depends Lipschitz continuously on the contraction, with sensitivity modulus \((1-q)^{-1}\). This modulus diverges as \(q\uparrow1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly perturbing contractions by at most eta moves their fixed points by at most eta divided by one minus the common contraction factor.
assumptions_latex: \(T,S:X\to X\) are contractions with a common factor \(q\in[0,1)\), having fixed points \(x_T^*\) and \(x_S^*\).

notation.meaning: Fixed points of T and S

source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization
source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16

source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization
source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine scalar contractions attaining the perturbation modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q\in[0,1)\) and \(\eta>0\), define
\[
T(x)=qx,\qquad S(x)=qx+\eta
\]
on \(\mathbb R\). Both maps have contraction factor \(q\), \(\sup_x|T(x)-S(x)|=\eta\), and fixed points \(x_T^*=0\) and \(x_S^*=\eta/(1-q)\). Hence
\[
|x_T^*-x_S^*|=\frac{\eta}{1-q},
\]
so the uniform sensitivity modulus cannot be reduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel affine contractions attain the fixed-point perturbation bound exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of Contraction Perturbation Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation estimates using map disagreement only at the fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_T^*\) and \(x_S^*\) be the fixed points of contractions \(T\) and \(S\) with factors \(q_T,q_S<1\). Then
\[
d(x_T^*,x_S^*)\le
\min\left\{
\frac{d(Tx_S^*,Sx_S^*)}{1-q_T},
\frac{d(Sx_T^*,Tx_T^*)}{1-q_S}
\right\}.
\]
Consequently, if \(\sup_xd(Tx,Sx)\le\eta\), then
\[
d(x_T^*,x_S^*)\le\frac{\eta}{1-\min\{q_T,q_S\}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-point displacement can be bounded using map disagreement at either fixed point; unequal contraction factors yield a refined uniform estimate.
assumptions_latex: \(T,S:X\to X\) are contractions with factors \(q_T,q_S\in[0,1)\) and fixed points \(x_T^*,x_S^*\).

notation.meaning: Contraction factors of the two maps

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point-Localized Perturbation Bounds

children.title: Error Certificates
children.top_down_role: Computable indicators controlling distance to the fixed point.

knowledge_statements.title: Error Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori certificate allowing an inexact evaluation of the contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(y\) is an inexact evaluation of \(Tx\) satisfying \(d(y,Tx)\le\eta\), then
\[
d(x,x^*)\le\frac{d(x,y)+\eta}{1-q}.
\]
Consequently, the condition \(d(x,y)+\eta\le(1-q)\varepsilon\) certifies \(d(x,x^*)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate map evaluation and its known evaluation error give a computable upper bound on the distance to the contraction's fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) is a contraction with factor \(q\in[0,1)\) and fixed point \(x^*\).

source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization
source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16

source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization
source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of the universal coefficient in the inexact contraction certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The coefficient \((1-q)^{-1}\) in the inexact-evaluation certificate is best possible. Let \(X=\mathbb R\), \(T(t)=qt\), \(x>0\), and choose \(0\le\eta\le(1-q)x\) and \(y=qx+\eta\). Then \(x^*=0\), \(|y-Tx|=\eta\), and
\[|x-x^*|=\frac{|x-y|+\eta}{1-q}.\]
Thus no smaller universal coefficient can replace \((1-q)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar contraction with an admissible inexact evaluation attains the certificate bound, so its coefficient cannot be uniformly improved.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Inexact-Evaluation Certificate

children.title: Residual-Based Certification
children.top_down_role: Certification based on observable fixed-point residuals.

assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) is a contraction with factor \(q<1\) and fixed point \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-q)d(x,x^*)\le d(x,Tx)\le(1+q)d(x,x^*)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided equivalence between residual and fixed-point error for contractions.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\), the residual \(r(x)=d(x,Tx)\) and the fixed-point error satisfy
\[
(1-q)d(x,x^*)\le r(x)\le(1+q)d(x,x^*).
\]
Therefore
\[
d(x,x^*)\le\frac{r(x)}{1-q}.
\]
A stopping test \(r(x)\le(1-q)\varepsilon\) certifies \(d(x,x^*)\le\varepsilon\). Conversely, a small fixed-point error forces a proportionally small residual, making the residual quantitatively equivalent to the error throughout the contractive regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a contraction, the fixed-point residual is equivalent to distance from the unique fixed point and directly supplies a stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Based Certification

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16
source_witnesses.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar contractions attaining both sides of the residual estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let \(x^*=0\). For \(T_+(x)=qx\),
\[
|x-T_+(x)|=(1-q)|x-x^*|,
\]
whereas for \(T_-(x)=-qx\),
\[
|x-T_-(x)|=(1+q)|x-x^*|.
\]
Both maps have contraction factor \(q\in[0,1)\). Thus neither constant in the two-sided residual–error equivalence can be improved uniformly over contractions with factor \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar contractions with slopes q and minus q attain the lower and upper residual–error constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constants \(1-q\) and \(1+q\) in the residual–error estimate are uniformly sharp.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Residual–Error Equivalence Constants

children.title: Inexactness Accumulation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Qualitative effects of persistent, diminishing, or bounded perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete and \(T:X\to X\) satisfies \(d(Tx,Ty)\le qd(x,y)\) for some \(q\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q^{n-1-k}\varepsilon_k\); hence \(\varepsilon_n\to0\) implies \(x_n\to x^*\), while \(\sup_n\varepsilon_n\le\bar\varepsilon\) implies \(\limsup_n d(x_n,x^*)\le\bar\varepsilon/(1-q)\).

notation.meaning: Unique fixed point of the contraction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic additive errors in an inexact Banach contraction iteration.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.4 Fixed-point theorems p. 141
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Banach's theorem gives a unique \(x^*\in X\) with \(Tx^*=x^*\). The inexact iterates satisfy
\[
d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q^{n-1-k}\varepsilon_k.
\]
Consequently, vanishing errors imply convergence to \(x^*\). Uniformly bounded errors give
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}d(x_n,x^*)\le \frac{\bar\varepsilon}{1-q}
\]
whenever \(\varepsilon_n\le\bar\varepsilon\). In particular, summable errors also imply convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contraction errors are geometrically filtered: vanishing or summable errors preserve convergence, while uniformly bounded errors produce a computable asymptotic neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexactness Accumulation Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.4 Fixed-point theorems p. 141
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rates for additive evaluation errors that decay geometrically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\varepsilon_k\le C\rho^k\), where \(C\ge0\) and \(q,\rho\in(0,1)\), then
\[
d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*)+C\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q^{n-1-k}\rho^k.
\]
For \(q\ne\rho\), the sum equals \((q^n-\rho^n)/(q-\rho)\), so the error is \(O(\max\{q,\rho\}^n)\). For \(q=\rho\), it equals \(nq^{n-1}\), so the error is \(O(nq^n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometrically decaying evaluation errors preserve geometric convergence, with a polynomial factor when their decay factor equals the contraction factor.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete and \(T:X\to X\) is a contraction with factor \(q\in(0,1)\) and fixed point \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(x_n,x^*)\le q^n d(x_0,x^*)+C\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q^{n-1-k}\rho^k, with the stated closed forms and rates.

notation.meaning: Geometric decay factor of the inexactness

knowledge_statements.title: Geometrically Decaying Inexactness Rates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness and nonconvergence under persistent additive error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\mathbb R\), \(T(x)=qx\), where \(q\in[0,1)\), and
\[
x_{n+1}=qx_n+\bar\varepsilon,
\qquad \bar\varepsilon>0.
\]
Then \(x^*=0\), \(d(x_{n+1},Tx_n)=\bar\varepsilon\), and
\[
x_n=q^n x_0+\bar\varepsilon\frac{1-q^n}{1-q}
\longrightarrow\frac{\bar\varepsilon}{1-q}\ne x^*.
\]
Thus bounded errors need not yield convergence to the fixed point, and the asymptotic-neighborhood constant \((1-q)^{-1}\) is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant additive error can make the iterates converge to the boundary of the guaranteed error neighborhood instead of to the fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\to\bar\varepsilon/(1-q)\), so convergence to the fixed point fails and the bounded-error estimate is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Persistent-Error Neighborhood

children.title: Hilbert-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Nonexpansive fixed-point existence in inner-product spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex.
\(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive: \(\|Tx-Ty\|\le\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{x\in C:Tx=x\}\neq\varnothing\).

source_refs.locator: 2.1.4 Fixed-point theorems p. 141
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\). If \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive, meaning
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|\le \|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in C),
\]
then \(T\) has at least one fixed point:
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T:=\{x\in C:Tx=x\}\ne\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonexpansive self-map of a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a Hilbert space has a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space Regime

children.title: Uniformly Convex Regime
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point existence supported by uniform convexity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a uniformly convex Banach space and \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformly convex Banach-space form of the Browder–Göhde–Kirk theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a uniformly convex Banach space \(X\). If \(T:C\to C\) satisfies
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|\le\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in C),
\]
then there exists \(x^*\in C\) such that \(Tx^*=x^*\); equivalently, \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convexity guarantees a fixed point for every nonexpansive self-map of a nonempty closed bounded convex set.

children.title: Geometric Hypothesis Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparison of the geometric mechanisms available in the two regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space with \(\dim H\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_H(\varepsilon)=1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2/4}>0\) for \(0<\varepsilon\le2\); thus the Hilbert-space regime is a specialization of the uniformly convex regime.

notation.meaning: Modulus of convexity of a normed space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison through the Hilbert modulus of convexity and theorem specialization.

source_refs.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(0<\varepsilon\le2\), the Hilbert-space modulus of convexity is
\[
\delta_H(\varepsilon)=1-\sqrt{1-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}}>0.
\]
Hence every Hilbert space is uniformly convex. The Hilbert fixed-point theorem for nonexpansive mappings on nonempty closed bounded convex sets therefore follows as a specialization of the uniformly convex Browder–Göhde–Kirk regime; the latter applies to Banach spaces without requiring an inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hilbert spaces have an explicit positive convexity modulus, so their nonexpansive fixed-point theorem is a special case of the uniformly convex Banach-space result.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Hypothesis Comparison

children.title: Beyond-Uniform-Convexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limitations when the relevant convexity geometry is weakened.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex, and \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(X\) is not uniformly convex, \(T\) has a fixed point; therefore uniform convexity is sufficient but not necessary for the nonexpansive fixed-point property.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example showing that uniform convexity is not necessary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The space \((\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\) is not uniformly convex. Nevertheless, every nonempty closed bounded convex subset \(C\subset\mathbb R^2\) is compact, and every nonexpansive map \(T:C\to C\) is continuous. The finite-dimensional fixed-point theorem therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing.
\]
Thus uniform convexity is a sufficient geometric hypothesis for the Browder–Göhde–Kirk theorem, but it is not necessary for a Banach space to possess the nonexpansive fixed-point property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum-norm plane is not uniformly convex but still has the nonexpansive fixed-point property on closed bounded convex sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Beyond-Uniform-Convexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The finite-dimensional compactness mechanism showing uniform convexity is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex. Every nonexpansive map \(T:C\to C\) is continuous, and \(C\) is compact. Brouwer's fixed-point theorem in the affine hull of \(C\) therefore gives
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing.
\]
Hence every finite-dimensional normed space has the nonexpansive fixed-point property, whether or not its norm is uniformly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-dimensional normed space has the nonexpansive fixed-point property, including spaces whose norm is not uniformly convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Nonexpansive Fixed-Point Property

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Banach space \(X\) has the nonexpansive fixed-point property if, for every nonempty closed bounded convex set \(C\subset X\) and every mapping \(T:C\to C\) satisfying
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|\le\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in C),
\]
there exists \(x^*\in C\) with \(Tx^*=x^*\). Failure of this property means that at least one such pair \((C,T)\) has \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach space has the nonexpansive fixed-point property when every nonexpansive self-map of every nonempty closed bounded convex subset has a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Property Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of the Fixed-Point Property in Sequence Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-point-free nonexpansive map on a closed bounded convex subset of a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(X=\ell^1\), let
\[
C=\left\{x=(x_n)_{n\ge1}:x_n\ge0,\ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n=1\right\}
\]
and define
\[
S(x_1,x_2,\ldots)=(0,x_1,x_2,\ldots).
\]
The set \(C\) is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex, and \(S:C\to C\) is an isometry. A fixed point would have every coordinate equal to zero, contradicting \(\sum_nx_n=1\). Hence \(\ell^1\) lacks the nonexpansive fixed-point property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The right shift on the probability simplex of l1 is an isometric self-map without a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}S=\varnothing\), so \(\ell^1\) fails the nonexpansive fixed-point property.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of the Fixed-Point Property in Sequence Space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Fixed-Point Property and Reflexive Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between the weakly compact and bounded-set fixed-point properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Banach space \(X\) has the weak fixed-point property if every nonexpansive self-map of every nonempty weakly compact convex subset of \(X\) has a fixed point. The fixed-point property on all nonempty closed bounded convex subsets implies the weak fixed-point property. If \(X\) is reflexive, the two properties are equivalent because every closed bounded convex subset of \(X\) is weakly compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded-set fixed-point property implies its weakly compact version, and the two coincide in reflexive Banach spaces.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space; reflexivity is additionally assumed for the equivalence assertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{FPP}(X)\Rightarrow\mathrm{WFPP}(X)\), and reflexivity gives \(\mathrm{FPP}(X)\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{WFPP}(X)\).

notation.meaning: Nonexpansive fixed-point property on closed bounded convex sets
Nonexpansive fixed-point property on weakly compact convex sets

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Fixed-Point Property and Reflexive Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general geometric sufficient condition for nonexpansive fixed-point existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty weakly compact convex subset of a Banach space. Suppose \(C\) has normal structure: every convex subset \(D\subset C\) with \(\operatorname{diam}D>0\) contains \(z\in D\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{y\in D}\|z-y\|<\operatorname{diam}D.
\]
Then every nonexpansive mapping \(T:C\to C\) has a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak compactness together with normal structure guarantees a fixed point for every nonexpansive self-map.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, weakly compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Kirk Normal-Structure Fixed-Point Theorem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\ne\{0\}\) be a real Hilbert space, choose \(v\ne0\), and take the unbounded closed convex set \(C=H\). The translation \(T:C\to C\), defined by \(T(x)=x+v\), is an isometry because
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|=\|x-y\|.
\]
However, \(Tx=x\) would imply \(v=0\), so \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\). Thus boundedness is essential in the general nonexpansive existence theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\in H:\|x\|=1\}\), the unit sphere of a real Hilbert space with \(\dim H\ge2\). The set \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and bounded, but not convex. The antipodal map \(T:C\to C\), \(T(x)=-x\), satisfies
\[
\|Tx-Ty\|=\|x-y\|.
\]
It has no fixed point because \(-x=x\) implies \(x=0\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipodal isometry on a Hilbert-space unit sphere has no fixed point, showing that boundedness without convexity is insufficient.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take \(C=\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb R\) and define \(T(n)=n+1\). The set \(C\) is nonempty and closed, but it is both unbounded and nonconvex. Moreover,
\[
|T(m)-T(n)|=|m-n|\qquad(m,n\in C),
\]
so \(T\) is nonexpansive. Since \(n+1\ne n\) for every \(n\in\mathbb Z\), one has \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shift on the integers is an isometric fixed-point-free map on a closed set that is both unbounded and nonconvex.

Let \(D\) be a subset of a uniformly convex Banach space \(X\), and let \(T:D\to D\) be nonexpansive. If there exists a nonempty closed bounded convex subset \(K\subset D\) such that
\[

\]

\[
\operatorname{Fix}T\cap K\ne\varnothing.
\]

children.title: Averaged-Mapping Regime
children.top_down_role: The averaged and firmly nonexpansive specializations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space inequality equivalent to the convex-combination representation of an averaged map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). A mapping \(T:H\to H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged if and only if, for all \(x,y\in H\), \[\|Tx-Ty\|^2\leq\|x-y\|^2-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|(I-T)x-(I-T)y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alpha-averagedness is equivalent to a quantitative distance-decrease inequality involving the displacement map I minus T.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is }\alpha\text{-averaged}\iff \|Tx-Ty\|^2\leq\|x-y\|^2-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|(I-T)x-(I-T)y\|^2\quad(\forall x,y\in H).
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Inequality Characterization of Averagedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space inequality and complementary-map characterizations of the firmly nonexpansive specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T:H\to H\) on a real Hilbert space, the following are equivalent: \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive; \(\|Tx-Ty\|^2\leq\langle Tx-Ty,x-y\rangle\) for all \(x,y\in H\); and \(I-T\) is firmly nonexpansive. Consequently, every firmly nonexpansive map is nonexpansive and \(1\)-cocoercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Firm nonexpansiveness is equivalent to its standard inner-product inequality and is preserved by replacing T with I minus T.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is firmly nonexpansive}\iff \|Tx-Ty\|^2\leq\langle Tx-Ty,x-y\rangle\quad(\forall x,y\in H).
knowledge_statements.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness Characterizations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrelaxed Picard iteration of an averaged Hilbert-space mapping with a nonempty fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged, where \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). If \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\), then \(x_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|\to0\), and, for every \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), \[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\|x_n-Tx_n\|^2\leq\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\|x_0-z\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iteration of an averaged mapping with a fixed point converges weakly, is asymptotically regular, and has a square-summable residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T,\qquad \|x_n-Tx_n\|\to0.

notation.meaning: Fixed-point residual at the nth iterate

knowledge_statements.title: Picard Convergence for Averaged Mappings

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged exactly when \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\) for some nonexpansive \(R\); it is firmly nonexpansive exactly when it is \(1/2\)-averaged.

notation.meaning: Identity mapping on the Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of averaged mappings and the firmly nonexpansive specialization.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mapping \(T:H\to H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged if and only if there exists a nonexpansive mapping \(R:H\to H\) such that
\[
T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R.
\]
Equivalently, \((1-1/\alpha)I+(1/\alpha)T\) is nonexpansive. The firmly nonexpansive mappings are precisely the \(1/2\)-averaged mappings; equivalently, \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive if and only if \(2T-I\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged map is a convex combination of the identity and a nonexpansive map; firm nonexpansiveness is exactly one-half averaging.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaged-Mapping Regime

children.title: Under-Relaxed Regime
children.top_down_role: Conservative relaxation choices within the Krasnoselskii–Mann family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon residual guarantee for constant under-relaxed Krasnoselskii–Mann iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive with \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and let \(x_{n+1}=(1-\lambda)x_n+\lambda Tx_n\) for a constant \(0<\lambda<1\). Then, for every \(N\geq0\), \[\lambda(1-\lambda)\sum_{n=0}^{N}\|Tx_n-x_n\|^2\leq d(x_0,F)^2,\] and therefore \[\min_{0\leq n\leq N}\|Tx_n-x_n\|\leq\frac{d(x_0,F)}{\sqrt{(N+1)\lambda(1-\lambda)}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant under-relaxation gives a summable squared-residual estimate and an order-one-over-square-root-of-iterations best-residual guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\leq n\leq N}\|Tx_n-x_n\|\leq d(x_0,F)/\sqrt{(N+1)\lambda(1-\lambda)}\).

notation.meaning: distance from the initial point to the fixed-point set

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Under-Relaxation Residual Bound

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive, and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
\(x_0\in H\) and the constant relaxation satisfies \(0<\lambda<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unless a zero residual occurs finitely, the iterates \(x_{n+1}=(1-\lambda)x_n+\lambda Tx_n\) converge weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant under-relaxed Krasnoselskii–Mann iteration in Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in H\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), generate
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda(Tx_n-x_n)=(1-\lambda)x_n+\lambda Tx_n.
\]
At iteration \(n\), stop and output \(x_n\) if \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|=0\). Otherwise continue indefinitely and take the weak limit as the output. If \(T\) is nonexpansive and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), then \((x_n)\) converges weakly to some \(x^*\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant under-relaxation averages each iterate with its image; for a nonexpansive map with fixed points, the sequence converges weakly to one.
knowledge_statements.title: Under-Relaxed Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fejér decrease and cumulative residual control in the ordinary Krasnoselskii–Mann range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive, let \(p\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and set \(x^+=(1-\lambda)x+\lambda Tx\), where \(0<\lambda<1\). Then \[\|x^+-p\|^2\leq\|x-p\|^2-\lambda(1-\lambda)\|Tx-x\|^2.\] Hence variable standard-relaxation iterates satisfy \[\sum_{n=0}^{N}\lambda_n(1-\lambda_n)\|Tx_n-x_n\|^2\leq d(x_0,\operatorname{Fix}T)^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard relaxed nonexpansive step is Fejér decreasing and yields weighted cumulative residual control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{n=0}^{N}\lambda_n(1-\lambda_n)\|Tx_n-x_n\|^2\leq d(x_0,\operatorname{Fix}T)^2\).

children.title: Relaxation Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Transitions between stable relaxation ranges and unstable behavior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure at zero and negative relaxation, even for a firmly nonexpansive scalar mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\mathbb R\), let \(T=0\), which is firmly nonexpansive and has \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\). The relaxed map is \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)\operatorname{Id}\). At \(\lambda=0\), every initial point is stationary, so a nonzero orbit never approaches the fixed point. For \(\lambda<0\), \(|1-\lambda|>1\), and every nonzero orbit diverges in norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero relaxation can stagnate away from the fixed point, while negative relaxation can diverge, even for the scalar zero mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda=0\) permits stagnation away from \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), while \(\lambda<0\) permits divergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower Relaxation Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\lambda\) is averaged exactly within the general stability interval \(0<\lambda<1/\alpha\); the endpoint cannot guarantee Krasnoselskii–Mann convergence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sharp scalar example establishes the averaged-operator relaxation boundary
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp uniform relaxation boundary for the class of \(\alpha\)-averaged operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R\) with \(R\) nonexpansive, then \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\alpha R\), hence \(T_\lambda\) is averaged whenever \(0<\lambda<1/\alpha\). This interval is sharp uniformly over all \(\alpha\)-averaged mappings. Indeed, on \(H=\mathbb{R}\), choosing \(R=-\operatorname{Id}\) gives \(T=(1-2\alpha)\operatorname{Id}\); at \(\lambda=1/\alpha\), one has \(T_\lambda=-\operatorname{Id}\), whose iterates oscillate unless initialized at zero, while \(\lambda>1/\alpha\) yields an expansive scalar multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uniform stable range is below the reciprocal averagedness constant. At the endpoint, a reflected scalar example oscillates; beyond it, the relaxed map can be expansive.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Stability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform boundary and scalar counterexample are mathematically plausible and fit a failure-boundary leaf, but no citation supports the sharpness claim. The explanatory derivation should also be reduced to a declarative boundary statement when sourced.

children.title: Composition Common-Fixed-Point Calculus

children.title: Operator Compositions
children.top_down_role: Composed mappings arising within fixed-point iteration.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Modulus of an Ordered Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric closure law for finite ordered compositions of Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T_i:H\to H\) is \(L_i\)-Lipschitz for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), then \(T=T_m\circ\cdots\circ T_1\) satisfies \[\|Tx-Ty\|\leq\left(\prod_{i=1}^mL_i\right)\|x-y\|.\] In particular, a finite composition of nonexpansive mappings is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz constants multiply under ordered composition, so finite compositions preserve nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_m\circ\cdots\circ T_1\) is \(\prod_{i=1}^mL_i\)-Lipschitz.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz modulus of the ith component

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Modulus of an Ordered Composition

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=T_m\circ\cdots\circ T_1\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged for \(\alpha=\theta/(1+\theta)\), where \(\theta=\sum_i\alpha_i/(1-\alpha_i)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard closure bound for finite compositions of averaged operators
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averagedness closure and a valid parameter bound for finite operator compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_i:H\to H\) be \(\alpha_i\)-averaged for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(0<\alpha_i<1\). Define \(\theta=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_i/(1-\alpha_i)\) and \(\alpha=\theta/(1+\theta)\). Then the ordered composition \(T=T_m\circ\cdots\circ T_1\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and therefore nonexpansive. For \(m=2\), this bound becomes \(\alpha=(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2)/(1-\alpha_1\alpha_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite composition of averaged operators remains averaged, with an explicit averagedness parameter determined by the component parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator Compositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-composition averagedness parameter is standard and algebraically consistent, but this nontrivial closure property has no inspectable source.

children.title: Common Fixed-Point Structure
children.top_down_role: Shared fixed points of operator families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separate Fixed Points Need Not Be Common
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample distinguishing individual nonemptiness from common nonemptiness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\mathbb R\), let \(T_1x=0\) and \(T_2x=1\). Both mappings are firmly nonexpansive, with \(\operatorname{Fix}T_1=\{0\}\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}T_2=\{1\}\), but \[\operatorname{Fix}T_1\cap\operatorname{Fix}T_2=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two firmly nonexpansive mappings can each have a fixed point while having no common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T_1\neq\varnothing\), \(\operatorname{Fix}T_2\neq\varnothing\), but \(\operatorname{Fix}T_1\cap\operatorname{Fix}T_2=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Separate Fixed Points Need Not Be Common

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Geometry of Common Fixed Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of the common fixed-point set for a finite nonexpansive family on Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T_i:H\to H\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are nonexpansive on a real Hilbert space, then each \(\operatorname{Fix}T_i\) is closed and convex. Consequently, \[F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Fix}T_i\] is closed and convex, possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common fixed-point set of finitely many nonexpansive Hilbert-space mappings is closed and convex, though it may be empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Fix}T_i\) is closed and convex, possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Geometry of Common Fixed Points

assumptions_latex: \(T_i:H\to H\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) are mappings on a common Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common fixed-point set is \(F=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}T_i\).

notation.meaning: fixed-point set of the ith mapping

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common fixed points of a finite family of self-mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For mappings \(T_i:H\to H\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), their common fixed-point set is \[F=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}T_i=\{x\in H:T_i x=x\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,m\}.\] Thus \(F\neq\varnothing\) means that a single point is invariant under every member of the family; this is stronger than requiring each set \(\operatorname{Fix}T_i\) to be nonempty separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common fixed-point set consists of points fixed simultaneously by every operator in the family.
knowledge_statements.title: Common Fixed-Point Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise, notation is complete, and the definition content kind fits the leaf. A source with a specific locator is nevertheless required by the evidence contract.

children.title: Fixed-Point Preservation under Composition
children.top_down_role: Relations between component fixed points and fixed points of a composition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure without a Common Fixed Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of composition fixed-point preservation when the component family has no common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\mathbb R\), define \(T_1x=x+1\) and \(T_2x=x-1\). Each translation is averaged, since for every \(0<\alpha<1\) it can be written as \((1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R_i\) with a nonexpansive translation \(R_i\). Neither component has a fixed point, whereas \[T_2\circ T_1=\operatorname{Id},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(T_2\circ T_1)=\mathbb R.\] Thus the composition fixed-point set need not equal the common fixed-point set when the latter is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two averaged translations can have no common fixed point while their composition is the identity and fixes every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T_1\cap\operatorname{Fix}T_2=\varnothing\) but \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_2\circ T_1)=\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure without a Common Fixed Point

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_m\circ\cdots\circ T_1)=F\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality follows from averaged-operator descent with a common fixed point
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point equality for a finite composition having a nonempty common fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1,\ldots,T_m:H\to H\) be averaged operators and suppose \(F=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}T_i\neq\varnothing\). Then \[\operatorname{Fix}(T_m\circ\cdots\circ T_1)=F.\] In particular, composition introduces no additional fixed points under these hypotheses. The nonemptiness assumption is essential: without a common fixed point, the fixed-point set of a composition need not equal the intersection of the individual fixed-point sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For averaged operators sharing a fixed point, the fixed points of their ordered composition are exactly their common fixed points.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Preservation under Composition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-point equality is correctly scoped to averaged operators with a nonempty common fixed-point set and fits a theorem leaf, but it is a nontrivial result without a citation.

children.title: Perturbed Krasnoselskii–Mann Variants
children.top_down_role: Iterations affected by controlled evaluation or implementation errors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Errors Need Not Preserve Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary showing that pointwise error decay does not replace an accumulation-control condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\mathbb R\), let \(T=I\), \(\lambda_n=1/2\), and \(e_n=1/(n+1)\). Then the perturbed recurrence \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(Tx_n+e_n-x_n)\) gives \(x_n=x_0+\frac12\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(k+1)^{-1}\to+\infty\), although \(e_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additive errors may tend to zero yet accumulate and make the perturbed Krasnoselskii–Mann iterates diverge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_n\to0\) while \(x_n\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Errors Need Not Preserve Convergence

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed iterates converge weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), and their fixed-point residuals vanish.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard summably perturbed Krasnoselskii–Mann formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive, summably weighted errors in Hilbert-space Krasnoselskii–Mann iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in H\), relaxation parameters \(0<\lambda_n<1\), and errors \(e_n\in H\), compute \[x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(Tx_n+e_n-x_n).\] Stop when a prescribed residual or iteration criterion is met; otherwise output the weak limit when the infinite process converges. If \(T\) is nonexpansive, \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), \(\sum_n\lambda_n(1-\lambda_n)=+\infty\), and \(\sum_n\lambda_n\|e_n\|<+\infty\), then \(x_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(\|Tx_n-x_n\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perturbed iteration evaluates the operator with additive errors. Summable weighted errors preserve weak fixed-point convergence under the standard relaxation condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Krasnoselskii–Mann Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic variant fits the container, but its weak-convergence and residual conclusions require a specific inexact Krasnoselskii–Mann theorem supporting the weighted-error hypothesis.

children.title: Block Krasnoselskii–Mann Variants
children.top_down_role: Partial-coordinate or componentwise fixed-point updates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial Residual Is Not a Fixed-Point Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate boundary for deterministic partial-coordinate activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\), let \(T:H\to H\), and define \(r_I(x)=(T_i x-x_i)_{i\in I}\) for \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). If \(I=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), then \(r_I(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). For a proper subset this implication can fail: with \(H=\mathbb R^2\), \(T=0\), \(I=\{1\}\), and \(x=(0,1)\), one has \(r_I(x)=0\) but \(x\notin\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero residual on only the active coordinates does not certify a full fixed point unless all block equations are tested.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is the set of tested coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_I(x)=0\) need not imply \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) when \(I\) is a proper subset.

notation.meaning: Fixed-point residual restricted to the tested blocks

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Residual Is Not a Fixed-Point Certificate

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\), and \(T:H\to H\) has coordinate maps \(T_i\).
Each activation set \(I_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is nonempty, and every block is activated infinitely often.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only activated coordinates receive Krasnoselskii–Mann updates; convergence requires activation and operator hypotheses beyond the update rule itself.

notation.meaning: set of blocks activated at iteration n

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic block-coordinate update rule; no asynchronous delays are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0=(x_{1,0},\ldots,x_{m,0})\in H\). At iteration \(n\), select a nonempty activation set \(I_n\) and compute, for each \(i\), \[x_{i,n+1}=\begin{cases}x_{i,n}+\lambda_n\bigl(T_i x_n-x_{i,n}\bigr),&i\in I_n,\\x_{i,n},&i\notin I_n.\end{cases}\] Stop according to a prescribed residual or iteration criterion and output the current block vector. Convergence to a fixed point requires, in addition, suitable averagedness, relaxation, and coverage conditions, such as every block being activated infinitely often with uniformly bounded activation gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block variant updates selected coordinates toward their operator images while leaving inactive coordinates unchanged. Convergence needs suitable averagedness, relaxation, and block-coverage conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Block Krasnoselskii–Mann Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic block update is well defined and correctly classified as an algorithm. Its discussion of sufficient coverage and convergence conditions remains unsourced.

children.title: Randomized Krasnoselskii–Mann Variants
children.top_down_role: Randomly selected updates within the iteration family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling boundary separating marginal positivity from conditional or pathwise persistent activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R^2\), \(T=0\), \(x_0=(1,1)\), and \(\lambda_n=1/2\). Sample one uniform random index \(J\in\{1,2\}\) and activate only block \(J\) at every iteration. Each block has marginal activation probability \(1/2\) at every time, but almost surely the unselected coordinate remains equal to \(1\). Hence \(x_n\) does not converge to the unique fixed point \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive marginal activation probability at every time is insufficient when block selections are perfectly dependent across time.
assumptions_latex: One uniform index \(J\) is sampled once and used at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P[x_n\not\to0]=1\), although each block has marginal activation probability \(1/2\) at every iteration.

notation.meaning: Single random block selected for every iteration

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Activation Probabilities Are Insufficient

assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\), and \(T:H\to H\) has coordinate maps \(T_i\).
The random activation vectors \(\varepsilon_n\in\{0,1\}^m\setminus\{0\}\) activate every block with positive conditional probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is a stochastic block Krasnoselskii–Mann scheme; almost-sure convergence needs explicit averagedness, sampling, and relaxation assumptions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical randomized block Krasnoselskii–Mann update
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random block activation without delays or stochastic operator-evaluation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in H\). At iteration \(n\), sample \(\varepsilon_n=(\varepsilon_{1,n},\ldots,\varepsilon_{m,n})\in\{0,1\}^m\setminus\{0\}\) and set \[x_{i,n+1}=x_{i,n}+\varepsilon_{i,n}\lambda_n\bigl(T_i x_n-x_{i,n}\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Stop according to a prescribed residual or iteration budget and output \(x_n\). Almost-sure weak convergence to a fixed point is obtained only under additional conditions, typically averagedness of \(T\), admissible relaxations, adapted sampling, and a uniform positive lower bound on each block's conditional activation probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized variant samples active blocks and applies relaxed coordinate updates. Almost-sure convergence requires averagedness, admissible relaxation, and persistent positive activation probabilities.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Krasnoselskii–Mann Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The randomized block update is well defined and fits the algorithm container, but the stated typical conditions for almost-sure weak convergence need a specifically located stochastic fixed-point source.

children.title: Fejér Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Exact distance-control structure relative to a target set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness, reference-distance convergence, and convergence from a strong cluster point in the reference set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, and let \((x_n)\) be Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\). Then \((x_n)\) is bounded and, for every \(z\in C\), the sequence \(\|x_n-z\|\) converges. If a subsequence converges strongly to some \(\bar x\in C\), then \(x_n\to\bar x\) strongly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fejér sequence is bounded, has a limiting distance to every reference point, and converges strongly once it has a strong cluster point in the reference set.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, and \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_n)\) is bounded; every \(\|x_n-z\|\) with \(z\in C\) converges; a strong cluster point in \(C\) is the strong limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Consequences of Fejér Monotonicity

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\) exactly when \(\|x_{n+1}-z\|\leq\|x_n-z\|\) for every \(z\in C\) and every \(n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical definition of Fejer monotonicity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric Fejér monotonicity relative to a nonempty reference set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq0}\subseteq H\) is Fejér monotone with respect to a nonempty set \(C\subseteq H\) if \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|\leq\|x_n-z\|\qquad\text{for every }z\in C\text{ and every }n\geq0.\] Equivalently, for each \(z\in C\), the scalar sequence \((\|x_n-z\|)_{n\geq0}\) is nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence is Fejér monotone relative to a set when its distance to every point of that set never increases.
knowledge_statements.title: Fejér Monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the canonical Fejér-monotonicity definition and is internally consistent, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fejér monotonicity with respect to a set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General distance-monotonicity definition for a sequence relative to a target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence \(\{x^k\}_{k\geq0}\subseteq\mathbb E\) is Fej\'er monotone with respect to \(S\subseteq\mathbb E\) if
\[
\|x^{k+1}-y\|\leq\|x^k-y\|\qquad\text{for every }k\geq0\text{ and }y\in S.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence is Fejér monotone with respect to S when its distance to every point of S never increases from one iterate to the next.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x^k\}\text{ is Fej\'er monotone with respect to }S\iff\forall k\geq0\;\forall y\in S,\ \|x^{k+1}-y\|\leq\|x^k-y\|.
