children.title: Quasi-Fejér Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Distance-control structure accommodating summable perturbations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness, reference-distance convergence, and convergence from a strong cluster point in the reference set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, and suppose \((x_n)\) and a summable sequence \((\eta_n)\subset[0,+\infty)\) satisfy \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|^2\leq\|x_n-z\|^2+\eta_n\qquad\text{for every }z\in C.\] Then \((x_n)\) is bounded and, for every \(z\in C\), the limit \(\lim_n\|x_n-z\|\) exists. If a subsequence converges strongly to some \(\bar x\in C\), then \(x_n\to\bar x\) strongly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable quasi-Fejér errors preserve boundedness and convergence of all reference-point distances; a strong cluster point in the target set forces strong convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty.
\(\eta_n\geq0\), \(\sum_n\eta_n<\infty\), and the common squared-distance inequality holds for every \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_n)\) is bounded, every \(\|x_n-z\|\) converges, and any strong cluster point in \(C\) is the strong limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Consequences of Quasi-Fejér Monotonicity

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_n)\) is quasi-Fejér monotone when its squared-distance increases are bounded by a common summable nonnegative error sequence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard additive squared-distance definition of quasi-Fejer monotonicity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error quasi-Fejér monotonicity in squared-distance form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq0}\subseteq H\) is quasi-Fejér monotone with respect to a nonempty set \(C\subseteq H\) if there exists a sequence \((\eta_n)_{n\geq0}\subseteq[0,+\infty)\) satisfying \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\eta_n<+\infty\) such that \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|^2\leq\|x_n-z\|^2+\eta_n\qquad\text{for every }z\in C\text{ and every }n\geq0.\] Fejér monotonicity is recovered by taking \(\eta_n=0\) for all \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-Fejér monotonicity permits summable increases in squared distance to each reference point; zero errors recover ordinary Fejér monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Fejér Monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common summable squared-distance-error formulation is coherent, but quasi-Fejér definitions vary across sources as to squared versus unsquared distance and whether errors may depend on the reference point. A specific source is required.

children.title: Perturbation Tolerance Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits beyond which quasi-Fejér control no longer supports convergence analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Tolerance Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summability as a uniform sufficient threshold for bounded reference sets, with a nonsummable harmonic-drift failure example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and bounded, and suppose \(\delta_n\geq0\) and \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|\leq\|x_n-z\|+\delta_n\qquad\text{for every }z\in C\text{ and }n\geq0.\] If \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\delta_n<+\infty\), define \[D=\sup_{z\in C}\|x_0-z\|+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\delta_n\quad\text{and}\quad\eta_n=2D\delta_n+\delta_n^2.\] Then \(\sum_n\eta_n<+\infty\) and \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|^2\leq\|x_n-z\|^2+\eta_n\qquad\text{for every }z\in C\text{ and }n\geq0,\] so \((x_n)\) is quasi-Fejér monotone in the common-error squared-distance sense. Summability cannot be omitted as a uniform safeguard: for \(H=\mathbb{R}\), \(T=\operatorname{Id}\), \(C=\{0\}\), \(x_0=0\), and \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n+1/(n+1)\), the perturbations are nonsummable and \(x_n\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded reference set, summable additive distance perturbations produce a common summable squared-distance error and hence quasi-Fejér control. Without summability, harmonic errors can make an identity-map iteration diverge.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty and bounded.
\(\delta_n\geq0\) and \(\|x_{n+1}-z\|\leq\|x_n-z\|+\delta_n\) for every \(z\in C\) and every \(n\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\sum_n\delta_n<+\infty\), then a common summable sequence \((\eta_n)\) gives squared-distance quasi-Fejér control; nonsummable perturbations admit divergent examples even for \(T=\operatorname{Id}\).

notation.meaning: uniform distance bound determined by the initial point and total perturbation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded-reference-set correction for common squared-distance errors

children.title: Asymptotic Regularity
children.top_down_role: Vanishing-displacement mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Picard Displacements Do Not Imply Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that asymptotic regularity alone gives neither boundedness nor convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(T(t)=\log(e^t+1)\), let \(x_0=0\), and set \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\). Then \(x_n=\log(n+1)\), so \[|x_n-Tx_n|=|x_n-x_{n+1}|=\log\!\left(1+\frac1{n+1}\right)\to0,\] while \(x_n\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Picard orbit can have a vanishing fixed-point residual while diverging to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|x_n-Tx_n|\to0\) while \(x_n\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Picard Displacements Do Not Imply Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Regularity of Averaged Picard Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual decay and finite-iteration residual bound for an averaged fixed-point mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(0<\alpha<1\), suppose \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and set \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\). For every \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), \[\|x_{n+1}-z\|^2\leq\|x_n-z\|^2-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|x_n-Tx_n\|^2.\] Consequently, \(\sum_n\|x_n-Tx_n\|^2<\infty\), \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|\to0\), and for every \(N\geq0\), \[\min_{0\leq n\leq N}\|x_n-Tx_n\|\leq\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)(N+1)}}\,\operatorname{dist}(x_0,\operatorname{Fix}T).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iteration of an averaged mapping with a fixed point has square-summable residuals and an order-one-over-square-root-N best-iterate residual bound.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(0<\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_n\|x_n-Tx_n\|^2<\infty\), \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|\to0\), and the displayed \(O(N^{-1/2})\) best-iterate bound holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Regularity of Averaged Picard Iteration

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_n-Tx_n\rVert\to 0\).

notation.meaning: displacement residual of T at x_n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard fixed-point definition, but no supplied locator directly supports this formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses residual asymptotic regularity relative to a fixed-point operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) is asymptotically regular with respect to \(T\) if its fixed-point residual vanishes, that is,
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert x_n-Tx_n\rVert=0.\]
When the sequence is generated by the Picard rule \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\), this condition is equivalently
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert x_{n+1}-x_n\rVert=0.\]
This property concerns vanishing displacement and, by itself, does not assert convergence of \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence is asymptotically regular when its fixed-point residual tends to zero; for Picard iteration, successive iterates become arbitrarily close.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-based formulation is mathematically coherent and fits the vanishing-displacement container, but asymptotic regularity has multiple conventions and no citation supports this particular relative-to-T definition.

children.title: Opial-Demiclosedness Identification Principles
children.top_down_role: Weak cluster-point identification and sequential convergence.

children.title: Opial Lemma Family
children.top_down_role: Weak-limit uniqueness mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the target-set conclusion without membership of weak cluster points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(C=\{0\}\), and \(x_n=1\) for every \(n\). Then \(\lim_n\|x_n-z\|\) exists for every \(z\in C\), but \(x_n\rightharpoonup1\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence of every distance to the target does not force the weak limit to belong to that target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All distances to \(C\) converge, while the weak limit lies outside \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Point Membership Is Essential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of weak convergence when distances to target points need not converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(C=\{0,1\}\), and set \(x_{2n}=0\), \(x_{2n+1}=1\). Every weak sequential cluster point belongs to \(C\), but \(\|x_n\|\) does not converge and \((x_n)\) has no weak limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternation between two target points shows that cluster-point membership alone does not imply weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega_w(x_n)=C\), but \((x_n)\) does not converge weakly.

notation.meaning: set of weak sequential cluster points

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Limit Hypothesis Is Essential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space property underlying uniqueness of weak sequential limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Banach space \(X\) has Opial's property if every sequence \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) satisfies
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|x_n-x\|<\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|x_n-y\|\qquad(y\ne x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opial's property says that a weakly convergent sequence is asymptotically strictly closer to its weak limit than to any other fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_n\|x_n-x\|<\liminf_n\|x_n-y\|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Opial Property

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Squared-distance identity yielding strict Opial separation in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) in a Hilbert space \(H\), then for every \(y\ne x\),
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|x_n-y\|^2=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|x_n-x\|^2+\|x-y\|^2.\]
Consequently, every Hilbert space has Opial's property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hilbert-space squared-distance identity makes every competing point asymptotically farther away than the weak limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_n\|x_n-x\|<\liminf_n\|x_n-y\|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert Spaces Have Opial's Property

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space variant of the Opial weak-convergence lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a reflexive Banach space with Opial's property and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty. If \(\lim_n\|x_n-z\|\) exists for every \(z\in C\) and every weak sequential cluster point of \((x_n)\) belongs to \(C\), then \((x_n)\) converges weakly to a point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a reflexive Opial space, convergent distances to the target and membership of every weak cluster point imply whole-sequence weak convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is reflexive and has Opial's property.
Every weak sequential cluster point of \((x_n)\) belongs to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in C\) such that \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Reflexive Opial-Space Convergence Lemma

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty.
\((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\subset H\) is such that \(\lim_n\lVert x_n-z\rVert\) exists for every \(z\in C\).
Every weak sequential cluster point of \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) belongs to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in C\) such that \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\).

notation.meaning: set of weak sequential cluster points

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Hilbert-space Opial lemma formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space weak-convergence form commonly used with Fejer monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that for every \(z\in C\), the limit \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert x_n-z\rVert\) exists, and that every weakly convergent subsequence of \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) has its weak limit in \(C\). Then there exists a unique \(\bar x\in C\) that can occur as a weak sequential cluster point, and the entire sequence converges weakly to it:
\[x_n\rightharpoonup \bar x.\]
In particular, the distance-limit property supplies uniqueness of weak cluster points, while membership of all such points in \(C\) identifies the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all distances to a target set converge and every weak cluster point lies in that set, the entire sequence converges weakly to one point there.
knowledge_statements.title: Opial Lemma Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard Hilbert-space Opial lemma formulation with sufficient hypotheses, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Demiclosedness Principle
children.top_down_role: Residual-based identification of weak cluster points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Continuity Does Not Ensure Demiclosedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional failure of weak-limit fixed-point identification without a demiclosedness-producing hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \((e_n)\) be an orthonormal sequence, and fix a unit vector \(v\in H\). Define
\[T(x)=x+(1-\|x\|)_+v.\]
Then \(T:H\to H\) is norm-continuous, \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\), and \(e_n-Te_n=0\) for every \(n\), but \(T0=v\ne0\). Thus norm continuity alone does not make \(\operatorname{Id}-T\) demiclosed at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-continuous map can have fixed points converging weakly to a nonfixed point, so continuity alone does not imply the demiclosedness principle.
assumptions_latex: \((e_n)\) is orthonormal and \(v\in H\) is a unit vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) and \(e_n-Te_n\to0\), whereas \(0-T0=-v\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Continuity Does Not Ensure Demiclosedness

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), equivalently \(Tx=x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical demiclosedness principle for nonexpansive mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Hilbert-space demiclosedness of the residual at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonexpansive mapping \(T:C\to C\), the residual operator \(\operatorname{Id}-T\) is demiclosed at zero: whenever \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\subset C\), \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), and
\[\lVert x_n-Tx_n\rVert\to 0,\]
then \(x\in C\) and
\[x-Tx=0.\]
Consequently, every weak cluster point along which the fixed-point residual converges strongly to zero belongs to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonexpansive map, a weak limit of points whose residuals vanish is a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Demiclosedness Principle

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical demiclosedness statement is precise and correctly placed, but it has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Weak-versus-Strong Convergence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Infinite-dimensional limitations on convergence upgrades.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact additional condition upgrading weak convergence to norm convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a sequence \((x_n)\) in a Hilbert space \(H\) and \(x\in H\),
\[x_n\to x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_n\rightharpoonup x\ \text{ and }\ \|x_n\|\to\|x\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Hilbert space, weak convergence upgrades to strong convergence exactly when the norms also converge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\to x\) if and only if \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) and \(\|x_n\|\to\|x\|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Radon–Riesz Upgrade in Hilbert Space
Weak-versus-Strong Convergence Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical infinite-dimensional obstruction to upgrading weak convergence to norm convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((e_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be an orthonormal sequence in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space \(H\). Then
\[e_n\rightharpoonup 0,\]
whereas
\[\lVert e_n\rVert=1\quad\text{for every }n.\]
Thus \((e_n)_{n\geq 1}\) does not converge strongly to zero. Weak convergence of a bounded sequence in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space therefore does not, by itself, imply strong convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal sequence converges weakly to zero but remains norm one, so weak convergence alone does not imply strong convergence in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_n\rightharpoonup 0\) but \(e_n\not\to 0\) in norm.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical Hilbert-space counterexample to weak-to-strong upgrading

children.title: Single-Operator Zero Problems
children.top_down_role: Zeros of monotone and maximal monotone operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Find \(\bar x\in H\) satisfying \(0\in A\bar x\), equivalently \(\bar x\in\operatorname{zer}A\).

notation.meaning: set-valued operator from H to subsets of H

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The basic zero problem for a single monotone operator.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The single-operator zero problem associated with \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is to find \(\bar x\in H\) such that
\[0\in A\bar x.\]
Its solution set is
\[\operatorname{zer}A=\{x\in H\mid 0\in Ax\}.\]
If \(A\) is maximal monotone, maximality concerns the graph of \(A\) and does not itself guarantee that \(\operatorname{zer}A\) is nonempty; solvability is the separate condition \(\operatorname{zer}A\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-operator zero problem seeks a point whose operator value contains zero; maximal monotonicity alone does not guarantee existence.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Operator Zero Problems

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Two-Operator Sum Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Inclusions formed from two separately accessible operator components.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Find \(\bar x\in H\) such that \(0\in A\bar x+B\bar x\).

notation.meaning: pointwise Minkowski sum of A and B
zero set of the sum operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sum inclusion for two monotone components.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in H\), define the pointwise sum by
\[(A+B)x=\{a+b\mid a\in Ax,\ b\in Bx\}.\]
The two-operator sum inclusion is the problem of finding \(\bar x\in H\) satisfying
\[0\in A\bar x+B\bar x,\]
equivalently, finding \(a\in A\bar x\) and \(b\in B\bar x\) with \(a+b=0\). Its solution set is \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). Monotonicity of both components implies monotonicity of their sum, although maximal monotonicity of the sum can require an additional qualification condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-operator sum inclusion seeks a point with selections from two monotone values that cancel each other.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Operator Sum Inclusions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Multi-Operator Sum Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Finite sums involving three or more operator components.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m\geq 2\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Find \(\bar x\in H\) such that \(0\in\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i\bar x\).

notation.meaning: pointwise Minkowski sum of the component values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-arity pointwise sum of monotone operators on one Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(x\in H\), the finite pointwise sum is
\[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i\right)x=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_i\mathrel{\middle|}a_i\in A_i x\text{ for every }i\right\}.\]
The multi-operator sum inclusion asks for \(\bar x\in H\) such that
\[0\in\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i\bar x.\]
Equivalently, there must exist selections \(a_i\in A_i\bar x\) whose sum is zero. The associated solution set is \(\operatorname{zer}(\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite multi-operator inclusion seeks a common argument at which one value from each monotone component can be selected to sum to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Operator Sum Inclusions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Component Accessibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem organization by available evaluations, resolvents, or block access.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) are monotone.
For each component, the algorithm is granted either a resolvent oracle or a single-valued evaluation oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each component is classified by which oracle \(J_{\gamma A_i}\) or \(A_i\) is available.

notation.meaning: resolvent of A_i with parameter gamma

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard splitting-oracle distinction, but the intended taxonomy may require a narrower accessibility classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-level distinction between backward and forward access to components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A component \(A_i\) is backward accessible when, for every requested \(\gamma>0\) and query \(x\in H\), an oracle returns
\[J_{\gamma A_i}x=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A_i)^{-1}x.\]
It is forward accessible when \(A_i\) is single-valued on the queried domain and an oracle returns \(A_i x\). A sum-inclusion model has componentwise accessibility when each \(A_i\) is assigned at least one of these regimes. Convergence of a forward use generally requires additional regularity, such as Lipschitz continuity or cocoercivity, whereas resolvent access is naturally associated with maximal monotone components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component is accessed backward through its resolvent or forward through direct evaluation; forward use typically needs additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Component Accessibility Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward/backward oracle distinction is coherent and the condition content kind fits, but no source establishes that these two regimes exhaust the intended local accessibility classification or supports the associated regularity claims.

children.title: Composite Linear-Coupling Inclusion Family
children.top_down_role: Composite, adjoint-coupled, and block models.

children.title: Composite Monotone Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Inclusions containing operator compositions with mappings between spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(L:H\to G\) is bounded linear and \(r\in G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Find \(\bar x\in H\) such that \(0\in A\bar x+L^*B(L\bar x-r)\).

notation.meaning: set-valued composition through the affine map

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard composite monotone inclusion template
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single linear composition with an adjoint pullback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The composite monotone inclusion determined by \(A\), \(B\), \(L\), and \(r\) is
\[0\in A\bar x+L^*B(L\bar x-r).\]
Thus \(\bar x\in H\) is a solution precisely when there exist \(a\in A\bar x\) and \(b\in B(L\bar x-r)\) such that
\[a+L^*b=0.\]
The expression \(L^*B(L\cdot-r)\) denotes an adjoint pullback of a set-valued operator; it is not ordinary scalar composition. Additional hypotheses may be needed for this composite operator or its sum with \(A\) to be maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite inclusion balances a monotone value in the primal space with the adjoint pullback of a monotone value after linear transformation.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Monotone Inclusions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composite inclusion and selection-based interpretation are mathematically coherent and correctly placed, but no inspectable source is supplied for this template.

children.title: Linearly Coupled Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Inclusions linked through linear operators and adjoint couplings.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) and \(G\) are real Hilbert spaces, and \(L:H\to G\) is bounded linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled system is equivalent to \(0\in Ax+L^*B(Lx-r)\).

notation.meaning: coupling variable in the range space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard primal-dual lifting of a linearly composite inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-space lifting of a linear-composite monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((x,v)\in H\times G\), consider the linearly coupled system
\[0\in Ax+L^*v,\qquad 0\in B^{-1}v-Lx+r.\]
The second inclusion is equivalent to \(v\in B(Lx-r)\). Consequently, every solution \((x,v)\) yields
\[0\in Ax+L^*B(Lx-r).\]
Conversely, if \(x\) solves this composite inclusion, then any \(v\in B(Lx-r)\) satisfying \(-L^*v\in Ax\) makes \((x,v)\) a solution of the coupled system. This representation exposes the linear interaction through \(L\) and \(L^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite inclusion can be lifted to two coupled inclusions by introducing a range-space variable linked through a linear operator and its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearly Coupled Inclusions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted system and its existential equivalence with the composite inclusion are correct, and representation is the appropriate content kind, but no source is cited.

children.title: Block-Coupled Inclusion Models
children.top_down_role: Structured systems organized into interacting operator blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Coupled Inclusion Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite product-space model with multiple primal and coupling blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p,m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}\). A finite block-coupled inclusion model seeks \((\bar x_j)_{j=1}^{p}\in H_1\times\cdots\times H_p\) such that, for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\),
\[0\in A_j\bar x_j+\sum_{i=1}^{m}L_{ij}^*B_i\left(\sum_{k=1}^{p}L_{ik}\bar x_k-r_i\right).\]
Here each \(A_j\) acts on the primal block \(H_j\), each \(B_i\) acts on the coupling block \(G_i\), and \(L_{ij}^*\) maps the corresponding coupling values back to \(H_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite block-coupled model seeks finitely many primal variables satisfying simultaneous inclusions formed by linear block combinations, monotone coupling operators, and adjoint pullbacks.
assumptions_latex: \(H_j\) for \(j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and \(G_i\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) are real Hilbert spaces.
\(L_{ij}:H_j\to G_i\) are bounded linear and \(r_i\in G_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Find \((\bar x_j)_{j=1}^{p}\in H_1\times\cdots\times H_p\) satisfying all \(p\) displayed block inclusions.

notation.meaning: bounded linear map from primal block j to coupling block i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: representative finite block-coupled monotone inclusion model

children.title: Primal–Dual Inclusion Systems
children.top_down_role: Coupled primal and dual zeros in product spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Inclusion Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite product-space primal-dual representation with linear couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}\). The primal-dual inclusion system is to find \(x\in H\) and \(v_i\in G_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that
\[z-\sum_{i=1}^{m}L_i^*v_i\in Ax,\qquad v_i\in B_i(L_i x-r_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
Eliminating the variables \((v_i)_{i=1}^{m}\) yields the primal inclusion
\[0\in Ax+\sum_{i=1}^{m}L_i^*B_i(L_i x-r_i)-z.\]
Equivalently, the dual compatibility inclusions can be written as
\[L_i x-r_i\in B_i^{-1}v_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual variables satisfy coupled inclusions whose elimination recovers the zero problem for the shifted composite operator.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) and \(G_i\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) are real Hilbert spaces.
\(L_i:H\to G_i\) are bounded linear, \(r_i\in G_i\), and \(z\in H\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, and let \(\lambda>0\). The resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is single-valued on \(H\), and for every \(x\in H\), \[0\in Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in x+\lambda Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J_{\lambda A}x=x.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zeros of a maximally monotone operator are exactly the fixed points of any positive-parameter resolvent.

children.title: Convex Optimization Formulations

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimization problem is \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\), with solution set \(\operatorname{Argmin}f\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Constrained Optimization and Equilibria p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Banach space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. The associated convex optimization problem is \[\inf_{x\in X}f(x).\] Its solution set is \[\operatorname{Argmin}f=\{\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f:f(\bar x)\le f(x)\ \text{for every }x\in X\},\] where \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in X:f(x)<+\infty\}\). If \(C\subset X\) is a nonempty closed convex set, define its indicator by \(\iota_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\iota_C(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin C\). Minimization over \(C\) is then represented by minimizing \(f+\iota_C\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a proper lower-semicontinuous convex extended-real function; a nonempty closed convex constraint set can be represented by adding its explicitly defined indicator function.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Optimization Formulations

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\in C\times D\) is a saddle point of \(L\) when \[L(\bar x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y)\le L(x,\bar y)\qquad\text{for all }(x,y)\in C\times D.\] With the convex-analytic convention \(-\partial_yL=\partial_y(-L)\), this is equivalently encoded by the primal–dual inclusion \[0\in \bigl(\partial_xL(\bar x,\bar y),-\partial_yL(\bar x,\bar y)\bigr)+N_{C\times D}(\bar x,\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex–concave saddle point is encoded as a zero of its signed primal–dual subdifferential plus the product constraint normal cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real reflexive Banach space and let \(A:X\to X^*\) be monotone, hemicontinuous, and bounded on bounded sets. Assume that \(A\) is coercive in the sense that \[\frac{\langle Ax,x\rangle}{\|x\|}\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad\text{as }\|x\|\to\infty.\] Then \(A\) is surjective: for every \(f\in X^*\), there exists \(x\in X\) such that \(Ax=f\). Equivalently, \(A(X)=X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coercive, hemicontinuous monotone operator on a reflexive Banach space attains every dual-space value.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(A(x)=\arctan x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(A\) is continuous and strictly monotone, it is not surjective because coercivity fails.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample showing that monotonicity and continuity do not replace coercivity.

source_refs.locator: III.2 Noncoercive Operators p. 87
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), defined by \(A(x)=\arctan x\), is continuous and strictly monotone, but \(A(\mathbb R)=(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\). Its normalized radial pairing satisfies \(A(x)x/|x|\to\pi/2\) as \(|x|\to\infty\), rather than tending to \(+\infty\). Thus \(A\) is noncoercive and is not surjective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arctangent map is continuous and strictly monotone but noncoercive, and its bounded range prevents global surjectivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncoercive Existence Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: III.2 Noncoercive Operators p. 87
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Unbounded-Domain Surjectivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Surjectivity failures associated with uncontrolled domain geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous strictly monotone map \(A\) is not surjective on its unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded-domain example showing that domain size alone does not imply surjectivity.

source_refs.locator: III.2 Noncoercive Operators p. 87
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(A(x)=e^x\) is continuous and strictly monotone on the unbounded domain \(\mathbb R\). Nevertheless, \(A(\mathbb R)=(0,+\infty)\), so \(A(x)=f\) has no solution for \(f\le0\). The missing negative-direction growth is decisive: as \(x\to-\infty\), one has \(A(x)x/|x|=-e^x\to0\), and the coercivity condition required for global Browder–Minty surjectivity fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded domain does not guarantee surjectivity: the exponential map is strictly monotone but reaches only positive values.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Domain Surjectivity Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: III.2 Noncoercive Operators p. 87
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Growth-Control Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Combined regimes where inadequate growth prevents range coverage.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sublinear saturation prevents coercivity and restricts \(\operatorname{ran}A\) to \((-1,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saturating growth as a concrete failure regime for global range conclusions.

source_refs.locator: III.2 Noncoercive Operators p. 87
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(A(x)=x/(1+|x|)\) is continuous and strictly monotone, but \(\operatorname{ran}A=(-1,1)\). Its normalized radial pairing satisfies \[\frac{A(x)x}{|x|}=\frac{|x|}{1+|x|}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{as }|x|\to\infty,\] so coercivity fails. Thus bounded or saturating growth can destroy global surjectivity even when continuity and strict monotonicity remain intact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saturating monotone operator has bounded range; without coercive growth, global surjectivity can fail despite continuity and strict monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Growth-Control Failure Regimes

children.title: Domain Qualification Geometry
children.top_down_role: Domain-intersection regimes supporting maximality.

children.title: Interior Qualification Regime
children.top_down_role: Domain-intersection geometry expressed through interior conditions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise sum \(A+B\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical reflexive-Banach-space interior qualification for the maximal-monotone sum theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \((A+B)(x)=\{a^*+b^*:a^*\in A(x),\ b^*\in B(x)\}\). If the domain of one operator meets the norm-topological interior of the other's domain, namely \(\operatorname{dom}A\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}B)\ne\varnothing\), then the Rockafellar sum conclusion holds: \(A+B\) is maximal monotone on \(X\). By symmetry, the analogous condition with \(A\) and \(B\) interchanged is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two maximal monotone operators have a maximal monotone sum when one domain meets the norm interior of the other domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Qualification Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reflexive-Banach-space interior qualification is a standard Rockafellar sum theorem variant and the theorem kind fits the leaf, but no source record or inspectable theorem-level locator is supplied. An authoritative citation identifying the exact Banach-space formulation is required.

children.title: Core Qualification Regime
children.top_down_role: Algebraic interior geometry supporting maximality of sums.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The core qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{core}(\operatorname{dom}A-\operatorname{dom}B)\).

notation.meaning: algebraic interior in the ambient vector space
Minkowski difference of the two domains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic core qualification, stated independently of any particular sum-theorem variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{dom}A-\operatorname{dom}B\). The core qualification holds precisely when \[0\in\operatorname{core}D,\] meaning that for every \(h\in X\) there exists \(\varepsilon_h>0\) such that \(th\in D\) whenever \(|t|<\varepsilon_h\). Equivalently, every ambient direction can be followed locally from the origin while remaining in the domain difference. Additional topological hypotheses may be required before this algebraic condition implies maximality of \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The core qualification requires the origin to be an algebraic interior point of the difference of the two operator domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Core Qualification Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed predicate is a recognizable algebraic-core qualification and the condition kind fits the leaf. However, conventions for the core and the additional hypotheses under which this predicate supports a maximal-monotone sum theorem vary. No source or exact variant locator is supplied.

children.title: Domain Qualification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Broader domain compatibility conditions for maximal-monotone sums.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interior and core qualifications are predicates on \(D=\operatorname{dom}A-\operatorname{dom}B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common domain-difference representation of standard maximal-monotone sum qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(D=\operatorname{dom}A-\operatorname{dom}B\). The usual interior qualification can be written as \[0\in\operatorname{int}D,\] and the algebraic variant as \[0\in\operatorname{core}D.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{dom}A\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}B)\ne\varnothing\) implies \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}A-\operatorname{dom}B)\). These predicates isolate domain geometry from monotonicity; the precise sum theorem determines which predicate, together with which closure or ambient-space assumptions, suffices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard sum qualifications can be expressed by requiring the origin to lie in the interior or algebraic core of the domain difference.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Qualification Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domain-difference representation and the stated implication from domain intersection to interior of the difference are plausible and locally relevant. Nevertheless, the phrase 'usual interior qualification' can refer to distinct sum-theorem formulations with different closure and ambient-space hypotheses, and no authoritative locator is supplied.

children.title: Qualification-Regime Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relative scope and strength of domain-intersection criteria.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}D	subseteq\operatorname{core}D\), while the reverse inclusion need not hold.

notation.meaning: algebraic interior in the ambient space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of topological-interior and algebraic-core domain qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every norm-interior point of \(D\) is an algebraic-core point, so \[\operatorname{int}D	subseteq\operatorname{core}D.\] Hence an interior qualification implies the corresponding core qualification. The converse can fail in infinite-dimensional spaces: if \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is a discontinuous linear functional and \(D=\{x	ext{:}|f(x)|	le1\}\), then \(0\in\operatorname{core}D\) but \(\operatorname{int}D=\varnothing\). Thus core qualification is algebraically weaker, although a sum theorem using it may require additional closure assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Topological interior qualification implies core qualification, but the converse can fail in infinite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification-Regime Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison is mathematically plausible, including the discontinuous-linear-functional example, but it lacks any source and depends on an infinite-dimensional pathological construction whose assumptions should be documented. The LaTeX also contains invalid commands such as `\tsubset`, `\tsubseteq`, and `\tle`; these must be repaired after authoritative sourcing.

children.title: Subdifferential Sum Specializations
children.top_down_role: Maximal-monotone sum results specialized to convex subdifferentials.

assumptions_latex: There exists \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) at which one of \(f,g\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)=\partial f+\partial g\), and this operator is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex subdifferential sum rule under a continuity qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Subdifferential Calculus and Related Topics p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), the continuity qualification yields
\[
\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).
\]
Consequently, since \(f+g\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, \(\partial(f+g)\) is maximally monotone; hence the pointwise operator sum \(\partial f+\partial g\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuity qualification makes the subdifferential of a convex sum equal the sum of the subdifferentials, which is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Sum Specializations

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Subdifferential Calculus and Related Topics p. 296
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Normal-Cone Sum Specializations
children.top_down_role: Maximal-monotone sum results specialized to normal-cone operators.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subset H\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{C\cap D}=N_C+N_D\), and \(N_C+N_D\) is maximally monotone.

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal-cone operator of a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-convex normal-cone sum rule under an interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\),
\[
N_{C\cap D}(x)=N_C(x)+N_D(x).
\]
Moreover, \(N_C+N_D\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If either closed convex set meets the interior of the other, the normal cone to their intersection equals the sum of their normal cones, and this sum is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Sum Specializations

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The qualification simultaneously validates convex subdifferential and normal-cone sum formulas.

children.title: Qualification-Maximality Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Pathologies caused by incompatible domains.

children.title: Domain Qualification Failure
children.top_down_role: Incompatible domain intersections that defeat standard sum criteria.

assumptions_latex: \(K=\ell^2\), \(H=K\oplus K\), and \(T:K\to K\) is defined by \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\notin\operatorname{sri}(U-V)\); thus the standard domain qualification fails.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional failure of the strong-relative-interior domain condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(T\) is bounded and injective, while \(\operatorname{ran}T\) is dense and nonclosed. Moreover,
\[
U-V=K\oplus\operatorname{ran}T.
\]
This is a nonclosed linear subspace of \(H\), so \(0\notin\operatorname{sri}(U-V)\). Hence the qualification \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}N_U-\operatorname{dom}N_V)\) fails for the two maximally monotone normal-cone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed subspaces can have a dense, nonclosed domain difference, causing the strong-relative-interior qualification to fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Qualification Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The infinite-dimensional construction and failure-boundary classification are plausible and internally precise, but no source record or inspectable locator is supplied for the example or the strong-relative-interior conclusion.

children.title: Nonmaximal Sum Operators
children.top_down_role: Monotone sums that fail to retain maximality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The monotone operator \(N_U+N_V\) is not maximally monotone.

notation.meaning: normal cone to a closed subspace

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-subspace counterexample to unconditional maximality of operator sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Both \(N_U\) and \(N_V\) are maximally monotone, and \(U\cap V=\{0\}\). At their common domain point,
\[
(N_U+N_V)(0)=U^\perp+V^\perp=\operatorname{ran}T\oplus K,
\]
up to the harmless sign on the first component. This is a proper dense nonclosed subspace of \(H\), whereas \(N_{U\cap V}(0)=H\). Thus \(N_U+N_V\) has the proper monotone extension \(N_{U\cap V}\) and is not maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two maximal normal-cone operators can have a nonmaximal sum when the associated orthogonal-complement sum is nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmaximal Sum Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-subspace construction plausibly gives a nonmaximal normal-cone sum and counterexample is the correct role for this leaf, but the exact computation and nonmaximality conclusion lack any cited authoritative source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Qualification-to-Maximality Failure Link
children.top_down_role: How domain incompatibility leads to loss of maximality.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximality of \(A+B\) is then not guaranteed, although qualification failure alone does not imply nonmaximality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between a sufficient qualification and maximality failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}A-\operatorname{dom}B)\) is sufficient for the standard maximal-monotone sum theorem, not necessary in general. Its failure therefore removes the theorem's guarantee without itself proving that \(A+B\) is nonmaximal. Nevertheless, closed-subspace normal cones with a nonclosed orthogonal-complement sum show that qualification failure can coincide with an actual proper monotone extension of \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of the domain qualification removes the maximality guarantee but does not logically force failure; infinite-dimensional examples show failure can occur.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification-to-Maximality Failure Link

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logical distinction between failure of a sufficient qualification and actual failure of maximality is correct and fits a failure-boundary leaf. However, neither the sufficiency statement nor the claimed infinite-dimensional failure example has a cited source.

children.title: Brézis–Haraux Range Theorem Family
children.top_down_role: Range geometry for sums involving rectangular operators.

children.title: Rectangular-Operator Sum Ranges
children.top_down_role: Range structure in the rectangular regime.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are rectangular maximally monotone operators on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ran}(A+B)\) and \(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B\) have the same closure and interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Brézis–Haraux near-equality in the two-rectangular-operator regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under these hypotheses, the Brézis–Haraux range conclusion is
\[
\overline{\operatorname{ran}(A+B)}=\overline{\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B}
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{int}\operatorname{ran}(A+B)=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B).
\]
Thus the range of the operator sum is nearly equal to the Minkowski sum of the individual ranges, where near equality means equality of both closures and interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For rectangular maximal operators whose sum is maximal, the sum range and the sum of individual ranges have equal closures and interiors.
knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular-Operator Sum Ranges

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem has the correct role and states the expected closure-and-interior near-equality conclusion, but the precise rectangularity and maximality hypotheses must be checked against an authoritative Brézis–Haraux theorem source. No citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Range Closure-Interior Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric comparisons among attainable ranges.

children.title: Range Closure Relations
children.top_down_role: Comparisons between closures of attainable operator ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are rectangular maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{ran}(A+B)}=\overline{\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure component of the Brézis–Haraux near-equality conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The rectangular range theorem gives
\[
\overline{\operatorname{ran}(A+B)}=\overline{\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B}.
\]
Equivalently, every point approximable by sums of individual range values is approximable by values of \(A+B\), and the reverse inclusion follows from \(\operatorname{ran}(A+B)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The range of the operator sum and the Minkowski sum of the individual ranges have identical norm closures.
knowledge_statements.title: Range Closure Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure relation is internally consistent and property is appropriate for this component leaf, but it inherits an unverified theorem hypothesis set and supplies no authoritative source locator.

children.title: Range Interior Relations
children.top_down_role: Comparisons between interiors of attainable operator ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are rectangular maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{ran}(A+B)=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior component of the Brézis–Haraux near-equality conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The rectangular range theorem yields
\[
\operatorname{int}\operatorname{ran}(A+B)=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B).
\]
Consequently, the two range sets contain exactly the same nonempty open subsets, even though their boundary points and exact set membership may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The range of the operator sum and the sum of the individual ranges have the same norm interior.
knowledge_statements.title: Range Interior Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interior relation is internally consistent and property is appropriate for this component leaf, but it inherits an unverified theorem hypothesis set and supplies no authoritative source locator.

children.title: Closure–Interior Range Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between approximate attainability and interior range coverage.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Near equality does not imply \(R=S\) or equality of boundary membership.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: What closure–interior range conclusions do not determine.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equality of closures and interiors leaves boundary membership undetermined. For example, in \(H=\mathbb R\), the sets \(R=(0,1)\) and \(S=(0,1]\) satisfy
\[
\overline R=\overline S=[0,1],\qquad \operatorname{int}R=\operatorname{int}S=(0,1),
\]
yet \(R\neq S\). Accordingly, Brézis–Haraux near equality does not generally assert exact equality of the two ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal closures and interiors do not determine boundary membership, so Brézis–Haraux near equality need not give exact range equality.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Interior Range Boundary

children.top_down_role: Dualized operator combinations for coupled systems.

children.title: Parallel Sum Operators
children.top_down_role: Dualized combinations formed through inverses and operator addition.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are set-valued operators on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parallel sum is \(A\mathbin{\Box}B=(A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation-theoretic definition of the parallel sum.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The parallel sum of \(A\) and \(B\) is the relation
\[
A\mathbin{\Box}B=(A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}.
\]
Equivalently, for \(x,u\in H\), one has \(u\in(A\mathbin{\Box}B)x\) exactly when there exist \(y,z\in H\) such that \(x=y+z\), \(u\in Ay\), and \(u\in Bz\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The parallel sum is the inverse of the pointwise sum of the inverse relations.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Sum Operators

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Parallel Composition Operators
children.top_down_role: Parallel combinations mediated by linear mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(L:H\to G\) is bounded linear, and \(B:G\rightrightarrows G\) is set-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parallel composition is \(L\mathbin{\triangleright}B=(L^*\circ B^{-1}\circ L)^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: adjoint of the bounded linear map
parallel composition of a linear map and an operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Hilbert-space parallel-composition convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The parallel composition of \(L\) and \(B\) is the operator on \(H\) defined by
\[
L\mathbin{\triangleright}B=(L^*\circ B^{-1}\circ L)^{-1}.
\]
Thus, for \(x,u\in H\), the membership \(u\in(L\mathbin{\triangleright}B)x\) holds exactly when \(x\in L^*(B^{-1}(Lu))\), equivalently when some \(v\in G\) satisfies \(Lu\in Bv\) and \(x=L^*v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel composition transports an inverse operator through a linear map and its adjoint, then inverts the resulting relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Composition Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed formula and membership equivalence are dimensionally consistent for the stated convention, and definition fits the leaf. Parallel-composition notation varies in the literature, however, and no authoritative source or locator is supplied to establish that this exact symbol and ordering are intended.

children.title: Coupled-System Representation
children.top_down_role: Use of parallel constructions in coupled monotone systems.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) and \(G_i\) are real Hilbert spaces; \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(B_i,D_i:G_i\rightrightarrows G_i\), and \(C:H\to H\).
Each \(L_i:H\to G_i\) is bounded linear, with adjoint \(L_i^*\), and \(r_i\in G_i\), \(z\in H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal inclusion is equivalent to the displayed coupled system in the variables \((x,y_1,\ldots,y_m)\).

notation.meaning: Parallel sum of two set-valued operators.
Hilbert-space adjoint of the bounded linear map.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard primal-dual representation for a finite sum of parallel-composite monotone terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m\geq 1\), consider
\[
z\in Ax+Cx+\sum_{i=1}^m L_i^*(B_i\mathbin{\square}D_i)(L_ix-r_i).
\]
A point \(x\in H\) solves this inclusion if and only if there exist \(y_i\in G_i\) such that
\[
z-\sum_{i=1}^mL_i^*y_i\in Ax+Cx,
\qquad
L_ix-r_i\in B_i^{-1}y_i+D_i^{-1}y_i
\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).
\]
Equivalently, the second relation is \(y_i\in(B_i\mathbin{\square}D_i)(L_ix-r_i)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone inclusion containing parallel-composite terms is equivalent to a primal-dual system obtained by introducing one dual variable for each term.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-System Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent and fits the terminal container, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator supporting the finite parallel-composite equivalence.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusion \(0\in Tx\) is solvable exactly when \(0\in\operatorname{ran}T\); maximal strong monotonicity is a sufficient existence regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence criteria for zeros of maximal monotone operators on Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution set of \(0\in Tx\) is nonempty if and only if
\[
0\in\operatorname{ran}T.
\]
In particular, suppose that for some \(\mu>0\),
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq \mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2
\]
whenever \(u\in Tx\) and \(v\in Ty\). Then maximality and \(\mu\)-strong monotonicity imply \(\operatorname{ran}T=H\), so \(\operatorname{zer}T\neq\varnothing\). Thus range membership is the exact existence condition, while maximal strong monotonicity supplies a standard sufficient regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero exists exactly when zero lies in the operator range. A maximally strongly monotone operator always has a zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution Existence Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Solution Uniqueness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings distinguished by uniqueness versus multiplicity of solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict monotonicity makes \(\operatorname{zer}T\) a singleton; maximal \(\mu\)-strong monotonicity additionally guarantees its existence.

notation.meaning: Set of solutions to the zero inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of a zero under strict or strong monotonicity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(T\) is strictly monotone, meaning
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle>0
\]
for all distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}T\), \(u\in Tx\), and \(v\in Ty\), then \(T\) has at most one zero. Consequently, under the stated nonemptiness assumption, \(\operatorname{zer}T\) is a singleton. More strongly, if \(T\) is maximally \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for some \(\mu>0\), then existence and uniqueness both hold, so there is exactly one \(\bar x\in H\) satisfying \(0\in T\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict monotonicity permits at most one zero. Maximal strong monotonicity guarantees that this unique zero exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution Uniqueness Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Solution-Set Boundedness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings distinguished by bounded or unbounded solution geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space and \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set is bounded exactly when its recession cone is \(\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the solution set.
notation.symbol_latex: \(S^\infty=\{d\in H:x+td\in S\ \text{for every }x\in S\text{ and every }t\geq0\}\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional recession characterization of bounded maximal-monotone zero sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The zero set \(S=\operatorname{zer}T\) is closed and convex. Its recession cone is
\[
S^\infty=\{d\in H:x+td\in S\text{ for every }x\in S\text{ and every }t\geq0\}.
\]
Then
\[
S\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S^\infty=\{0\}.
\]
Hence a nonzero recession direction is precisely the obstruction to boundedness in this finite-dimensional regime. In particular, if \(T\) is strongly monotone, then \(S\) is a singleton and is therefore bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite-dimensional zero set is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession direction; strong monotonicity yields a bounded singleton.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Boundedness Regimes

children.title: Subregularity-Error-Bound Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Residual-to-solution-set control.

children.title: Metric Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Local regularity of the operator relative to its zero set.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) maps metric spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric subregularity is the stated local distance estimate with the target fixed at \(\bar y\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to infinity.
Inverse image of the fixed target value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric subregularity of a set-valued mapping at a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) with modulus \(\kappa\geq0\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
d\bigl(x,F^{-1}(\bar y)\bigr)\leq \kappa\,d\bigl(\bar y,F(x)\bigr)
\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
Here \(d(\bar y,F(x))=+\infty\) when \(F(x)=\varnothing\). Unlike metric regularity, the estimate fixes the range value at \(\bar y\) and varies only \(x\) locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity bounds local distance to the solution set by the residual distance to one fixed target value.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard local definition of metric subregularity with a fixed range value, and the definition kind fits the leaf. No source or exact locator is supplied.

children.title: Residual Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Control of solution-set distance through computable residuals.

assumptions_latex: \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is an operator on a real Hilbert space and \(S=\operatorname{zer}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A local residual error bound is the inequality \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa d(0,Tx)\) near \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Residual magnitude of the zero inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local error bound using the natural set-valued residual of a zero inclusion.

source_refs.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar x\in S\). The zero inclusion for \(T\) admits a local residual error bound at \(\bar x\) with constant \(\kappa\geq0\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
d(x,S)\leq \kappa r_T(x)=\kappa d(0,Tx)
\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
The convention \(d(0,\varnothing)=+\infty\) makes the inequality meaningful outside \(\operatorname{dom}T\). A global error bound uses the same inequality for every \(x\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual error bound controls distance to the zero set by the smallest norm of a value returned by the operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475
source_witnesses.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed condition is a coherent natural-residual error bound, but the cited section concerns linear complementarity and does not reliably support the stated general Hilbert-space set-valued-operator formulation.

children.title: Subregularity–Error-Bound Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between metric subregularity and residual-based distance control.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(\bar x\in\operatorname{zer}T\), and \(S=T^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric subregularity of \(T\) at \((\bar x,0)\) is equivalent to the local residual error bound for \(0\in Tx\).

notation.meaning: Natural residual for the zero inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence for the natural residual of a set-valued zero inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a constant \(\kappa\geq0\), the following statements are equivalent:
\[
T\text{ is metrically subregular at }\bar x\text{ for }0\text{ with constant }\kappa;
\]
\[
\text{there exists a neighborhood }U\text{ of }\bar x\text{ such that }d(x,S)\leq\kappa r_T(x)\text{ for every }x\in U.
\]
Indeed, both statements are the same inequality
\[
d\bigl(x,T^{-1}(0)\bigr)\leq\kappa d(0,Tx)
\]
near \(\bar x\). Thus the subregularity modulus equals the best local error-bound constant for this residual convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the natural operator residual, metric subregularity and a local residual error bound are exactly the same inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Subregularity–Error-Bound Correspondence

children.title: Perturbation Conditioning Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity under strong monotonicity and regularity.

children.title: Solution-Map Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Quantitative sensitivity of inclusion solutions to problem data.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is a set-valued mapping between metric spaces and \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local conditioning is quantified by the smallest \(\kappa\) in the displayed Aubin estimate.

notation.meaning: Closed ball of radius r about a point.
One-sided excess of one set over another.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aubin conditioning of a set-valued solution map near a reference parameter-solution pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution map \(F\) is Lipschitz-like, or has the Aubin property, around \((\bar p,\bar x)\) with modulus \(\kappa\geq0\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
e\bigl(F(p_1)\cap V,F(p_2)\bigr)\leq\kappa d(p_1,p_2)
\qquad\text{for all }p_1,p_2\in U.
\]
The infimum of admissible \(\kappa\) is the local conditioning modulus. Finite modulus means that nearby solution branches lying in \(V\) vary at most linearly with parameter perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution map is well conditioned when nearby local solution branches move at most linearly with changes in the parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Map Conditioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The excess-form Aubin estimate correctly describes local Lipschitz-like conditioning and the condition kind fits the leaf. No inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Perturbation Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence and movement of solutions under operator perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution map between normed spaces and \((0,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Calmness gives a linear local displacement bound for perturbed solutions relative to \(S(0)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to the unperturbed solution set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local calmness stability of solutions under additive or abstract parameter perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution map \(S\) is calm at \((0,\bar x)\) with modulus \(\kappa\geq0\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(0\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
d(x,S(0))\leq\kappa\lVert p\rVert
\qquad\text{whenever }p\in U\text{ and }x\in S(p)\cap V.
\]
This condition permits multiple unperturbed and perturbed solutions, but requires every nearby selected solution to remain within a distance proportional to the perturbation magnitude from the unperturbed solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calm perturbation stability means every nearby perturbed solution stays linearly close to the unperturbed solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The calmness inequality is mathematically precise and appropriately represents a perturbation-stability condition, but it lacks a cited source and exact locator.

children.title: Strong-Monotonicity Stability Regime
children.top_down_role: Enhanced sensitivity control supplied by strong monotonicity.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed solution map \(T^{-1}:H\to H\) is single-valued and globally \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz.

notation.meaning: Unique solution of the perturbed inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hilbert-space stability for additive right-hand-side perturbations of a strongly monotone inclusion.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(p\in H\), the perturbed inclusion
\[
p\in Tx
\]
has a unique solution \(x(p)\). Moreover, for all \(p,q\in H\),
\[
\lVert x(p)-x(q)\rVert\leq\frac{1}{\mu}\lVert p-q\rVert.
\]
Consequently, \(T^{-1}\) is everywhere defined, single-valued, and globally Lipschitz with modulus at most \(1/\mu\). In particular, the zero \(x(0)\) is unique and additive right-hand-side perturbations produce proportionally bounded solution displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximal strong monotonicity gives a unique solution for every right-hand side and a global Lipschitz sensitivity bound of one over the modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Stability Regime

children.title: Solution-Set Pathology Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes for existence and stability.

children.title: Empty Solution Sets
children.top_down_role: Inclusion regimes lacking any solution.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximally monotone operator \(T\) has \(\operatorname{zer}T=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional maximal-monotone operator whose range omits zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(x\mapsto e^x\) is continuous, everywhere defined, and strictly increasing, so the single-valued operator
\[
T(x)=e^x
\]
is maximally monotone on \(\mathbb R\). Nevertheless, \(e^x>0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), and hence
\[
0\notin\operatorname{ran}T
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{zer}T=\varnothing.
\]
Thus maximal monotonicity alone does not ensure solvability of the zero inclusion; an additional range, coercivity, or strong-monotonicity condition is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential operator is maximally monotone on the real line but never attains zero, so its zero set is empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Empty Solution Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential map is a valid one-dimensional maximally monotone operator whose range omits zero, and a counterexample is appropriate for this pathology leaf. No source or exact locator is supplied.

children.title: Unbounded Solution Sets
children.top_down_role: Inclusion regimes with solutions lacking bounded geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nontrivial real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is the zero operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximally monotone operator \(T\) has the unbounded solution set \(\operatorname{zer}T=H\).

notation.meaning: Zero operator on the Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical failure of boundedness without strict or strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
T(x)=0\qquad\text{for every }x\in H.
\]
This operator is maximally monotone, but every point solves the zero inclusion. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{zer}T=H.
\]
Since \(H\) is nontrivial, for any nonzero \(d\in H\) the sequence \((nd)_{n\geq1}\) lies in \(\operatorname{zer}T\) and satisfies \(\lVert nd\rVert\to+\infty\). Hence a nonempty zero set of a maximally monotone operator need not be bounded when no coercivity or strictness assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero operator is maximally monotone, yet every point is a solution, producing an unbounded zero set.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Solution Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero operator is a valid maximally monotone counterexample with the unbounded zero set \(H\), and the content kind fits the pathology leaf. No source or exact locator is supplied.

children.title: Unstable Solution Sets
children.top_down_role: Inclusion regimes exhibiting severe sensitivity to perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb R\) and \(A_p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(A_p(x)=x^3-p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)=\{p^{1/3}\}\) is not Lipschitz-like at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: Solution mapping of the parameterized inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete monotone inclusion whose nonempty singleton solution set is unstable under parameter perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p\in\mathbb R\), the continuous increasing operator \(A_p(x)=x^3-p\) is maximally monotone and the inclusion \(0\in A_p(x)\) has the unique solution \(S(p)=\{p^{1/3}\}\). Nevertheless, \(S\) is not Lipschitz-like at \((0,0)\): no neighborhoods and constant \(L<\infty\) can satisfy \(|p^{1/3}-q^{1/3}|\le L|p-q|\) for all sufficiently small \(p,q\). Thus nonemptiness and uniqueness alone do not ensure stable solution dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximally monotone equations x³ = p have unique solutions, but their solution mapping is not locally Lipschitz at p = 0.
knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Solution Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct and fits the unstable-solution-set leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.
