children.top_down_role: Exact resolvent evaluation and controlled inexactness.

children.title: Exact Proximal Point Variant
children.top_down_role: Proximal iterations based on exact resolvent evaluations.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_k A}x_k\) and \((x_k-x_{k+1})/\lambda_k\in A(x_{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Hilbert-space proximal iteration for a maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in H\), generate \(x_{k+1}\) by solving exactly \[x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_k A}x_k=(I+\lambda_k A)^{-1}x_k.\] Equivalently, choose \(a_{k+1}\in A(x_{k+1})\) satisfying \(x_k-x_{k+1}=\lambda_k a_{k+1}\). Stop when \(0\in A(x_{k+1})\), or under a prescribed numerical tolerance when \(\|x_k-x_{k+1}\|/\lambda_k\) is sufficiently small; otherwise output the generated sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each step exactly evaluates the resolvent of the maximally monotone operator; the scaled displacement is an operator residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Proximal Point Variant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact resolvent iteration is correctly stated and algorithm is the appropriate content kind, but the record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Inexact Proximal Point Variant
children.top_down_role: Proximal iterations admitting controlled evaluation errors.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone and \(x_0\in H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_k A}x_k+e_k\) with \(\|e_k\|\le\eta_k\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent evaluation error at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error formulation of an inexact proximal point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(x_0\), at iteration \(k\) compute an approximation \(x_{k+1}\) satisfying \[x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_k A}x_k+e_k,\qquad \|e_k\|\le\eta_k.\] Equivalently, the exact resolvent value must lie in the closed ball centered at \(x_{k+1}\) with radius \(\eta_k\). Stop when an available inclusion residual meets a prescribed tolerance; otherwise output the inexact sequence together with the certified error bounds \((\eta_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each proximal step may deviate from the exact resolvent value by a certified, iteration-dependent error.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Proximal Point Variant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive-error iteration is coherent and fits the inexact-variant leaf, but its formulation lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Inexactness Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural categories of admissible proximal evaluation error.

assumptions_latex: \((x_k)\subset H\) is the associated inexact proximal sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Standard controls include \(\sum_k\|e_k\|<\infty\), \(\|e_k\|\le\sigma_k\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\), or \(\|e_k\|\le\eta_k\) with \(\sum_k\eta_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common absolute, summable, and relative controls for resolvent evaluation errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact proximal iteration is under absolute summable control when \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|e_k\|<\infty\). A prescribed-budget version requires \(\|e_k\|\le\eta_k\) with \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty\). A relative regime instead compares error with the computed displacement, for example \(\|e_k\|\le\sigma_k\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\), where the admissible upper bound on \(\sigma_k\) must be chosen according to the particular convergence theorem and error model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact proximal steps are commonly controlled by summable absolute errors, summable budgets, or errors bounded relative to the step length.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexactness Control Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute controls are clear, but the relative-error regime depends on a particular error model and convergence theorem. A source must specify its admissible coefficients and hypotheses.

children.title: Relaxed Proximal Point Variants
children.top_down_role: Relaxed resolvent iterations.

assumptions_latex: \(x_0\in H\), \(\lambda_k>0\), and relaxation parameters \(\theta_k\in(0,2)\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\theta_k(J_{\lambda_kA}x_k-x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Underrelaxed and overrelaxed resolvent iterations in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(x_0\), compute \(y_k=J_{\lambda_kA}x_k\) and update \[x_{k+1}=x_k+\theta_k(y_k-x_k).\] Values \(0<\theta_k<1\) give underrelaxation, \(\theta_k=1\) recovers the exact proximal point step, and \(1<\theta_k<2\) gives overrelaxation. Stop when \(y_k=x_k\), which implies \(0\in A(x_k)\), or when \(\|y_k-x_k\|/\lambda_k\) meets a prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxed proximal method moves a fraction, or an admissible overrelaxed multiple, of the displacement toward the resolvent point.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Proximal Point Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxed resolvent algorithm and relaxation classification fit the terminal container, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Variable-Metric Proximal Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Proximal Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal iterations using a changing strongly positive metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in H\), for every \(k\ge 0\) choose \(x_{k+1}\in H\) satisfying \[0\in A(x_{k+1})+\lambda_k^{-1}M_k(x_{k+1}-x_k).\] Equivalently, \[x_{k+1}=(M_k+\lambda_kA)^{-1}M_kx_k.\] The metric \(M_k\) may vary with \(k\), subject to the stated positivity and any additional compatibility conditions required by the applicable convergence theorem. A fixed point satisfies \(0\in A(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, the variable-metric proximal method solves the proximal inclusion using a strongly positive metric operator that may change with the iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
\(M_k:H\to H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive for every \(k\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=(M_k+\lambda_kA)^{-1}M_kx_k\) for every \(k\ge 0\).

notation.meaning: Squared norm induced by the metric operator.

children.title: Preconditioned Proximal Variants
children.top_down_role: Proximal iterations transformed by fixed or structured preconditioners.

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioned Proximal Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-metric proximal iteration expressed through a positive preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(x_0\in H\), for every \(k\ge 0\) compute \(x_{k+1}\in H\) from \[0\in A(x_{k+1})+P(x_{k+1}-x_k).\] Equivalently, \[x_{k+1}=(P+A)^{-1}Px_k=(I+P^{-1}A)^{-1}x_k.\] Moreover, \(P(x_k-x_{k+1})\in A(x_{k+1})\), and a fixed point solves \(0\in A(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every iteration, the method uses one fixed strongly positive preconditioner to rescale the proximal inclusion and its residual.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
\(P:H\to H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.

notation.meaning: Squared norm induced by the preconditioner.

children.title: Metric Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Metric choices compatible with proximal convergence mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: \(M_k:H\to H\) is bounded and self-adjoint for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(mI\preccurlyeq M_k\preccurlyeq MI\) and \(M_{k+1}\preccurlyeq(1+\eta_k)M_k\) with \(\sum_k\eta_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard sufficient uniform-equivalence and summable-variation regime for changing metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A standard compatible metric sequence satisfies constants \(0<m\le M<\infty\) and numbers \(\eta_k\ge0\) such that \[mI\preccurlyeq M_k\preccurlyeq MI,\qquad M_{k+1}\preccurlyeq(1+\eta_k)M_k,
\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty.\] The first inequalities make all induced norms uniformly equivalent to the ambient norm; the final two conditions limit cumulative metric growth. This is a sufficient compatibility regime, not a necessary characterization of every convergent variable-metric method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible changing metrics are uniformly positive and bounded, with their cumulative relative growth controlled by a summable sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Compatibility Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditions form a coherent sufficient compatibility regime and condition is the correct content kind, but their status and use require a specific authoritative locator.

children.title: Hybrid Proximal–Extragradient Family
children.top_down_role: Enlargement-based inexact proximal frameworks.

assumptions_latex: \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone and \(x_0\in H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_kv_k\) under the HPE relative-error inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical enlargement-based hybrid proximal–extragradient iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), find \((y_k,v_k,\varepsilon_k)\) with \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\), \(v_k\in T^{[\varepsilon_k]}(y_k)\), and \[\|\lambda_kv_k+y_k-x_k\|^2+2\lambda_k\varepsilon_k\le\sigma^2\|y_k-x_k\|^2.\] Then perform the extragradient update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_kv_k\). Stop when \(v_k=0\) and \(\varepsilon_k=0\), or when both satisfy prescribed tolerances; otherwise output the generated iterates and enlargement certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: HPE computes an enlargement-certified approximate proximal point, enforces a relative-error test, and then takes an extragradient update.
knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Proximal–Extragradient Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The HPE enlargement condition and extragradient update are appropriately presented as an algorithm, but the canonical formulation has no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Proximal Solvability-Error Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Insolvability and uncontrolled inexactness regimes.

children.title: Proximal-Point Insolvability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior of proximal iterations when the underlying inclusion has no solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Point Insolvability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal iterations need not converge when the underlying inclusion is insoluble.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(A(x)=e^x\). Then \(A\) is maximally monotone and \(A^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\). For any \(x_0\in\mathbb R\) and step sizes satisfying \(\lambda_k\ge\underline\lambda>0\), the exact proximal iteration \[x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kA}x_k\] is equivalently characterized by \[x_k=x_{k+1}+\lambda_ke^{x_{k+1}}.\] Its iterates satisfy \(x_{k+1}<x_k\) and \(x_k\to-\infty\). Thus exact, well-defined resolvent steps need not converge to a point when the inclusion has no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the insoluble monotone equation eˣ = 0, every exact proximal step is well defined, but step sizes bounded away from zero produce iterates that decrease to negative infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0\in\mathbb R\), exact proximal steps are used, and \(\lambda_k\ge\underline\lambda>0\) for every \(k\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\) and \(x_k\to-\infty\).

children.title: Uncontrolled Inexactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Error patterns outside convergence-compatible inexactness controls.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k/2+1\) converges to \(2\notin A^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A constant resolvent error can force convergence to a nonsolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=I\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(A^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\) and \(J_Ax=x/2\). With uncontrolled additive errors \(e_k=1\), the inexact iteration is \[x_{k+1}=J_Ax_k+e_k=\frac{x_k}{2}+1.\] For every starting point, \(x_k\to2\), although \(2\notin A^{-1}(0)\). Thus bounded but nonsummable errors need not preserve convergence to a zero, even for a strongly monotone linear operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant additive error makes the proximal method for the identity operator converge to 2 instead of its unique zero 0.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Inexactness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and directly demonstrates failure under uncontrolled additive error, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Solvability–Error Interaction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interaction between problem inconsistency and proximal evaluation error.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_k)\) converges weakly to a point of \(A^{-1}(0)\); removing solvability or error control invalidates this guarantee.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating standard convergence guarantees from insolvability and uncontrolled-error failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated hypotheses, the additive-error proximal point sequence \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kA}x_k+e_k\) converges weakly to some \(x_\star\in A^{-1}(0)\). Both solvability and cumulative error control are structural: if \(A^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\), an exact sequence may diverge; if errors are not suitably controlled, a sequence may converge to a nonsolution even when the zero is unique. Therefore the standard guarantee does not extend across either boundary without replacement assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty zeros plus summable errors yield standard weak convergence; insolvability or uncontrolled errors can respectively cause divergence or convergence to a nonsolution.
knowledge_statements.title: Solvability–Error Interaction Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-convergence boundary statement is plausible under the stated Hilbert-space hypotheses, but it is a nontrivial theorem and requires an exact authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Forward Splitting Correction Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Splittings distinguished by cocoercive or merely Lipschitz forward components.

children.title: Forward–Backward Splitting Family
children.top_down_role: Explicit-implicit splitting in the cocoercive regime.

children.title: Cocoercive Forward–Backward Regime
children.top_down_role: The standard averaged-operator regime.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space, and \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximally monotone.
\(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive: \(\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\|Bx-By\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\gamma\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha=2\beta/(4\beta-\gamma)\), and \(\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical cocoercive forward–backward averagedness formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-step Hilbert-space forward–backward splitting with a cocoercive explicit operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma B)\). Under the stated assumptions, \(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma B\) is \(\gamma/(2\beta)\)-averaged, and its composition with the firmly nonexpansive resolvent is \(\alpha\)-averaged, where \[\alpha=\frac{2\beta}{4\beta-\gamma}\in(0,1).\] Moreover, \[x=T_\gamma x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in Ax+Bx.\] Consequently, the unrelaxed iteration \(x_{n+1}=T_\gamma x_n\) is an averaged fixed-point iteration for solving the monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a cocoercive forward operator and stepsize below twice its cocoercivity constant, the forward–backward map is averaged and its fixed points solve the inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Forward–Backward Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The averagedness formula, fixed-point characterization, scope, and property kind are mathematically standard and internally consistent, but no inspectable citation supports the nontrivial claims.

children.title: Relaxation-Metric Variant Family
children.top_down_role: Relaxation and preconditioning extensions.

children.title: Relaxed Forward–Backward Variants
children.top_down_role: Forward–backward splittings modified by relaxation parameters.

assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(Tx_n-x_n)\) converges weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relaxed Krasnoselskii–Mann form of forward–backward splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar relaxation of an averaged forward–backward operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in\mathcal H\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute \(p_n=Tx_n\) and update \[x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(p_n-x_n).\] Stop when a prescribed tolerance satisfies \(\|p_n-x_n\|\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise return the last iterate. Under the stated relaxation condition, the iteration is a relaxed averaged fixed-point method; in a Hilbert space, \(x_n\) converges weakly to an element of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), while \(\|Tx_n-x_n\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relax each forward–backward step by a parameter below the reciprocal averagedness constant; the iterates converge weakly under the standard divergence condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Forward–Backward Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxed Krasnoselskii–Mann algorithm and convergence condition fit the leaf, but the weak-convergence and residual claims have no cited theorem or section.

children.title: Variable-Metric Forward–Backward Variants
children.top_down_role: Forward–backward splittings formulated in changing metric geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(U:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.
\(A\) is maximally monotone, and \(UB\) is \(\beta_U\)-cocoercive in the \(U^{-1}\)-metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\gamma,U}=J_{\gamma UA}(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma UB)\) is averaged in the \(U^{-1}\)-metric and has fixed-point set \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed strongly-positive preconditioning of forward–backward splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-metric preconditioned variant; variable metrics require additional inter-iteration control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in\mathcal H\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma UA}(x_n-\gamma UBx_n).\] Stop when \(\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|_{U^{-1}}\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise return the last iterate. The map \(T_{\gamma,U}\) is \(\alpha_U\)-averaged in the metric induced by \(U^{-1}\), with \[\alpha_U=\frac{2\beta_U}{4\beta_U-\gamma}.\] Its fixed points are precisely the zeros of \(A+B\), so the iteration is the metric analogue of cocoercive forward–backward splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly positive preconditioner replaces the ambient metric and scales both the resolvent and forward step while preserving the inclusion’s solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Forward–Backward Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas describe a fixed preconditioning metric, whereas the terminal title indicates variable-metric variants, which ordinarily require a metric sequence and inter-iteration controls. A source is needed to determine the intended variant and sufficient hypotheses.

children.title: Relaxation–Metric Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Joint parameter regimes supporting stable relaxed metric adaptations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\lambda<1/\alpha_U=2-\gamma/(2\beta_U)\) makes \((1-\lambda)\operatorname{Id}+\lambda T_{\gamma,U}\) averaged.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relaxation bound for an averaged operator in a Hilbertian metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for constant relaxation and a fixed preconditioning metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the relaxed metric update \[x^+=x+\lambda(T_{\gamma,U}x-x),\] admissibility is determined by the averagedness constant in the same metric. The complete constant-parameter condition is \[0<\gamma<2\beta_U,\qquad 0<\lambda<\frac{1}{\alpha_U}=2-\frac{\gamma}{2\beta_U}.\] Under this condition, the relaxed map is averaged in the \(U^{-1}\)-metric. Thus larger forward steps reduce the permitted overrelaxation, while smaller steps allow relaxation parameters approaching \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stepsize and relaxation are coupled: the relaxation must be below two minus the stepsize divided by twice the metric cocoercivity constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation–Metric Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-metric relaxation bound follows formally from the stated averagedness constant and the condition kind fits, but the underlying metric averagedness premise and compatibility claim lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Forward-Backward Admissibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of averagedness outside compatible regimes.

children.title: Cocoercivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Forward-component regularity supporting averaged splitting operators.

assumptions_latex: \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is single-valued on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive exactly when \(\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\|Bx-By\|^2\) for every \(x,y\in\mathcal H\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: defining inequality and its immediate Lipschitz consequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hilbert-space cocoercivity used by explicit forward steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(B\) lies in the \(\beta\)-cocoercive regime when \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\|Bx-By\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathcal H.\] This predicate implies monotonicity and, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz continuity. Equivalently, for each \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), the forward map \(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma B\) is \(\gamma/(2\beta)\)-averaged. Cocoercivity is stronger than monotonicity plus Lipschitz continuity for a general nonlinear operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity lower-bounds the monotonicity pairing by a squared operator difference and ensures that sufficiently short forward steps are averaged.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercivity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its monotonicity, Lipschitz, and averaged-forward consequences are standard and consistent, but no specific source locator is cited.

children.title: Admissible Stepsize Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stepsize ranges compatible with the available cocoercivity.

assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone, and \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\gamma<2\beta\) is the open stepsize regime guaranteeing averagedness of \(T_\gamma\) from cocoercivity alone.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sharp uniform forward-step interval under beta-cocoercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform constant-stepsize boundary derived solely from cocoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The admissible constant forward stepsizes are \[0<\gamma<2\beta.\] For every such \(\gamma\), the forward map is \(\gamma/(2\beta)\)-averaged and the forward–backward composition is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \[\alpha=\frac{2\beta}{4\beta-\gamma}<1.\] The endpoints are excluded: \(\gamma=0\) performs no forward correction, while at \(\gamma=2\beta\) averagedness with a constant strictly below \(1\) is not guaranteed uniformly over all \(\beta\)-cocoercive operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity alone guarantees an averaged forward–backward map precisely for positive stepsizes strictly below twice the cocoercivity constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Admissible Stepsize Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The open stepsize interval and averagedness formula are standard and the condition kind matches the boundary leaf, but the asserted sharp uniform interpretation requires a cited result or counterexample source.

children.title: Averagedness-Loss Boundary
children.top_down_role: Parameter transitions where the splitting operator loses averagedness.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\gamma=2\beta\), \(T_\gamma=-\operatorname{Id}\) is not \(\alpha\)-averaged for any \(\alpha<1\); for \(\gamma>2\beta\), it is expansive.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar identity operator gives the sharp averagedness boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar counterexample at and beyond the cocoercive stepsize boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(B=\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Id}\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and with \(A=0\) the forward–backward map is \[T_\gamma=(1-\gamma/\beta)\operatorname{Id}.\] At the boundary \(\gamma=2\beta\), this becomes \(-\operatorname{Id}\), which is nonexpansive but is not \(\alpha\)-averaged for any \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). If \(\gamma>2\beta\), then \(|1-\gamma/\beta|>1\), so \(T_\gamma\) is expansive. Hence the open upper bound \(2\beta\) cannot be enlarged using cocoercivity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled identity operator shows sharpness: the boundary step gives minus identity, and larger steps make the forward map expansive.
knowledge_statements.title: Averagedness-Loss Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled-identity example correctly exhibits loss of strict averagedness at the boundary and expansiveness beyond it, and failure_boundary is the proper kind. No source is supplied.

children.title: Corrected-Forward Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Corrective schemes for monotone Lipschitz components.

children.title: Korpelevich Extragradient Family
children.top_down_role: The classical predictor-corrector family.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space.
\(F:C\to\mathcal H\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, and the variational inequality has a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extragradient iteration uses two projected forward evaluations per step and converges weakly to a solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Korpelevich two-projection extragradient scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical constant-step projection form for monotone Lipschitz variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in C\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), form the predictor and corrector \[y_n=P_C(x_n-\gamma Fx_n),\qquad x_{n+1}=P_C(x_n-\gamma Fy_n).\] Stop when \(\|x_n-y_n\|\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise return the last iterate. The first projection predicts a feasible point, while the second uses the operator evaluated at that predictor. Under the stated monotonicity, Lipschitz, solvability, and stepsize assumptions, \(x_n\) converges weakly to a point \(x_\star\in C\) satisfying \(\langle Fx_\star,z-x_\star\rangle\geq0\) for every \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Korpelevich’s method projects a forward predictor and then corrects from the old iterate using the operator evaluated at that predictor.
knowledge_statements.title: Korpelevich Extragradient Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence is the classical Korpelevich extragradient algorithm and the stated Hilbert-space convergence claim is plausible under the listed hypotheses, but it lacks a theorem-level citation.

children.title: Tseng Forward–Backward–Forward Family
children.top_down_role: Corrected forward splitting with an implicit component.

assumptions_latex: \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, with \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tseng’s forward–backward–forward iteration converges weakly to a zero of \(A+B\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard constant-step Tseng forward–backward–forward scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-step Hilbert-space forward–backward–forward splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in\mathcal H\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[p_n=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Bx_n),\qquad x_{n+1}=p_n+\gamma(Bx_n-Bp_n).\] Stop when \(\|x_n-p_n\|\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise return the last iterate. The resolvent treats \(A\) implicitly, and the second forward evaluation corrects the Lipschitz monotone component. Under the stated assumptions, both \(x_n\) and \(p_n\) converge weakly to a point in \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tseng’s method takes a forward–backward predictor and corrects it by the difference between forward evaluations at the old and predicted points.
knowledge_statements.title: Tseng Forward–Backward–Forward Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward–backward–forward recurrence and algorithm kind fit the terminal container, but weak convergence of both sequences under the exact constant-step hypotheses needs an inspectable citation.

children.title: Gradient-Reuse Corrected-Forward Variants
children.top_down_role: Evaluation-reusing corrected-forward variants.

children.title: Popov Variants
children.top_down_role: Corrected-forward schemes associated with Popov-type evaluations.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:C\to\mathcal H\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz.
\(y_{-1}\in C\), \(x_0\in C\), and \(\gamma>0\) lies in a convergence range appropriate to the Popov scheme.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration reuses \(Fy_{n-1}\), evaluates \(F\) only once at \(y_n\), and produces \(x_{n+1}\) by a second projection.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common two-sequence Popov projection recurrence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sequence projection form emphasizing reuse of the preceding predictor evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0,y_{-1}\in C\) and store \(Fy_{-1}\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[y_n=P_C(x_n-\gamma Fy_{n-1}),\qquad x_{n+1}=P_C(x_n-\gamma Fy_n).\] Only the value \(Fy_n\) is newly evaluated during iteration \(n\); it is retained for the next predictor. Stop when \(\|x_n-y_n\|\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise return the last iterate. The admissible numerical bound on \(\gamma L\) depends on the precise Popov convergence theorem adopted and is therefore left as an explicit source-dependent assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Popov step predicts using the previous auxiliary gradient, evaluates one new gradient, and uses it in a correcting projection from the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Popov Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence is a plausible Popov-type evaluation-reuse scheme, but the convergence range is left undefined and Popov nomenclature varies. A precise theorem and source are required.

children.title: Past-Gradient Variants
children.top_down_role: Corrected-forward schemes reusing a previously computed gradient.

assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone, and \(B\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz.
\(p_{-1},x_0\in\mathcal H\), and \(\gamma>0\) satisfies the selected past-gradient convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence performs one new evaluation \(Bp_n\) per iteration and reuses it as the next iteration’s past gradient.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resolvent extension of past-extragradient evaluation reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent-form past-gradient scheme; naming overlaps with Popov methods in the literature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0,p_{-1}\in\mathcal H\) and store \(Bp_{-1}\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[p_n=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Bp_{n-1}),\qquad x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Bp_n).\] Evaluate \(Bp_n\) once and retain it for the next iteration. Stop when \(\|x_n-p_n\|\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise return the last iterate. The exact admissible range of \(\gamma L\) is theorem-dependent; it must be fixed when a specific past-gradient variant and convergence source are selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The past-gradient resolvent scheme reuses the previous auxiliary forward value to predict, then stores one newly evaluated forward value for correction and reuse.
knowledge_statements.title: Past-Gradient Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed two-resolvent recurrence and its distinction from Popov variants are not established, and the admissible stepsize is unspecified. The exact algorithmic variant must be fixed from a source.

children.title: Reflected-Gradient Variants
children.top_down_role: Corrected-forward schemes using reflected gradient information.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximally monotone, and \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forward-reflected-backward recurrence converges weakly to a zero of \(A+B\) while using one new evaluation of \(B\) per iteration.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: forward-reflected-backward recurrence with a conservative classical stepsize bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-value reflection, distinct from evaluating the operator at a reflected point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_{-1},x_0\in\mathcal H\) and store \(Bx_{-1}\) and \(Bx_0\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), update \[x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(x_n-\gamma(2Bx_n-Bx_{n-1})\bigr).\] Evaluate \(Bx_{n+1}\) once for the next iteration. Stop when \(\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|\leq\varepsilon\), and otherwise return the last iterate. Under the stated constant-step assumptions, the sequence converges weakly to an element of \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). The reflection is applied to stored operator values, not necessarily to their arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward-reflected-backward splitting extrapolates two consecutive operator values before applying one resolvent, requiring only one new forward evaluation per iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflected-Gradient Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence matches a forward-reflected-backward variant and the algorithm kind fits, but the exact bound and weak-convergence theorem require a specific source locator.

children.title: Evaluation-Reuse Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Structural comparison of oracle reuse across the three variant families.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone and \(B:H\to H\) is single-valued.
Both compared schemes perform \(K\) iterations from the same initialized oracle cache.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_B^{\mathrm{reuse}}(K)=K+1\), whereas a two-query forward-correction scheme has \(N_B^{\mathrm{two}}(K)=2K\).

notation.meaning: Number of distinct evaluations of the forward operator through iteration K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct oracle-count comparison for cached corrected-forward and two-query schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts only evaluations of the forward operator, not resolvent calls or vector operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. Suppose a corrected-forward scheme stores one previously computed value of \(B\), performs one initial evaluation, and queries \(B\) at exactly one new point during each iteration. After \(K\) iterations its forward-oracle cost is \(N_B^{\mathrm{reuse}}(K)=K+1\). A comparison scheme that queries \(B\) at two new points during every iteration has \(N_B^{\mathrm{two}}(K)=2K\). Thus evaluation reuse saves \(K-1\) forward evaluations over \(K\) iterations, while this count alone makes no assertion about convergence rates or admissible step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cached corrected-forward method uses one initial and one new forward evaluation per iteration, versus two new evaluations per iteration for a standard two-query correction.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Reuse Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle-count comparison fits the terminal container and the operational assumptions make the arithmetic precise, but no inspectable citation supports the characterization of the compared corrected-forward schemes.

children.title: Rachford Reflection Splitting Family
children.top_down_role: Reflection-based splitting for two resolvent-accessible components.

children.title: Douglas–Rachford Splitting
children.top_down_role: Averaged reflected-resolvent splitting.

children.title: Shadow-to-Solution Recovery Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Recovery of inclusion solutions from auxiliary fixed points.

children.title: Douglas–Rachford Shadow Sequences
children.top_down_role: Resolvent images derived from auxiliary Douglas–Rachford iterates.

assumptions_latex: \(\gamma>0\), and the Douglas–Rachford iteration is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequences \((J_{\gamma A}z_k)\) and \((J_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}z_k)\) are the two Douglas–Rachford shadow sequences.

notation.meaning: Reflected resolvent of an operator M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the ordering in which the resolvent of \(A\) is applied first.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z_0\in H\), define \(z_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{DR}}z_k\), where \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\). The associated shadow points are \(x_k=J_{\gamma A}z_k\) and \(y_k=J_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}z_k=J_{\gamma B}(2x_k-z_k)\). Equivalently, the auxiliary update is \(z_{k+1}=z_k+y_k-x_k\). The sequences \((x_k)\) and \((y_k)\), rather than the generally non-solution auxiliary sequence \((z_k)\), are called the Douglas–Rachford shadow sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford auxiliary iterates produce two shadows by applying the first resolvent and then the second resolvent to the reflected first shadow.
knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Shadow Sequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and ordering convention are mathematically consistent with Douglas–Rachford splitting, but the record has no source with a specific locator establishing the shadow-sequence terminology.

children.title: Inclusion Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Extraction of inclusion solutions from fixed points or shadow limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=J_{\gamma A}z\) satisfies \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-point recovery identity for Douglas–Rachford splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed auxiliary point yields a primal solution and an explicit opposing-operator certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(x=J_{\gamma A}z\) and \(u=\gamma^{-1}(z-x)\). The resolvent identity gives \(u\in Ax\). Since \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), one has \(J_{\gamma B}(2x-z)=x\), and hence \(-u=\gamma^{-1}(x-z)\in Bx\). Therefore \(0=u+(-u)\in Ax+Bx\). The pair \((x,u)\) is a directly checkable certificate for recovery of a zero of \(A+B\) from the auxiliary fixed point \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the first resolvent to a Douglas–Rachford fixed point recovers a solution, with the fixed-point residual decomposition providing an explicit inclusion certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion Solution Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits inclusion recovery, but the statement contains a derivation and supplies no inspectable source for the fixed-point recovery identity and certificate formulation.

children.title: Auxiliary-to-Primal Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relations connecting auxiliary fixed points to recovered primal solutions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}})=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\), with the stated fixed-point fibers.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard fixed-point and primal-solution correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes both the surjective shadow map and every auxiliary fixed-point fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The first-resolvent shadow maps Douglas–Rachford fixed points onto primal solutions according to \[J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}})=\operatorname{zer}(A+B).\] More precisely, for each \(x\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\), the auxiliary fixed points whose first shadow equals \(x\) form the fiber \[\{z\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}:J_{\gamma A}z=x\}=x+\gamma(Ax\cap(-Bx)).\] Thus an auxiliary point has the form \(z=x+\gamma u\), where \(u\in Ax\) and \(-u\in Bx\); auxiliary fixed points need not themselves be primal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first resolvent maps Douglas–Rachford fixed points onto inclusion solutions; each solution’s auxiliary fiber is determined by its compatible opposing operator values.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-to-Primal Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the auxiliary-to-primal terminal and the fiber formula is coherent, but this nontrivial equality requires an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Projection-Based Feasibility Specializations
children.top_down_role: Normal-cone and projection specializations.

children.title: Feasibility-Problem Specializations
children.top_down_role: Douglas–Rachford formulations for intersections of constraint sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fixed point shadow \(P_Cz\) lies in \(C\cap D\), and the iteration uses only projections onto \(C\) and \(D\).

notation.meaning: Metric projection onto a closed convex set S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex-feasibility specialization of Douglas–Rachford splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-set closed convex feasibility with the \(C\)-projection taken first.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z_0\in H\), compute \(x_k=P_Cz_k\), \(y_k=P_D(2x_k-z_k)\), and \[z_{k+1}=z_k+y_k-x_k.\] The reported primal candidate is the shadow \(x_k\). If a stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\) is prescribed, one may stop when \(\lVert y_k-x_k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) and output \(x_k\). For an exact fixed point \(z\), the identity \(P_D(2P_Cz-z)=P_Cz\) implies \(P_Cz\in C\cap D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two closed convex sets, Douglas–Rachford alternates a projection, a reflected projection, and an auxiliary correction; fixed-point shadows solve the feasibility problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Problem Specializations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection algorithm fits the feasibility specialization, but no source supports either the specialization or the stated stopping rule and output convention.

children.title: Projection-Operator Specializations
children.top_down_role: Realizations in which resolvents reduce to projection operators.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma N_S}=P_S\) and \(R_{\gamma N_S}=2P_S-I\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resolvent of a convex normal cone equals the metric projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the normal-cone resolvent and reflection used in feasibility splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z\in H\), the projection condition \(z-P_Sz\in N_S(P_Sz)\) is equivalent to \(P_Sz=(I+\gamma N_S)^{-1}z\), because the normal cone is positively homogeneous in its values. Consequently, \[J_{\gamma N_S}=P_S\qquad\text{and}\qquad R_{\gamma N_S}=2J_{\gamma N_S}-I=2P_S-I=R_S.\] Hence Douglas–Rachford splitting for normal cones can be written entirely with metric projections and reflected projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a closed convex set’s normal cone is its metric projection, and its reflected resolvent is the ordinary reflected projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Operator Specializations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection and reflected-projection identities are correct in the stated convex setting and the representation kind fits, but the record includes derivational text and has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Normal-Cone Feasibility Representation
children.top_down_role: Operator representation linking set feasibility to normal-cone inclusions.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap D=\operatorname{zer}(N_C+N_D)\).

notation.meaning: Normal-cone operator of a closed convex set S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary normal-cone formulation of convex feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents two-set convex feasibility as a monotone inclusion without requiring a constraint qualification.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Using the convention \(N_S(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\notin S\), two-set convex feasibility has the exact normal-cone representation \[x\in C\cap D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in N_C(x)+N_D(x),\] and hence \[C\cap D=\operatorname{zer}(N_C+N_D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding a point in two closed convex sets is exactly the problem of finding a zero of the sum of their normal-cone operators.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Feasibility Representation

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Douglas-Rachford-ADMM Duality Interface
children.top_down_role: The dual interpretation delegated to the ADMM chapter.

children.title: ADMM Interface
children.top_down_role: Douglas–Rachford connections delegated to the ADMM treatment.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
\(K:X\to Z\) and \(L:Y\to Z\) are bounded linear maps, \(c\in Z\), and \(\rho>0\).
The constrained problem has a saddle point and both displayed subproblems attain minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed alternating minimizations and multiplier update define the ADMM interface for \(Kx+Ly=c\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard two-block unscaled ADMM iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unscaled two-block ADMM for a linearly constrained convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For initial \(y^0\in Y\) and \(\lambda^0\in Z\), compute \[x^{k+1}\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{f(x)+\langle\lambda^k,Kx+Ly^k-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Kx+Ly^k-c\rVert^2\right\},\] \[y^{k+1}\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_{y\in Y}\left\{g(y)+\langle\lambda^k,Kx^{k+1}+Ly-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Kx^{k+1}+Ly-c\rVert^2\right\},\] and \(\lambda^{k+1}=\lambda^k+\rho(Kx^{k+1}+Ly^{k+1}-c)\). Stop under a prescribed primal-dual residual test and output the latest primal pair and multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: ADMM alternately minimizes the augmented Lagrangian in each primal block and then updates the multiplier by the current feasibility residual.
knowledge_statements.title: ADMM Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed iteration is a coherent unscaled two-block ADMM algorithm and fits the interface container, but no source with a specific locator supports the formulation and its Hilbert-space assumptions.

children.title: Dual Proximal-Point Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Dual-space interpretation through proximal-point structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Douglas–Rachford iteration is a proximal-point iteration \(z_{k+1}=J_Mz_k\) for the maximal monotone operator \(M=T_{\mathrm{DR}}^{-1}-I\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: every full-domain firmly nonexpansive mapping is a maximal-monotone resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-point interpretation of the Douglas–Rachford auxiliary iteration, including dual instances underlying ADMM.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Douglas–Rachford mapping \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) is firmly nonexpansive and has full domain. Hence \(M=T_{\mathrm{DR}}^{-1}-I\) is maximally monotone and \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=J_M\). Therefore its auxiliary iteration can be written as \[z_{k+1}=J_Mz_k,\] which is the proximal-point method with unit proximal parameter applied to \(0\in Mz\). When \(A\) and \(B\) are the dual operators associated with a convex program, this gives the corresponding dual proximal-point interpretation of the Douglas–Rachford, and hence ADMM, auxiliary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The firmly nonexpansive Douglas–Rachford map is itself a maximal-monotone resolvent, so its auxiliary iteration is a proximal-point method, including on ADMM dual operators.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Proximal-Point Interpretation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic resolvent representation of the firmly nonexpansive Douglas–Rachford map is plausible, but the record does not define the dual operators needed by this terminal container and gives no source for the asserted ADMM dual interpretation.

children.title: Douglas–Rachford–ADMM Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between reflection splitting and dual decomposition.

assumptions_latex: The consensus problem \(\min\{f(x)+g(y):x-y=0\}\) has a saddle point.
The standard convex-duality and subdifferential chain rules hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: ADMM for the consensus formulation is Douglas–Rachford splitting on the dual inclusion \(0\in\partial(f^*\circ(-I))(u)+\partial g^*(u)\), up to the standard affine iterate identification.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of a convex function h
Dual variable for the constraint x-y=0

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical ADMM and Douglas–Rachford equivalence on the Fenchel dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus-form convex duality; signs depend on the chosen multiplier convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel dual of \(\min\{f(x)+g(y):x-y=0\}\) is \[\min_{u\in H}\ f^*(-u)+g^*(u),\] whose optimality inclusion is \[0\in\partial(f^*\circ(-I))(u)+\partial g^*(u).\] With reciprocal scaling between the ADMM penalty and the Douglas–Rachford resolvents, Douglas–Rachford splitting of these two dual subdifferentials generates, after the standard affine identification of the auxiliary and scaled-multiplier variables, exactly the ADMM primal proximal subproblems and multiplier update. Reversing the multiplier sign reverses the order of the dual factors but not the correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a consensus convex problem, ADMM is Douglas–Rachford splitting applied to the two subdifferentials in the Fenchel-dual optimality inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford–ADMM Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual inclusion is consistent with the stated sign convention, but the claimed exact ADMM correspondence depends on an omitted affine iterate identification and reciprocal scaling that require a precise authoritative source.

children.title: Peaceman–Rachford Splitting
children.top_down_role: Unaveraged reflection splitting and its restricted regimes.

children.title: Strong-Monotonicity Contractivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stable regimes for unaveraged reflections.

children.title: Contractive Reflection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Peaceman–Rachford settings where the reflection composition is contractive.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\gamma A}\) is Lipschitz with factor at most \(q=\sqrt{(1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2)/(1+2\gamma\mu)}<1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct strong-monotonicity and Lipschitz estimate for a reflected resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient contractive regime for a single-valued strongly monotone and Lipschitz operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(p,q\in H\), set \(x=J_{\gamma A}p\) and \(y=J_{\gamma A}q\). Strong monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity imply \[\lVert(x-y)-\gamma(Ax-Ay)\rVert^2\leq(1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2)\lVert x-y\rVert^2\] and \[\lVert(x-y)+\gamma(Ax-Ay)\rVert^2\geq(1+2\gamma\mu)\lVert x-y\rVert^2.\] Since these expressions equal the reflected-output and input differences, respectively, \(\lVert R_{\gamma A}p-R_{\gamma A}q\rVert\leq q\lVert p-q\rVert\), where \(q<1\) under the stated step-size restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly monotone, Lipschitz operator has a contractive reflected resolvent when the step size is below the stated sufficient threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Reflection Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the contractive-reflection terminal and the stated sufficient regime is internally coherent, but the exact factor and threshold lack an inspectable source and the statement contains derivational text.

children.title: Strong-Monotonicity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stable unaveraged-reflection settings supported by strong monotonicity.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}\) is \((1+\gamma\mu)^{-1}\)-Lipschitz, and \(\operatorname{zer}A\) contains at most one point.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard resolvent consequence of strong monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates consequences of strong monotonicity from reflection contractivity, which needs additional regularity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}A\), strong monotonicity means \[\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq\mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2.\] The resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}\) is everywhere defined and satisfies \[\lVert J_{\gamma A}p-J_{\gamma A}q\rVert\leq\frac{1}{1+\gamma\mu}\lVert p-q\rVert\qquad(p,q\in H).\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{zer}A\) contains at most one point. Strong monotonicity alone does not generally imply that \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-I\) is contractive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximally strongly monotone operator has an everywhere-defined, strictly contractive resolvent and at most one zero, while contractivity of its reflected resolvent requires additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

children.title: Contractivity from Strong Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Links between operator regularity and contraction of reflected resolvents.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\to H\) is single-valued, maximally monotone, \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, and \(L\)-Lipschitz, where \(0<\mu\le L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\gamma A}\) is a contraction with modulus at most \(q<1\).

notation.meaning: resolvent and reflected resolvent of the scaled operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient Lipschitz–strong-monotonicity regime; strong monotonicity alone need not give uniform reflected-resolvent contractivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x,y\in H\),
\[
\|R_{\gamma A}x-R_{\gamma A}y\|\le q\|x-y\|,
\qquad
q=\sqrt{\frac{1-2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2L^2}{1+2\gamma\mu+\gamma^2\mu^2}}<1.
\]
Thus compositions containing \(R_{\gamma A}\) and a nonexpansive reflected resolvent inherit a contraction modulus no larger than \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly monotone, Lipschitz operator has a contractive reflected resolvent for sufficiently small steps; composing it with another nonexpansive reflection remains contractive.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractivity from Strong Monotonicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem, hypotheses, contraction modulus, and content kind are mathematically consistent, but no inspectable source supports the nontrivial quantitative bound.

children.title: Relaxed Peaceman–Rachford Variants
children.top_down_role: Interpolations among reflection schemes.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update interpolates between Douglas–Rachford at \(\lambda_n=\tfrac12\) and Peaceman–Rachford at \(\lambda_n=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation is applied to the composition of the two reflected resolvents.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Generalized Splitting Methods p. 445
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(z_n\), compute
\[
x_n=J_{\gamma A}z_n,
\qquad
y_n=J_{\gamma B}(2x_n-z_n),
\qquad
z_{n+1}=z_n+2\lambda_n(y_n-x_n).
\]
Equivalently, \(z_{n+1}=T_{\lambda_n}z_n\). A stopping rule may use \(\|z_{n+1}-z_n\|\le\varepsilon\); the associated primal output is \(x_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing the composition of two resolvent reflections continuously connects Douglas–Rachford splitting with the unaveraged Peaceman–Rachford method.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Peaceman–Rachford Variants

source_witnesses.locator: 5.7 Generalized Splitting Methods p. 445
source_witnesses.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

children.title: Unaveraged-Reflection Divergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Divergence boundaries for general maximal monotone sums.

assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R^2\), and \(U,V\subset H\) are distinct lines through the origin meeting at an angle \(\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\).
\(A=N_U\), \(B=N_V\), and the unrelaxed iteration starts from \(z_0\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Peaceman–Rachford orbit generally fails to converge although \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: normal-cone operator of a closed convex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-subspace counterexample isolates the failure of an unaveraged reflection composition.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Generalized Splitting Methods p. 445
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(J_A=P_U\) and \(J_B=P_V\), the Peaceman–Rachford map is
\[
R_BR_A=(2P_V-I)(2P_U-I),
\]
which is a rotation through angle \(2\theta\). Hence \(z_n=(R_BR_A)^nz_0\) has constant nonzero norm and does not converge whenever the resulting rotation orbit is nonconstant. Nevertheless, \(U\cap V=\{0\}\), so the underlying inclusion has the unique solution \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For normal cones to two intersecting lines, Peaceman–Rachford becomes a nontrivial rotation, so its iterates need not converge despite a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Unaveraged-Reflection Divergence Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 5.7 Generalized Splitting Methods p. 445
source_witnesses.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

children.title: Multi-Operator Primal-Dual Splitting Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Operator-theoretic interfaces for methods developed more fully in algorithm chapters.

children.title: Spingarn Partial-Inverse Method
children.top_down_role: Partial-inverse decomposition for constrained inclusions.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(V\subset H\) is a closed vector subspace, and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proximal iteration on the partial inverse yields a decomposition method for \(0\in Ax+N_Vx\).

notation.meaning: orthogonal projectors onto the subspace and its orthogonal complement
Spingarn partial inverse of the operator with respect to the subspace

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical partial-inverse formulation for a maximally monotone inclusion constrained to a closed subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the partial inverse by
\[
y\in A_Vx
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}x\in A\bigl(P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}y\bigr).
\]
Starting from \(z_0\), perform
\[
z_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A_V}z_n.
\]
A zero \(z\) of \(A_V\) produces \(x=P_Vz\in V\) and \(u=P_{V^\perp}z\in V^\perp\) satisfying \(u\in Ax\), equivalently \(0\in Ax+N_Vx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spingarn replaces a subspace-constrained inclusion by a zero problem for the operator’s partial inverse, then applies proximal iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Spingarn Partial-Inverse Method

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partial-inverse definition and its relation to the constrained inclusion are consistent, but this nontrivial algorithmic representation has no cited source.

children.title: Multi-Component Splitting Families
children.top_down_role: Splittings for multiple separately accessible components.

children.title: Three-Operator Splitting Families
children.top_down_role: Splittings designed for three separately structured operator components.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone and \(C:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive on a real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fixed point produces a solution of \(0\in Ax+Bx+Cx\) through \(x=J_{\gamma B}z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Davis–Yin-type splitting with two backward steps and one explicit forward evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute
\[
x_n=J_{\gamma B}z_n,
\qquad
y_n=J_{\gamma A}(2x_n-z_n-\gamma Cx_n),
\qquad
z_{n+1}=z_n+\lambda_n(y_n-x_n).
\]
Stop when a prescribed fixed-point residual, such as \(\|y_n-x_n\|\), is at most \(\varepsilon\), and return \(x_n\). The iteration uses each of \(J_{\gamma A}\), \(J_{\gamma B}\), and \(C\) separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three-operator splitting solves a sum of two maximally monotone operators and one cocoercive operator using two resolvents and one forward evaluation.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Operator Splitting Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Davis–Yin-type update and fixed-point shadow relation are correctly stated and fit the algorithm container, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Generalized Forward–Backward Families
children.top_down_role: Forward–backward architectures extended to multiple accessible components.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Forward–Backward Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted product-space generalized forward–backward splitting for a finite monotone sum; only the fixed-point solution relation is asserted without additional convergence hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(z_{i,0}\in H\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). For each \(n\), set
\[
x_n=\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i z_{i,n},
\qquad
p_{i,n}=J_{(\gamma/\omega_i)A_i}(2x_n-z_{i,n}-\gamma Bx_n),
\]
and update in parallel by
\[
z_{i,n+1}=z_{i,n}+\lambda_n(p_{i,n}-x_n).
\]
A stopping rule may use \(\max_{1\le i\le m}\|p_{i,n}-x_n\|\le\varepsilon\). If a state is fixed, so that \(p_i=x=\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i z_i\) for every \(i\), then
\[
0\in Bx+\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x.
\]
Convergence of the iterates requires additional solution-existence and relaxation assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized forward–backward splitting applies the component resolvents in parallel and shares one explicit cocoercive evaluation. Every fixed state yields a solution of the finite-sum inclusion; convergence requires further assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(m\ge1\) is an integer, and \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(p_i=x=\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i z_i\) for every \(i\), then \(0\in Bx+\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x\).

children.title: Multi-Component Accessibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Method organization by resolvent, forward-evaluation, or block access.

assumptions_latex: The target inclusion is \(0\in Bx+\sum_{i=1}^m A_ix\), where every \(A_i\) is maximally monotone and \(B\) is single-valued.
An oracle call may evaluate \(Bx\), apply scalar-vector operations, or compute \(J_{\gamma_iA_i}z\) for a chosen \(\gamma_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusion is componentwise accessible precisely when a splitting iteration can be formed from these permitted calls without evaluating a coupled resolvent.

notation.meaning: allowed resolvent oracle for component i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An oracle-level condition distinguishing genuine component splitting from direct solution of the coupled sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Componentwise accessibility holds when, for every iteration index \(n\), all new variables are computable using finitely many evaluations of \(B\), individual resolvents \(J_{\gamma_iA_i}\), inner products, and affine combinations, while no call to \(J_{\gamma(\sum_iA_i+B)}\) or to any unresolved multi-component resolvent is required. Parallel accessibility additionally requires that the individual resolvent calls at a fixed iteration depend only on previously available shared data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-component problem is accessible when iterations require only individual component resolvents, forward evaluations, and elementary operations—not a resolvent of the coupled sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Component Accessibility Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the accessibility leaf, but its claimed characterization depends on a formal oracle model that is neither cited nor fully formalized by an external source.

children.title: Projective Splitting Family
children.top_down_role: Separator-based decomposition of multi-operator systems.

assumptions_latex: \(T_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) are monotone for \(1\le i\le m\).
Graph points satisfy \(y_i\in T_ix_i\), and dual variables satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^m w_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Kuhn–Tucker set lies in an explicitly computable affine halfspace and can be approached by relaxed projections.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separator certificate underlying projective splitting for a finite sum of monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \((z,w_1,\ldots,w_m)\in S\), monotonicity gives
\[
\phi(z,w)=\sum_{i=1}^m\langle z-x_i,y_i-w_i\rangle\le0.
\]
Hence the affine halfspace
\[
H_\phi=\{(z,w):\phi(z,w)\le0\}
\]
contains \(S\). If a current primal-dual point has \(\phi>0\), projecting it, possibly with relaxation, toward \(H_\phi\) yields a verifiable separator-based projective-splitting step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph points from individual operators generate an affine halfspace containing every primal-dual solution; projection toward that halfspace supplies the splitting step.
knowledge_statements.title: Projective Splitting Family

children.title: Product-Space Primal–Dual Splitting Interface
children.top_down_role: Lifted primal-dual inclusions and their separable resolvents.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(B:G\rightrightarrows G\) are maximally monotone on real Hilbert spaces.
\(L:H\to G\) is bounded linear, with adjoint \(L^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal inclusion is equivalent to a zero of a product-space sum with separable nonlinear resolvents and skew linear coupling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical product-space lift for one primal operator, one composite dual operator, and a linear coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The primal inclusion
\[
0\in Ax+L^*B(Lx)
\]
is equivalent to the existence of \(v\in G\) such that
\[
0\in Ax+L^*v,
\qquad
0\in B^{-1}v-Lx.
\]
Equivalently, \((x,v)\) is a zero of \(M+S\) on \(H\times G\). Moreover,
\[
J_{\gamma M}(x,v)=\bigl(J_{\gamma A}x,J_{\gamma B^{-1}}v\bigr),
\]
so the nonlinear resolvent evaluations remain block-separable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearly coupled primal inclusion lifts to a product-space primal-dual system whose nonlinear resolvent splits into independent primal and dual blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Primal–Dual Splitting Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal–dual product-space equivalence and block-separable resolvent are correct and appropriately classified as a representation, but no source is provided.

children.title: Anchor Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric roles of anchor placement relative to the fixed-point set.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), \(T:C\to C\), and \(u,x_n\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each new iterate lies on the anchor-to-image segment with explicitly controlled distances to both endpoints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary segment geometry of the classical Halpern update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(n\),
\[
x_{n+1}\in[u,Tx_n],
\qquad
x_{n+1}-u=(1-\alpha_n)(Tx_n-u),
\]
and
\[
x_{n+1}-Tx_n=\alpha_n(u-Tx_n).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\|x_{n+1}-u\|=(1-\alpha_n)\|Tx_n-u\|,
\qquad
\|x_{n+1}-Tx_n\|=\alpha_n\|u-Tx_n\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Halpern iterate lies on the segment joining the anchor to the current operator image, with distances determined exactly by the anchor weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Anchor Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The segment identities and distance formulas are correct and fit the anchor-geometry property container, but the record supplies no citation.

There exists a unique \(p\in F\) satisfying

\|u-p\|=\inf_{y\in F}\|u-y\|.

p=P_Fu

Thus the displacement \(u-p\) belongs to the normal cone \(N_F(p)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Halpern recursion \(x_{n+1}=\alpha_nu+(1-\alpha_n)Tx_n\), a classical anchor-control regime is
\[
\alpha_n\to0,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n=\infty,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n|<\infty.
\]
The first condition removes persistent anchor bias, the second prevents premature loss of the anchor, and the third controls oscillation of successive weights.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive with nonempty fixed-point set.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\to q\), where \(q\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) uniquely satisfies \(\langle q-f(q),y-q\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contraction-based viscosity selection in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in C\), compute
\[
x_{n+1}=\alpha_nf(x_n)+(1-\alpha_n)Tx_n.
\]
Stop when a prescribed residual or iterate-change tolerance is met; otherwise output the strong limit. Under the stated controls, \(x_n\to q\), where \(q\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) is the unique solution of
\[
\langle q-f(q),y-q\rangle\ge0\qquad(y\in\operatorname{Fix}T).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Viscosity iteration replaces the fixed anchor by a contraction and converges to the uniquely selected fixed point solving an associated variational inequality.

children.title: Tikhonov-Regularized Variants
children.top_down_role: Strong-convergence variants driven by vanishing Tikhonov regularization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_\varepsilon\to P_Su\) strongly as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: zero set of the monotone operator
metric projection onto the zero set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Tikhonov selection for maximal monotone zeros
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static Tikhonov path selecting the anchor-nearest zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the strongly monotone inclusion
\[
0\in Az_\varepsilon+\varepsilon(z_\varepsilon-u)
\]
has a unique solution \(z_\varepsilon\). As the regularization vanishes,
\[
z_\varepsilon\longrightarrow P_Su\qquad\text{strongly as }\varepsilon\downarrow0.
\]
Thus the Tikhonov term selects the zero of \(A\) nearest to the anchor \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a vanishing quadratic Tikhonov term produces unique regularized zeros that converge strongly to the zero nearest the anchor.
knowledge_statements.title: Tikhonov-Regularized Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem matches Tikhonov-regularized variants and is standard, but uniqueness, existence, and strong convergence of the regularization path are nontrivial claims without an inspectable citation.

children.title: Vanishing-Regularization Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Common selection effects across viscosity and Tikhonov mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_\alpha\to P_Fu\) strongly as \(\alpha\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: fixed point of the constant-anchor contraction

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic equivalence between implicit anchoring and Tikhonov regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit Halpern anchors as regularized zeros of the displacement operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unique solution of
\[
z_\alpha=\alpha u+(1-\alpha)Tz_\alpha
\]
is equivalently characterized by
\[
0=(I-T)z_\alpha+\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}(z_\alpha-u).
\]
Hence the implicit anchored fixed-point path is exactly the Tikhonov path for the displacement operator \(I-T\), with parameter \(\varepsilon_\alpha=\alpha/(1-\alpha)\). Moreover, \(z_\alpha\to P_Fu\) strongly as \(\alpha\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant implicit anchoring equals Tikhonov regularization of the displacement operator, and its vanishing-parameter path selects the nearest fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Regularization Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic correspondence is correct and fits the representation leaf, but the strong limit-selection assertion is nontrivial and has no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Strong-Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle errors asymptotically negligible relative to anchoring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\), let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and let \(u,x_0\in C\). Suppose the Halpern controls satisfy \(\alpha_n\in(0,1)\), \(\alpha_n\to0\), \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n=\infty\), and \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n|<\infty\). Given inexact evaluations \(y_n=Tx_n+d_n\in C\), define
\[
x_{n+1}=\alpha_nu+(1-\alpha_n)y_n.
\]
If \(\|d_n\|/\alpha_n\to0\), then
\[
x_n\longrightarrow P_Fu\qquad\text{strongly}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated Hilbert-space Halpern iteration, strong convergence to the fixed point nearest the anchor persists when each oracle error is negligible relative to the current anchor weight.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\).

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Accumulation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent errors of anchor-weight order can shift the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(T=I\), \(u=0\), \(x_0=0\), \(\alpha_n=1/(n+2)\), and \(e_n=c\alpha_n\) for a fixed \(c\neq0\). For the perturbed Halpern recursion
\[
x_{n+1}=(1-\alpha_n)x_n+e_n,
\]
one has
\[
x_n\longrightarrow c\neq0=P_{\operatorname{Fix}T}u.
\]
Thus errors with \(e_n/\alpha_n=c\neq0\) can change the selected limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the identity mapping on the real line, errors equal to a nonzero constant times the anchor weight shift the limit away from the anchor-nearest fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\to c\neq P_{\operatorname{Fix}T}u=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Anchor-Control Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite total anchor mass permits persistent oscillation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=C=\mathbb R\), \(T=-I\), \(u=0\), and \(x_0=1\). Choose \(\alpha_n\in(0,1)\) with \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n<\infty\), and define
\[
x_{n+1}=\alpha_nu+(1-\alpha_n)Tx_n.
\]
Then \((x_n)\) does not converge, although
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}.
\]
Thus finite total anchor mass does not ensure convergence of Halpern iteration.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a bounded closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, with diameter \(D<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a universal constant \(K>0\) such that \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|\le KD/(n+1)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: harmonic Halpern controls yield an order-one-over-n residual rate on bounded domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order residual rate for harmonic Halpern weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the harmonic-control Halpern iteration, the pointwise fixed-point residual satisfies
\[
\|x_n-Tx_n\|\le \frac{KD}{n+1}
\]
for a universal constant \(K>0\). Thus achieving \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|\le\varepsilon\) requires at most \(O(D/\varepsilon)\) evaluations of \(T\), counting one mapping evaluation per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Harmonic Halpern iteration has pointwise residual order one over the iteration count, giving order one over epsilon oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Halpern Residual Rate Families

children.title: Optimized Halpern Families
